WEB-118.rootCause: When a team stops using some external service, they often forget to also remove the DNS record that was pointing to it. That leftover, 'dangling' record stays live and exploitable the moment someone else is able to claim that exact resource name on the same provider.
WEB-118.impact: Exploiting a Subdomain Takeover grants the attacker complete, authoritative control over a subdomain belonging to the target organization (e.g., `support.target.com`). This enables highly effective, practically undetectable phishing campaigns, as the URL belongs to the legitimate domain. It allows attackers to execute critical Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) against the apex domain, bypass Content Security Policies (CSP) that whitelist subdomains, and intercept sensitive session cookies (if scoped to `*.target.com`).
stepsToIdentify: Utilize aggressive subdomain enumeration techniques (using tools like Sublist3r, Amass, or crt.sh) to identify all subdomains associated with the target organization.

Resolve the identified subdomains to retrieve their DNS records. Specifically identify any CNAME records pointing to external, third-party cloud services (e.g., `.s3.amazonaws.com`, `.github.io`, `.azurewebsites.net`).
Navigate to the resolved subdomains via a web browser or utilize an automated tool like `subjack` or `nuclei`. Observe the HTTP responses.

Look for specific, provider-defined error messages that explicitly indicate the endpoint is unclaimed (e.g., an AWS response stating 'NoSuchBucket', or a GitHub Pages response stating 'There isn't a GitHub Pages site here'). If these signatures are detected alongside an active CNAME, the subdomain is highly vulnerable.
exploitationSteps: Identify the specific cloud service provider associated with the dangling CNAME (e.g., Azure App Service).
Create an account with the identified provider.
Attempt to provision a new resource (e.g., a new web app) and explicitly claim the exact endpoint name identified in the CNAME record.

If the provider allows the registration (meaning the name was truly abandoned), deploy a benign HTML proof-of-concept page to the resource (e.g., displaying the assessor's handle or a safe reporting message).

Navigate to the victim's vulnerable subdomain (e.g., `dev.target.com`). If the browser successfully loads the assessor's PoC page, the takeover is confirmed, proving complete control over the subdomain's content.
Document the successful takeover and immediately relinquish control or lock the resource to prevent actual malicious actors from claiming it post-assessment.

examplePayloads.label: Automated scanning for Dangling DNS and Subdomain Takeovers using Subjack
Automated verification utilizing Nuclei templates
Manual verification of an AWS S3 bucket takeover signature via curl

variants: CNAME Takeover: The most common variant, where a CNAME record points to an unclaimed SaaS or PaaS endpoint.

NS Takeover: A more severe variant where a delegation (NS record) points to an abandoned DNS zone on a cloud provider (e.g., Route53), allowing the attacker to control entire swaths of the DNS hierarchy.

A/AAAA Record Takeover: An IP address points to an ephemeral cloud IP (like an AWS Elastic IP) that has been released by the victim and subsequently dynamically assigned to an attacker's EC2 instance.
mitigation: Implement rigorous, automated Infrastructure as Code (IaC) practices. Ensure that the lifecycle of DNS records is intrinsically tied to the lifecycle of the underlying cloud infrastructure, guaranteeing that when a resource is spun down, the corresponding CNAME record is automatically and instantaneously deleted.

Conduct continuous, proactive monitoring of the organization's DNS zones. Utilize automated scripts or commercial Attack Surface Management (ASM) platforms to actively scan for dangling records and 'NoSuchBucket' signatures on a daily basis.
When migrating or decommissioning services, explicitly mandate the deletion of DNS records *before* releasing the resource back to the cloud provider's public pool.

Where supported by the cloud provider, utilize custom domain verification TXT records to assert domain ownership, preventing arbitrary accounts from aggressively claiming endpoints associated with the organization's domain.

WEB-119.prerequisites: A web application endpoint vulnerable to Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) that attempts to mitigate the flaw by explicitly checking the resolved IP address against a blacklist (e.g., blocking `127.0.0.1` or `10.0.0.0/8`). The attacker requires control over an authoritative DNS server (or a specialized tool like `rbndr.us` or `singularity`) capable of returning dynamic, alternating A records with extremely low Time-to-Live (TTL) values.
WEB-119.whatItIs: This is a clever trick to defeat security checks meant to stop the app from reaching internal systems. An attacker's domain first answers with a safe, public address (passing the security check), then almost immediately switches its answer to point at a restricted internal address instead — timing it so the actual connection happens using the second, unsafe answer instead of the one that was checked.
WEB-119.rootCause: The app checks whether a web address is safe by looking it up once, but then the actual connection code looks the address up again, separately, right before connecting. If the attacker's domain gives a different answer on that second lookup (which they can control by setting it to expire almost instantly), the safety check and the actual connection end up using two completely different addresses.
WEB-119.impact: DNS Rebinding completely neutralizes standard SSRF mitigation strategies (like IP blacklisting), re-exposing the application to the full catastrophic impact of SSRF. It allows the attacker to reliably pivot through the web server to systematically scan the internal network, interact with sensitive, unauthenticated internal microservices, extract highly confidential cloud metadata credentials, and achieve Remote Code Execution via internal daemon exploitation.
stepsToIdentify: Identify an SSRF-susceptible endpoint (e.g., a webhook URL processor or image fetcher).

Provide a direct internal IP (e.g., `http://127.0.0.1`) and observe if the application blocks the request with a specific security error (e.g., 'Internal IP addresses are not permitted'), indicating a blacklist is in place.
Provide a safe public URL (e.g., `http://example.com`) to confirm the application successfully fetches external content.

Determine if the application's backend architecture is susceptible to TOCTOU flaws by evaluating if the validation logic is separated from the execution logic, which makes it a prime candidate for a rebinding attack.
exploitationSteps: Set up an authoritative DNS server (or utilize a public rebinding service like `rbndr.us`) configured to return two distinct IP addresses sequentially with a TTL of 0 seconds.

Configure the rebinding server so the FIRST resolution returns a benign public IP address (e.g., `8.8.8.8`), and the SECOND resolution returns the highly restricted internal target IP (e.g., `127.0.0.1` or `169.254.169.254`).
Generate the malicious rebinding hostname (e.g., `c0a80001.7f000001.rbndr.us`).
Submit the crafted hostname to the target application's SSRF endpoint.

The application's security filter resolves the hostname, receives the benign IP (`8.8.8.8`), and permits the request. Microseconds later, the HTTP client resolves the hostname again to initiate the connection, receives the restricted IP (`127.0.0.1`), and successfully fetches the internal resource.
Document the successful bypass and capture the extracted internal data as proof of concept.

examplePayloads.label: Generating a DNS Rebinding domain utilizing the rbndr.us public service
examplePayloads.command:
echo "Benign IP: 8.8.8.8 | Target IP: 127.0.0.1" 
# Target Domain: 08080808.7f000001.rbndr.us

examplePayloads.label: Exploiting the SSRF endpoint utilizing the rebinding domain
Automated comprehensive testing utilizing NCC Group's Singularity

variants: Server-Side Rebinding (SSRF Bypass): Exploiting TOCTOU race conditions in backend URL processing to pivot internally.

Client-Side Rebinding (Browser Exploitation): Running malicious JavaScript in a victim's browser that forces a DNS rebind, bypassing the Same-Origin Policy to allow external sites to query internal corporate intranets or local IoT devices.

Multi-A Record Rebinding: Supplying both a safe and an internal IP in a single DNS response and relying on the application's fallback logic to cycle to the internal IP if the safe IP connection intentionally times out.
mitigation: The only foolproof mitigation against DNS Rebinding is to architecturally eliminate the Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use (TOCTOU) race condition. The application MUST resolve the hostname to an IP address exactly once, perform the strict allowlist/denylist validation on that specific IP address, and then explicitly use that resolved, validated IP address (not the hostname) to initiate the HTTP connection.

If overriding the HTTP client's connection behavior is impossible, enforce network-level egress filtering. The application server must be strictly firewalled and categorically denied the ability to route traffic to internal subnets or cloud metadata endpoints at the OS network layer.

Configure the backend environment to forcibly ignore dangerously low DNS TTLs (pinning DNS caches for a minimum of 60 seconds), significantly increasing the difficulty of executing the rebinding race condition.

When evaluating the `Host` header of incoming requests to internal services, explicitly validate it against expected internal hostnames to prevent malicious requests dynamically routed via rebinding from succeeding.

WEB-120.prerequisites: Access to a web application protected by web server configuration files (like Apache `.htaccess`, IIS `web.config`, or Java EE `web.xml`) or application-layer routing that implements Role-Based Access Control (RBAC). An intercepting proxy like Burp Suite is required to arbitrarily modify HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, HEAD, etc.) on the fly.
WEB-120.whatItIs: A permission rule only protects specific request types — say, it blocks GET and POST requests to an admin page — but forgets to account for every other possible request type. An attacker can simply switch to an unprotected request type the rule never anticipated, and the request sails right past the check entirely, straight to the app behind it.
WEB-120.rootCause: Permission rules were written to explicitly list which request types they protect, rather than protecting the page itself no matter what type of request is used. Anything not on that explicit list is implicitly left completely unprotected — and the app behind it often processes the request anyway, regardless of what type it technically was.
WEB-120.impact: Exploiting Verb Tampering results in catastrophic Authentication and Authorization Bypass. An attacker can access highly restricted administrative dashboards, exfiltrate confidential data, or execute state-changing operations (like deleting accounts or altering system configurations) without supplying any valid credentials or possessing the requisite administrative roles.
stepsToIdentify: Identify an endpoint protected by an authentication or authorization barrier (e.g., a request to `/admin/dashboard` returning a `401 Unauthorized` or `403 Forbidden`).
Intercept the request using Burp Suite Repeater.
Systematically cycle through standard alternative HTTP methods. Change the original `GET` request to `POST`, `HEAD`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, `OPTIONS`, and `TRACE`.

Observe the HTTP response. If changing the method from `GET` to `HEAD` bypasses the `403` error and the server returns a `200 OK` (along with the response headers indicating success), the access control is improperly scoped.
Attempt to inject completely fabricated, arbitrary methods (e.g., `HACK /admin/dashboard HTTP/1.1`) to see if the web server relies on an explicit allowlist or a flawed denylist.
exploitationSteps: To exploit an Authentication Bypass via HEAD: If the application blocks `GET /api/v1/users/export` but permits `HEAD /api/v1/users/export`, use the `HEAD` method. While `HEAD` does not return a body, if the backend application executes the logic (e.g., generating the export file on the server) before realizing it shouldn't send the body, the logic is successfully manipulated.

To exploit Action Execution via Arbitrary Verbs: Intercept a state-changing request, such as `POST /admin/delete_user?id=10`. Change the method to an arbitrary string like `BYPASS /admin/delete_user?id=10`. If the web server filter only inspects `GET` and `POST`, it will ignore the request and pass it to the backend framework (like PHP or Node.js). If the backend framework routes requests based purely on the path and processes query parameters regardless of the method, the user will be deleted.
Document the specific bypassed method, the bypassed endpoint, and verify that the intended action was successfully executed on the backend.

Report the specific HTTP verb(s) that bypassed the intended access control, and recommend the application explicitly allowlist permitted methods per route rather than relying on a security layer that only inspects a subset of verbs.

examplePayloads.label: Identifying Verb Tampering by altering GET to HEAD to bypass ACLs
examplePayloads.command:
curl -I -X HEAD https://<target-url>/admin_portal
# Check if the response returns a 200 OK instead of the expected 401 Unauthorized.

examplePayloads.label: Exploiting insecure routing by injecting an arbitrary HTTP method
examplePayloads.command:
curl -X HACK_METHOD "https://<target-url>/api/delete_record?id=55"
# If the backend framework executes the deletion logic regardless of the method, bypass is confirmed.

variants: Filter Bypass via HEAD/OPTIONS: Utilizing valid but unexpected standard HTTP methods to circumvent narrowly scoped authorization rules.
Arbitrary Verb Injection: Submitting completely fabricated method strings (e.g., `TEST` or `G3T`) to bypass filters that rely on hardcoded method denylists.
Method Override Abuse: Manipulating custom HTTP headers designed to override methods (e.g., `X-HTTP-Method-Override: PUT`) to bypass front-end WAFs that only inspect the primary request line.
mitigation: Architecturally enforce a 'Default Deny' posture for all access control configurations. Authorization rules must be applied universally to the requested resource (the URL path), completely irrespective of the HTTP method utilized. Avoid using method-specific limiting directives (like `<Limit>` in Apache) unless absolutely necessary, and instead rely on `<LimitExcept>` to explicitly block everything not explicitly permitted.

Configure the web server or API Gateway to strictly reject any request utilizing an unrecognized, arbitrary, or unsupported HTTP method with a `405 Method Not Allowed` or `501 Not Implemented` status code before the request ever reaches the backend application logic.

Ensure backend web frameworks explicitly map routes to specific HTTP methods (e.g., explicitly defining `app.post('/delete')` rather than a generic `app.all('/delete')`) to ensure actions are only executed when the correct verb is utilized.

WEB-121.prerequisites: Access to a Python-based web application (utilizing frameworks like Flask, Django, or FastAPI) that natively ingests and processes serialized binary streams via Python's built-in `pickle` module (frequently transmitted via custom session cookies, authorization tokens, or internal RPC payloads). An intercepting proxy like Burp Suite Professional to capture and modify requests, alongside a controlled Python execution environment to generate and serialize malicious bytecode gadget payloads.
WEB-121.whatItIs: The app uses Python's pickle format to save and restore data, including data that might come from — or be tampered with by — a user. Unlike safer formats like JSON, pickle can be crafted to run a specific function the instant it's loaded back in — including one that runs operating-system commands — giving an attacker a direct way to execute their own code.
WEB-121.rootCause: Python's own documentation is explicit that pickle was never designed to be safe against untrusted data — loading a pickle file is allowed to run arbitrary code by design. Using it anyway to handle session data, cached results, or anything a client can influence, without adding a way to verify the data hasn't been tampered with, opens the door directly to this.
WEB-121.impact: Exploitation leads directly, reliably, and instantaneously to full Remote Code Execution (RCE) on the application server running with the privileges of the web process user (e.g., `www-data` or `uwsgi`). Because Python's execution model provides native access to powerful system libraries during the unpickling phase, an attacker can execute arbitrary operating system commands, establish persistent interactive reverse shells, exfiltrate internal configuration files, and completely compromise the underlying server infrastructure.
stepsToIdentify: Meticulously analyze all incoming HTTP requests and outgoing response headers for indicators of Python pickling, such as cookies, hidden parameters, or API bodies containing Base64-encoded strings that decode to binary headers beginning with known Python pickling opcodes (e.g., `\x80\x03`, `\x80\x04`, or `gASV`).

Attempt to subtly modify a byte or character within the serialized token and observe whether the backend application throws a verbose Python exception containing stack traces referencing `pickle.UnpicklingError`, `EOFError`, or `AttributeError`, definitively confirming backend processing of pickled data.

Test for remote code execution capability by constructing a benign, non-destructive pickle payload containing an Out-of-Band (OOB) DNS lookup or an HTTP interaction via `os.system('nslookup ...')` and submitting it through the identified vector.
Check for secondary serialization mechanisms like `cPickle` or `dill` which share identical architectural insecurities when processing untrusted byte streams.
Review application source code repositories (if accessible via static analysis) for explicit imports of `pickle`, `cPickle`, or `shelve` combined with unauthenticated input sinks.
exploitationSteps: Develop a custom, isolated Python script leveraging the native `pickle` library to construct a malicious object payload utilizing the `__reduce__` magic method.

Define a custom exploit class where the `__reduce__` method returns a callable execution target (e.g., `os.system`) alongside a tuple containing the exact shell command string to execute on the target server (e.g., `('id > /tmp/assessor_proof.txt',)`).
Serialize the exploit class instance into a binary byte stream using `pickle.dumps()` and encode the resulting binary data using standard Base64 encoding.
Inject the resulting Base64-encoded string into the vulnerable application vector (such as replacing the existing `session` cookie value).
Trigger the application to process and deserialize the modified payload by submitting an authenticated or state-dependent request.
Verify execution via observable application behavior, output file generation, or capturing the resulting interaction on your OOB listener.
Document the successful RCE capability and immediately cease execution to prevent infrastructure corruption.

examplePayloads.label: Python script generating a malicious Pickle RCE payload for Base64 cookie injection
Transmitting the generated malicious pickle payload via curl to a vulnerable cookie parameter
Python script generating a reverse shell pickle payload
Out-of-Band DNS Exfiltration pickle payload

variants: Cookie-Based Pickle Deserialization: Utilizing unencrypted pickled payloads stored within browser session cookies to achieve persistent RCE.
API-Based Pickle Deserialization: Ingesting pickled objects within custom REST API endpoints, WebSockets, or internal RPC microservice communication channels.
File-Upload Pickle Deserialization: Parsing uploaded state files, backup archives, or configuration caches that insecurely leverage the pickle format.
Celery/Redis Backend Deserialization: Exploiting task queues that utilize pickle serialization for message passing between workers.
mitigation: The primary, absolute mitigation is to never use the `pickle` module to parse or process untrusted data under any circumstances. Immediately refactor and migrate all data serialization workflows to safe, data-only serialization formats such as JSON, Protocol Buffers, or MessagePack.

If object serialization is an unavoidable architectural requirement, implement robust cryptographic message signatures (e.g., HMAC utilizing a cryptographically strong, securely stored secret key) to ensure the pickled data has not been tampered with or generated by an untrusted client *before* passing the stream to `pickle.loads()`.

Enforce strict least privilege on the web application service account at the operating system level, ensuring that even if RCE is achieved via deserialization, the attacker's ability to read system files or execute lateral movement is heavily restricted.

WEB-122.prerequisites: Access to a web application feature that generates downloadable PDF reports, invoices, user data exports, or certificates based on user-supplied content, HTML inputs, or dynamic URLs. An intercepting proxy like Burp Suite Professional and an Out-of-Band listener (such as Burp Collaborator or interactsh) are required.
WEB-122.whatItIs: The app converts HTML into PDF files using a tool that renders web pages behind the scenes — and that renderer will happily fetch any images, stylesheets, or scripts referenced in the HTML it's converting, just like a real browser would. If a user can influence the HTML being converted, they can point it at internal, normally unreachable systems, and get the server to fetch from them on the attacker's behalf.
WEB-122.rootCause: The PDF-rendering tool actively fetches external content referenced in whatever HTML it's given, by design — that's just how it renders pages accurately. If the app lets users supply raw HTML or custom links that get fed directly into that renderer with no restriction on where it's allowed to fetch from, the renderer treats the server's own internal network as fair game.
WEB-122.impact: Exploitation allows an attacker to bypass perimeter firewalls, scan internal network ports, access unauthenticated internal microservices, and retrieve sensitive cloud provider metadata (e.g., AWS IAM credentials via `169.254.169.254`). Furthermore, if the rendering engine executes embedded JavaScript (like Puppeteer), attackers can extract local files via `file://` URIs or perform advanced cross-site scripting attacks against the PDF parser.
stepsToIdentify: Inventory the application for any features that generate and export PDF documents (e.g., profile downloads, invoice generators, report exports).
Determine if the PDF generation feature accepts raw HTML input, rich-text fields, or user-supplied URLs.
Inject an HTML tag containing an external asset reference pointing to your controlled OOB listener, such as `` or a CSS import statement (``).

Trigger the PDF generation and download the resulting document. Simultaneously, monitor your OOB listener to confirm whether the backend rendering engine fetched the external resource, and analyze the incoming request headers for clues regarding the rendering engine's user-agent and internal IP address.
Test for local file inclusion by injecting `file:///etc/passwd` or `file:///C:/Windows/win.ini` into image sources or iframe paths.
exploitationSteps: To exploit for Internal Network Scanning: Craft an HTML payload containing multiple image tags or iframe elements pointing to standard internal ports (e.g., `` or internal service ports like Redis on 6379).
Generate the PDF and analyze the response. If the PDF successfully renders internal error pages, internal service banners, or captures time-delay variations, map the internal network topology.
To exploit for Cloud Metadata Extraction: Inject an iframe pointing to the AWS metadata endpoint (`<iframe src="http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/"></iframe>`).
Download the resulting PDF. If the metadata JSON is successfully rendered as text within the document pages, the sensitive credentials are fully compromised.
To exploit Local File Inclusion: Construct an HTML payload utilizing `file:///` URIs to read sensitive system files and render them directly into the output document.
Document the successful extraction and report the vulnerability without weaponizing the obtained metadata.

examplePayloads.label: Basic OOB SSRF payload via HTML image injection in a PDF export
Extracting AWS IAM credentials via an injected iframe in the PDF template
Local File Inclusion (LFI) via wkhtmltopdf file:// URI read
Internal port scanning payload via multiple img tags

variants: HTML-to-PDF Injection: Injecting malicious tags (``, `
URL-to-PDF SSRF: Supplying an arbitrary internal or external URL directly to a headless browser tool (like wkhtmltopdf) for conversion.
JavaScript Execution SSRF: Leveraging headless browsers (Puppeteer/Chromium) to execute advanced scripts that read local files or interact with internal APIs.
mitigation: Implement strict input sanitization on all user-supplied data destined for PDF templates. Strip out dangerous HTML tags (`<iframe>`, `<script>`, `<object>`, `<embed>`) and restrict image sources exclusively to trusted, local storage paths.

Configure headless rendering engines (e.g., Puppeteer, wkhtmltopdf) to operate with security flags enabled: explicitly disable local file access (e.g., disabling `file://` URI loading), disable JavaScript execution during rendering if dynamic scripts are unnecessary, and block remote resource loading where possible.

Enforce rigorous network-level egress filtering (Zero Trust) on the dedicated server nodes responsible for PDF generation. Firewalls must categorically block these nodes from initiating outbound connections to internal subnets, management interfaces, and cloud metadata endpoints.

WEB-123.prerequisites: Access to a web application utilizing JSON Web Tokens (JWT) for authentication, session management, or access control assertions. An intercepting proxy like Burp Suite Professional, the JWT Editor extension, or command-line utilities like `jwt_tool` to decode, modify, and re-encode token structures.
WEB-123.whatItIs: The server accepts a JWT login token that explicitly says 'no signature was used to verify this,' and goes along with it anyway. Since there's no real signature check happening at all in that case, an attacker can just edit the token's contents directly — like changing their account role to admin — with nothing stopping them.
WEB-123.rootCause: The verification code trusts what the token itself claims about how it should be checked, instead of insisting on one specific, hardcoded method regardless of what the token says. Older libraries or loose configurations sometimes still allow this 'no signature needed' option to be honored at all, which should never be accepted.
WEB-123.impact: Exploitation grants an attacker total authentication bypass and vertical privilege escalation. By simply changing the algorithm header to `none`, stripping the signature, and altering claims, an attacker can impersonate any user, including root administrators, and take over the application.
stepsToIdentify: Capture a valid JWT from an authenticated session.
Decode the header and payload segments to understand the structure.
Modify the header to explicitly declare the none algorithm: `{"alg":"none","typ":"JWT"}`.
Modify the payload claims (e.g., changing `"role":"user"` to `"role":"admin"`).
Strip the signature segment entirely, ensuring the token retains its trailing dot structure (e.g., `header.payload.`), and submit it to an authenticated endpoint.
Test case-insensitive variations like `None`, `NONE`, or `nOnE` to evaluate parser robustness.
exploitationSteps: Use `jwt_tool` or Burp Suite JWT Editor to quickly generate the modified `alg: none` token.
Inject the crafted token into the `Authorization: Bearer` header of a restricted request.
Observe the HTTP response; if the server responds with a `200 OK` and honors the elevated claims, the vulnerability is confirmed.
Test privilege escalation against admin-only API routes or user management endpoints.
Document the bypass technique and the vulnerable library version.

examplePayloads.label: Manually constructed JWT with alg=none and elevated claims
Automated jwt_tool exploitation command for alg=none
Testing case-insensitive variations (alg=None)

variants: Case-Insensitive Bypass: Exploiting weak parsers by supplying variations like `None`, `NONE`, or `nOnE` to evade primitive blocklists.
Signature Stripping: Omitting the signature block while retaining the delimiter dots.
mitigation: Hardcode the expected cryptographic algorithm on the server side (e.g., strictly enforce `RS256` or `HS256`) and explicitly reject any token specifying `none` or missing a signature.
Update all authentication libraries to modern versions that reject unencrypted tokens by default.
Additionally validate the JWT header's `alg` field against an explicit allow-list before invoking any cryptographic verification, rejecting the token outright on mismatch.

WEB-124.prerequisites: Network access to the target web server and a standard web browser or command-line tool like `curl` to inspect directory paths.
WEB-124.whatItIs: When you visit a folder on the site that doesn't have a default page in it, the server shows a plain list of every file in that folder instead of a blank page or an error.
WEB-124.rootCause: The web server's setting that auto-generates this kind of folder listing is turned on — either for specific folders or across the whole site — instead of being switched off.
WEB-124.impact: While classified as a low-severity information disclosure finding, directory listing reveals the internal structural layout of the application, source code backups (`.bak`, `.zip`), configuration files, and hidden administrative scripts that can be leveraged to discover compounding vulnerabilities.
stepsToIdentify: Navigate to common predictable directories or asset folders (e.g., `/images/`, `/uploads/`, `/backup/`, `/js/`) that lack an index page.
Observe if the server responds with a structured directory tree listing filenames, sizes, and modification dates.
Utilize automated content discovery tools (like gobuster or dirb) with wordlists targeting backup directories and asset folders.
exploitationSteps: Browse the directory index to identify sensitive artifacts, old documentation, or source code files.
Download discovered files using `wget` or `curl` for offline code review.
Identify hidden backup archives or configuration files exposed via the index.
Document the exposed directories as an information disclosure finding.

examplePayloads.label: Checking for directory indexing via curl
Automated discovery of indexable directories using gobuster
Recursing into exposed backup directories with wget

variants: Global Indexing: Enabled across the entire server root.
Localized Indexing: Enabled only on specific storage directories like uploads or asset folders.
mitigation: Disable auto-indexing globally and locally within the web server configuration (e.g., set `Options -Indexes` in Apache or `autoindex off;` in Nginx).
Ensure every directory contains a default index file if direct browsing is not required.
Deploy automated configuration-drift scanning in CI/CD to catch any web server or infrastructure-as-code change that re-enables directory indexing.

WEB-125.prerequisites: Access to a web application password reset workflow. Burp Suite Professional to capture request parameters and analyze token entropy.
WEB-125.whatItIs: The password-reset process uses a reset code that's guessable — maybe it's a sequential number, based on the current time, or drawn from a weak set of possibilities — or fails to properly tie that code to the specific account it's meant for. That lets an attacker systematically reset other people's passwords.
WEB-125.rootCause: The reset code isn't generated using a genuinely unpredictable method — it's built using something predictable like a counter or timestamp instead of a proper cryptographically secure random generator. On top of that, there's often no limit on how many times a code can be tried, and no expiration forcing it to become useless after one use.
WEB-125.impact: Exploitation results in full Account Takeover. An attacker can request a password reset for any registered user, predict or brute-force the generated token, and reset the password to gain permanent unauthorized access.
stepsToIdentify: Initiate a password reset for a test account and capture the generated reset link.
Generate multiple reset tokens sequentially and analyze their entropy, length, and generation patterns.
Check if the token expires rapidly after a single use or persists indefinitely.
Test if the token can be guessed or brute-forced without hitting account lockouts.
Check if reset tokens leak via the `Referer` header to third-party analytics.
exploitationSteps: Trigger a password reset for the victim account.
Utilize Burp Intruder or a custom script to test token predictability or brute-force the recovery token if entropy is low.
Submit the validated token along with a new password to seize control of the account.
Document the lack of cryptographic entropy or expiration controls.

examplePayloads.label: Analyzing sequential password reset tokens in Burp Sequencer
examplePayloads.command: # Capture 100 reset links and evaluate token randomness using Burp Sequencer.

examplePayloads.label: Brute-forcing weak numeric reset tokens using ffuf
Testing token persistence by replaying a used token

variants: Predictable Tokens: Tokens generated via timestamps or weak PRNGs.
Token Leakage via Referer: Reset tokens passed via URL query parameters that leak to third-party analytics via the `Referer` header.
mitigation: Generate password reset tokens using cryptographically secure PRNGs with high entropy (minimum 128 bits of randomness).
Enforce strict token expiration (e.g., valid for a maximum of 15 minutes) and ensure tokens are permanently invalidated upon single use or after a password change.
Transmit tokens exclusively via POST request bodies or securely scoped headers to prevent leakage via the `Referer` header.

WEB-126.prerequisites: Access to a web application session authentication workflow. Browser Developer Tools (Application/Storage tab) or Burp Suite Professional to intercept responses and inspect `Set-Cookie` response headers.
WEB-126.whatItIs: Session cookies get issued without important protective settings — flags that would stop them from being read by JavaScript, stop them from being sent over an unencrypted connection, or stop them from being sent along with requests from other websites. Missing any of these makes the cookie easier to steal or misuse.
WEB-126.rootCause: These protective flags have to be explicitly set when the cookie is created — they're not automatically added. Developers often just rely on whatever the framework does by default, which isn't always secure out of the box.
WEB-126.impact: Missing `HttpOnly` allows malicious JavaScript executed via XSS to read `document.cookie` and exfiltrate session identifiers. Missing `Secure` allows cookies to be intercepted over plaintext HTTP connections. Missing `SameSite` exposes the application to Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) by permitting cookies to be sent across cross-origin requests.
stepsToIdentify: Authenticate to the web application and capture the initial response setting the session cookie.
Inspect the `Set-Cookie` header for the presence and configuration of `Secure`, `HttpOnly`, and `SameSite` attributes.
Verify if the cookie can be accessed via client-side JavaScript by executing `console.log(document.cookie)` in the browser developer console.
Check whether the application permits fallback over unencrypted HTTP connections where session cookies might be leaked.
Evaluate cross-origin request handling to see if missing `SameSite` attributes permit cross-site context inclusion.
exploitationSteps: Demonstrate impact by running a basic XSS script in the browser console to access the session cookie if `HttpOnly` is missing.
Simulate cookie interception over an unencrypted channel if the `Secure` flag is omitted.
Construct a cross-origin proof-of-concept form to show that cookies are attached to third-party requests if `SameSite` is absent.
Document each missing attribute and its corresponding risk vector in the security assessment report.

examplePayloads.label: Inspect Set-Cookie headers using curl
Checking cookie accessibility via browser console XSS simulation

variants: Missing HttpOnly: Allows cookie access via client-side scripts.
Missing Secure: Allows cookie transmission over plaintext HTTP.
Missing SameSite: Leaves session vulnerable to cross-site requests.
mitigation: Explicitly configure all session and sensitive cookies with `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, and `SameSite=Strict` or `SameSite=Lax` attributes within the application's session management configuration.

Adopt the `__Host-` cookie name prefix for session cookies where possible — browsers refuse to accept a `__Host-` cookie unless it also carries `Secure`, has no `Domain` attribute, and uses `Path=/`, which makes misconfiguration browser-enforced rather than reliant on developer discipline.

Enforce the cookie attributes at the reverse proxy / CDN layer as well as in application code, so a future framework upgrade or new endpoint can't silently ship a cookie missing the required flags; add an automated header-assertion check to the CI pipeline.

WEB-127.prerequisites: Access to web application endpoints containing state-changing operations. Burp Suite Professional or browser DevTools to inspect security headers.
WEB-127.whatItIs: The app never tells the browser whether it's okay to be embedded inside another website's page. Without that setting, any website can load this app inside a frame and trick users into clicking something they didn't mean to (see Clickjacking).
WEB-127.rootCause: The specific header that controls whether a page can be framed by another site was never added, so the browser falls back to its default, permissive behavior — allowing any site to embed it.
WEB-127.impact: Attackers can construct transparent overlays on external sites to force authenticated users into clicking hidden buttons, resulting in unauthorized actions or state changes. Combined with a real-world target's UI (e.g., a bank's 'disable 2FA' or 'transfer funds' button hidden under the overlay), a single click can produce an irreversible financial or security-relevant action the user never consciously took.
stepsToIdentify: Inspect response headers for `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors` and `X-Frame-Options`.
Test framing viability by embedding the application inside a local HTML `<iframe>` file.
Verify browser console logs for frame blocking notifications.
Assess whether subdomains or proxy layers strip out framing protections.
exploitationSteps: Create an HTML PoC file embedding the target URL in an invisible iframe over a decoy button.
Test user interaction flow locally to verify click redirection.
Document the missing headers and provide proof-of-concept overlay code.
Report the specific pages missing frame-protection headers and recommend a Content-Security-Policy frame-ancestors directive as the modern, more flexible replacement for X-Frame-Options alone.

examplePayloads.label: Basic framing test HTML snippet
Working invisible-overlay PoC (opacity trick over a real button)

variants: Missing X-Frame-Options
Missing CSP frame-ancestors directive
mitigation: Deploy `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self';` alongside `X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN` across all web responses.
Add clickjacking protection to the WAF/CDN layer as a second control, not just the application's own headers, so a misconfigured or bypassed origin server is still covered.
Include a `frame-ancestors` regression test in CI/CD so a future refactor that drops the header is caught before release rather than discovered in production.

WEB-128.prerequisites: Access to an application download feature that references files via predictable identifiers (e.g., `file_id=105` or `path=invoices/inv_998.pdf`). Burp Suite Professional to capture requests and iterate parameters.
WEB-128.whatItIs: A file-download feature fetches whatever file matches the ID given in the request, without checking whether the person asking actually owns that file. Swap in a different ID, and you can download someone else's confidential file.
WEB-128.rootCause: The code fetching the file relies entirely on the ID supplied in the request, with no matching check confirming the logged-in user is actually allowed to access that specific file.
WEB-128.impact: An attacker can horizontally escalate privileges to harvest sensitive documents, PII, financial statements, or legal contracts belonging to other users simply by iterating through sequential file identifiers.
stepsToIdentify: Initiate a legitimate file download and capture the request in Burp Suite.
Modify the file identifier or filename parameter to point to a file belonging to another user.
Observe if the server returns the unauthorized file content with a `200 OK` status.
Test for parameter pollution and alternate encoding mechanisms.
Check if unauthenticated sessions can invoke the download function directly.
exploitationSteps: Automate the parameter iteration using Burp Intruder or a script to harvest multiple files.
Verify file contents to ensure cross-account data isolation is broken.
Document the successful extraction of unauthorized files.

Report the specific parameter/pattern used to enumerate files (sequential ID, predictable filename, UUID guessed via a separate leak) and recommend an ownership check enforced server-side on every download request, not just at initial listing.

examplePayloads.label: Modifying file ID parameter to download unauthorized document
Automated sequential-ID sweep with ffuf

variants: Sequential IDOR on file records
Predictable filename enumeration
mitigation: Implement centralized authorization checks verifying file ownership before serving downloads, and utilize unguessable UUIDs instead of sequential IDs.

Rate-limit and alert on abnormal sequential-access patterns against download endpoints (e.g., the same session requesting many different `file_id` values in a short window), since this is a strong IDOR-sweep signature even before any single request looks malicious.
Log every file access with the requesting user and the file's actual owner, so a retrospective audit can identify how many other records were harvested if the flaw was already exploited.

WEB-129.prerequisites: Access to an administrative logging or analytics dashboard that displays raw HTTP request headers (such as the `User-Agent` string) submitted by visitors. Burp Suite Professional to inject malicious payloads into HTTP headers.
WEB-129.whatItIs: The app logs details from incoming requests — like the browser's self-reported identity string — and later displays those logs in an admin panel, without cleaning them up first. Since that string is fully controlled by whoever's sending the request, an attacker can put malicious script code inside it, and it runs the moment an admin views the logs.
WEB-129.rootCause: Developers assume this kind of request detail, since it comes from the browser itself, is automatically safe and not something a user could manipulate — but it's just as attacker-controlled as any other input. The app doesn't clean it up before displaying it in an admin view.
WEB-129.impact: Allows attackers to target administrators viewing application logs, leading to session hijacking, administrative account takeover, and full system compromise. Because the payload persists in log storage, it can also fire against any other internal tool that renders the same log data — SIEM dashboards, ticketing integrations, or a support engineer's browser — turning one injection point into a foothold across multiple internal systems.
stepsToIdentify: Intercept a normal HTTP request and modify the `User-Agent` header to include an XSS payload.
Log into the administrative dashboard where visitor logs are displayed and observe if the payload executes.
Test other non-standard request headers like `Referer` or custom tracking headers for similar reflection.
exploitationSteps: Craft a targeted XSS payload within the User-Agent header.
Trigger the request against a public endpoint logged by the backend.
Confirm execution when an administrator reviews the activity log.
Document the vulnerable log-viewing endpoint.

examplePayloads.label: Injecting XSS payload via User-Agent header
Blind stored XSS via X-Forwarded-For with an out-of-band callback

variants: Stored XSS via Referer header
Stored XSS via X-Forwarded-For header
mitigation: Apply strict context-aware output encoding to all request headers when rendering them in administrative interfaces or logs.
Sanitize or encode header values at ingestion time (when they're first written to logs/storage), not only at render time, so any other tool that later reads the raw log data is protected too.
Restrict who can view raw request logs in the administrative interface to the smallest practical group, since this class of stored XSS specifically targets that audience.

WEB-130.prerequisites: Access to a password reset workflow where user identifiers or email addresses are passed as modifiable parameters during the token generation or submission phase. Burp Suite Professional.
WEB-130.whatItIs: The password-reset process includes an account identifier in the request, but doesn't check whether the person making the request actually has any connection to that account. An attacker can trigger — or even complete — a password reset for someone else's account just by supplying their identifier.
WEB-130.rootCause: The reset process trusts whatever account identifier is supplied in the request, without requiring the person to already be logged in as that account, or otherwise proving they actually own it.
WEB-130.impact: An attacker can systematically initiate and complete password resets for any registered user on the platform, leading to widespread account takeovers. Because the flaw requires nothing more than a valid username, it is straightforward to automate at scale — an attacker with a breached username list (from an unrelated leak) can attempt mass account takeover across the entire user base in a single scripted run.
stepsToIdentify: Initiate a password reset for your own account and intercept the request in Burp Suite.
Modify the target user identifier (e.g., changing `user_id=101` to `user_id=102`) while keeping your own reset token or email confirmation destination.
Observe if the reset token is successfully issued for the victim account.
Check if the token submission step allows overriding the target user context.
exploitationSteps: Inject the victim's account identifier into the password reset request.
Capture the generated reset link or token.
Complete the reset process to seize control of the victim's account.
Document the lack of binding between the token generator and the account ID.

examplePayloads.label: Modifying username parameter in password reset request
Sweep the reset endpoint across a username list

variants: IDOR during reset token generation
IDOR during final password update submission
mitigation: Implement rigorous server-side authorization checks ensuring the reset workflow strictly targets the verified owner of the account.
Rate-limit password-reset requests per account and per source IP to slow down username-sweeping attacks against the endpoint.
Require a second verification factor beyond the username alone before completing a reset — e.g., a link sent to the verified email/phone on file rather than accepting a submitted identifier directly.

WEB-131.prerequisites: Access to an e-commerce platform or shopping cart checkout workflow where item quantities can be modified dynamically via numerical inputs. An intercepting proxy like Burp Suite Professional to capture and alter numeric parameters before backend processing.
WEB-131.whatItIs: The shopping cart calculates the total cost using a number type that can only hold values up to a certain size. If someone enters an enormous quantity — bigger than that number type can actually hold — the value 'wraps around' to something tiny, zero, or even negative, letting them check out with a massively discounted or completely free order.
WEB-131.rootCause: There's no upper limit enforced on how many of an item someone can add to their cart, and the calculation uses a number type with a fixed maximum size instead of properly validating the input first. When that maximum gets exceeded, the math just breaks in an exploitable way.
WEB-131.impact: Exploitation leads directly to severe financial fraud and inventory abuse. An attacker can purchase massive quantities of high-value goods for minimal cost, bypass payment gateways entirely, or generate negative invoice totals that result in processing errors or unintended refunds.
stepsToIdentify: Add an item to the shopping cart and navigate to the quantity update interface.
Capture the update request in Burp Suite and modify the quantity parameter to a value near the boundary limits of a 32-bit signed integer (e.g., `2147483647` or `2147483648`).

Observe the calculated total cost in the application's response. If the total cost wraps around into a negative value, drops to zero, or becomes inexplicably small, an integer overflow condition is confirmed.
Test if the application allows submission of the order under the anomalous financial calculation.
exploitationSteps: Inject the overflowing quantity value into the cart update payload.
Proceed through the checkout workflow up to the final payment confirmation screen while monitoring the displayed order total.
Verify if the backend payment gateway evaluates and accepts the wrapped negative or zero total.
Document the exact parameter manipulated, the data type limits of the backend framework, and the resulting financial calculation anomaly.

examplePayloads.label: Injecting an overflowing integer value into cart item quantity
Testing boundary limits via form-data manipulation

variants: Integer Underflow: Supplying values below the minimum allowable boundary of a signed integer type.
Floating-Point Arithmetic Errors: Manipulating currency values to exploit precision rounding errors during multi-item tax calculations.
mitigation: Implement strict server-side bounds validation on all numerical inputs, explicitly establishing maximum and minimum allowable limits for item quantities (e.g., restricting quantities between 1 and 99).

Utilize arbitrary-precision arithmetic libraries or large integer data types (such as 64-bit integers or native currency decimal types) for all financial calculations to completely eliminate integer overflow risks.
Ensure the backend calculation logic explicitly validates that final order totals, item subtaxes, and unit prices remain non-negative prior to authorizing any payment workflow.

WEB-132.prerequisites: Access to a file upload feature that reflects the uploaded filename back to the user within the web application's user interface (e.g., profile document lists, attachment viewers, or gallery management screens). An intercepting proxy like Burp Suite Professional to manipulate multipart form data headers.
WEB-132.whatItIs: The app checks the actual content of uploaded files carefully to block dangerous uploads — but doesn't clean up the file's name the same way. If someone names their file something like a chunk of malicious script code, that name gets displayed as-is in a file list or admin panel, running the script the moment someone views it.
WEB-132.rootCause: Developers focus their validation on the file's actual content and extension, since that's the more obvious risk, but completely overlook that the filename itself — which the uploader also fully controls — gets displayed elsewhere without being cleaned up first.
WEB-132.impact: Exploitation allows an attacker to achieve Stored XSS via an indirect vector. When an administrator reviews uploaded user documents or logs into a management portal, the malicious filename executes in their browser context, leading to session hijacking, administrative account takeover, and full application compromise.
stepsToIdentify: Locate a file upload mechanism and prepare a harmless file (e.g., a blank text file or small image).
Rename the file to include an HTML/JavaScript payload in place of the filename (e.g., `"/><script>alert(document.domain)</script>.png`).
Upload the file and navigate to the application page or user profile where uploaded files are listed or managed.
Observe if the filename is rendered raw as executable HTML/JavaScript, triggering the alert or executing console logic.
exploitationSteps: Craft an advanced payload within the filename designed to extract session cookies or execute DOM manipulation.
Upload the file while intercepting and modifying the `filename` parameter within the multipart `Content-Disposition` header in Burp Suite.
Lure an administrator to view the uploads management dashboard, or wait for automated review workflows to process the list.
Confirm payload execution and document the lack of output sanitization on file metadata.

examplePayloads.label: Multipart form upload modifying filename parameter for XSS injection
examplePayloads.command:
POST /upload HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundary

------WebKitFormBoundary
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="file"; filename="<script>alert(1)</script>.png"
Content-Type: image/png

[binary data]
------WebKitFormBoundary--

examplePayloads.label: Attribute breakout payload within filename

variants: Stored XSS via File Metadata (EXIF data): Injecting XSS payloads into image EXIF metadata fields that are extracted and displayed by the application.
Stored XSS via Document Title / PDF Metadata: Injecting scripts into PDF internal document properties that render in web-based PDF viewers.
mitigation: Apply strict context-aware output encoding to all user-supplied metadata—including filenames, file sizes, and descriptions—prior to rendering them in the web application's DOM.

Implement aggressive sanitization or normalization on filenames upon upload: strip out all special characters, spaces, and HTML tags, or automatically overwrite uploaded filenames with randomized UUID strings combined with safe extensions.
Validate uploaded filenames server-side against a strict allow-list of characters and enforce a maximum length before persisting or displaying them anywhere in the UI.

WEB-133.prerequisites: Access to a GraphQL API endpoint supporting state-changing mutations (e.g., `updateUser`, `deletePost`, `changePassword`). Two distinct user accounts at the same privilege level. Burp Suite Professional to inspect and modify GraphQL query and mutation payloads.
WEB-133.whatItIs: In a GraphQL app, an action that changes data (like updating a document) takes an object's ID as part of the request, but doesn't check whether the person making the request actually owns or has permission to modify that specific object.
WEB-133.rootCause: This is the same broken-ownership problem that shows up in regular APIs, but it's especially easy to miss in GraphQL — teams often focus their security review on traditional endpoints and wrongly assume that just needing to know the right ID is protection enough on its own.
WEB-133.impact: An attacker can horizontally escalate privileges to modify, overwrite, or delete data belonging to other users across the entire platform. In mutations handling sensitive account properties, this leads directly to unauthorized account takeovers or data destruction.
stepsToIdentify: Map the GraphQL schema via Introspection or traffic analysis to identify sensitive state-changing mutations accepting object IDs.
Establish two distinct user sessions (User A and User B).
While authenticated as User A, capture a mutation request intended to modify User A's data (e.g., `mutation { updateUser(id: "USER_A_ID", email: "new@email.com") { success } }`).
Modify the `id` argument in the mutation payload to point to User B's identifier (`USER_B_ID`).
Execute the request and check if the server returns a successful execution status, indicating User B's record was modified by User A.
exploitationSteps: Craft a malicious GraphQL mutation targeting User B's object ID.
Execute the mutation utilizing User A's session token.
Verify via User B's session that the targeted record was successfully altered.
Document the lack of resolver-level authorization checks and list the affected mutation fields.

examplePayloads.label: GraphQL mutation exploiting BOLA to update another user's email
examplePayloads.command: curl -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "Authorization: Bearer USER_A_TOKEN" -d '{"query": "mutation { updateProfile(input: {id: "USER_B_ID", email: "attacker@evil.com"}) { user { id email } } }"}' https://<target-url>/graphql

examplePayloads.label: GraphQL mutation deleting another user's post
examplePayloads.command: curl -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "Authorization: Bearer USER_A_TOKEN" -d '{"query": "mutation { deletePost(postId: \"VICTIM_POST_ID\") { status } }"}' https://<target-url>/graphql

variants: Horizontal BOLA: Modifying objects belonging to peers at the same privilege level.
Vertical BOLA: Invoking administrative mutations (e.g., `promoteToAdmin`) as a standard user.
mitigation: Implement centralized authorization logic within every GraphQL resolver function, explicitly verifying that the authenticated session possesses permissions to access or mutate the requested object ID.
Derive user context implicitly from the secure session token within the resolver rather than blindly trusting client-supplied ID arguments for mutation targets.
Apply the same object-level authorization checks consistently across all GraphQL operation types (queries, mutations, and subscriptions) rather than only the most commonly tested mutations.

WEB-134.prerequisites: Access to a Python web application utilizing the Tornado web framework's native templating engine where user input is unsafely interpolated into rendered templates. Burp Suite Professional or `curl` for payload delivery.
WEB-134.whatItIs: A Python web framework called Tornado lets template files run Python code written inside double curly braces. If user input gets mixed directly into the template text itself instead of being passed in as a separate, safe value, an attacker can inject their own code inside those braces and have it run on the server.
WEB-134.rootCause: User input gets pasted directly into the template's text before it's compiled and run, instead of being passed in safely as a separate variable to fill into a fixed, pre-written template.
WEB-134.impact: Exploitation yields immediate Remote Code Execution (RCE) on the server, allowing attackers to execute operating system commands, read sensitive files, and achieve total system compromise.
stepsToIdentify: Fuzz input parameters with basic mathematical evaluation payloads compatible with Tornado, such as `{{7*7}}` or `{{2+2}}`.
Observe the HTTP response; if the server evaluates and reflects '49' or '4', template injection is confirmed.
Test for access to Python built-ins or execution modules through Tornado's expression syntax.
exploitationSteps: Construct a Tornado-specific RCE payload leveraging Python's `os` or `subprocess` module via expression evaluation.
Submit the payload through the vulnerable input vector.
Verify command execution via reflected output or OOB interaction.
Document the vulnerability and provide the verified proof-of-concept payload.

examplePayloads.label: Tornado SSTI math evaluation test
Tornado SSTI Remote Code Execution payload

variants: Reflected Tornado SSTI
Sandboxed Tornado Template Escape
mitigation: Never concatenate user input directly into Tornado template strings; always pass parameters securely via context dictionaries.
Migrate to logic-less rendering frameworks or strictly sandbox template execution environments.
Apply automatic sandboxing/allow-listing of template functions and disable access to Python builtins and OS-level modules within the Tornado template execution context.

WEB-135.prerequisites: A web application deployed behind a caching proxy that processes and reflects cookie values into responses without including those cookies in the cache key definition. Burp Suite Professional with the Param Miner extension.
WEB-135.whatItIs: A caching system is set up to ignore certain cookies when deciding what to cache — but the app itself still reads those same cookies and displays their contents back on the page. An attacker can set a cookie containing malicious script code, get that poisoned page cached (since the cache doesn't realize the cookie mattered), and have it served to every other visitor.
WEB-135.rootCause: There's a mismatch: the caching system was configured to ignore specific cookies for efficiency, while the app behind it is still using those same cookies to build the actual page content — so the cache has no idea the response actually varies based on something it's not accounting for.
WEB-135.impact: Attackers can poison the cache to persistently execute Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) against any user who visits the affected page, leading to widespread session hijacking and credential theft.
stepsToIdentify: Use Burp Param Miner to test common unkeyed headers and cookies against cached endpoints.
Inject a unique canary string into a test cookie and check if it appears reflected in the response body.
Verify that the caching layer returns `X-Cache: HIT` on subsequent requests while retaining the reflected canary string.
exploitationSteps: Craft an XSS payload encapsulated within an unkeyed cookie value.
Issue requests with a cache-buster parameter until the cache stores the poisoned response.
Remove the cache-buster and confirm the cache serves the XSS payload to unauthenticated visitors.
Document the unkeyed cookie vector and caching behavior.

examplePayloads.label: Injecting XSS payload via unkeyed cookie header
Two-step proof: poison once, confirm a clean second request is served the poisoned response

variants: Cache Poisoning via unkeyed language cookies
Cache Poisoning via unkeyed tracking cookies
mitigation: Include all request headers and cookies that influence response content within the cache key definition at the proxy/CDN layer.
Never reflect cookie values directly into the HTML response body without rigorous context-aware output encoding.
Deploy cache-poisoning detection tooling (e.g. periodic differential probing) against the CDN/proxy layer to catch regressions where a new header or cookie becomes unkeyed.

WEB-136.prerequisites: Access to an e-commerce web application featuring a promotional discount system where single-use or limited-use coupon codes can be applied during checkout. Burp Suite Professional equipped with Turbo Intruder to execute synchronized multi-threaded request bursts.
WEB-136.whatItIs: If someone submits the exact same one-time discount code multiple times at almost the same instant, the server can check whether it's still valid for each request in parallel, before any of them has actually marked it as used — letting the same single-use code get applied more than once.
WEB-136.rootCause: The check ('is this code still valid?') and the action ('mark it as used') happen as two separate database steps instead of one combined, protected operation. That gap gives simultaneous requests a window where they all see the code as still valid.
WEB-136.impact: Exploitation leads directly to financial loss and promotional abuse. An attacker can apply a single-use coupon multiple times within a single order, or reuse a limited-use promotional code hundreds of times concurrently, acquiring expensive goods for free or deep discounts.
stepsToIdentify: Add an item to the shopping cart and navigate to the checkout discount input field.
Apply a valid single-use or limited-use promotional coupon code normally and capture the submission request in Burp Suite.
Transfer the request to Turbo Intruder and configure a Python script to send a synchronized burst of 20 to 50 identical requests concurrently.
Analyze the resulting responses and the final order total. If multiple concurrent requests successfully apply the discount, the application's coupon validation logic contains a race condition.
exploitationSteps: Capture the valid discount code application HTTP request.
Construct a Turbo Intruder concurrency script utilizing HTTP/2 single-packet attack techniques to minimize network jitter.
Execute the script to release 30 parallel requests simultaneously targeting the checkout discount endpoint.
Inspect the order summary to verify if the discount was multiplied or applied repetitively.
Document the exact concurrency timing, the absence of database locking, and the financial impact.

examplePayloads.label: Turbo Intruder python script for concurrent coupon code application
examplePayloads.command:
def queueRequests(target, wordlists):
    engine = RequestEngine(endpoint=target.endpoint,
                           concurrentConnections=30,
                           engine=Engine.BURP2)
    for i in range(30):
        engine.queue(target.req, to_string=True)
    engine.start(timeout=5)

examplePayloads.label: Concurrent curl bash loop for basic race condition testing
examplePayloads.command: seq 1 20 | xargs -n1 -P20 -I{} curl -s -X POST -H "Cookie: session=USER" -d "code=WELCOME50" https://<target-url>/apply_discount

variants: Single-Use Coupon Duplication: Reusing a one-time code multiple times across concurrent threads.
Loyalty Point Double-Spending: Redeeming loyalty points concurrently across multiple checkouts to spend the same balance multiple times.
mitigation: Implement pessimistic locking (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`) at the database layer when querying and updating coupon status, ensuring concurrent threads queue up and evaluate the code sequentially.

Enforce unique constraints and atomic database updates (e.g., `UPDATE coupons SET status = 'used' WHERE code = 'X' AND status = 'active'`) so that only a single thread can successfully modify the record.
Utilize distributed caching locks (such as Redis RedisLock) at the application layer to serialize checkout operations per user or per coupon entity.

WEB-137.prerequisites: Access to a web application API that processes user input and returns verbose error messages with `Content-Type: application/json` or text-based MIME types when invalid input is submitted. Burp Suite Professional for payload injection.
WEB-137.whatItIs: An API sends back an error message that includes unfiltered user input, formatted as JSON. If the browser or the app's own front-end code ends up treating that response as HTML instead of plain data, whatever malicious script was in the input runs.
WEB-137.rootCause: The error message isn't cleaned up before including user input in it, and either the response isn't correctly labeled as JSON, or the front-end code that displays API errors inserts the raw text directly into the page instead of treating it as plain, harmless text.
WEB-137.impact: Exploitation allows attackers to achieve Reflected XSS through API error channels, leading to session hijacking or credential harvesting when users or administrators interact with the vulnerable application interface.
stepsToIdentify: Identify API parameters that trigger error messages upon receiving invalid input (e.g., malformed JSON, invalid characters, or out-of-range integers).
Inject an XSS payload into the parameter (e.g., `?search=<script>alert(1)</script>`).

Inspect the response headers and body. Determine if the payload is reflected verbatim in the error message and check if the frontend application renders this error message into the DOM using unsafe sinks.
exploitationSteps: Craft a targeted XSS payload designed to break out of JSON string contexts or target frontend error-handling sinks.
Trigger the API error response containing the reflected payload.
Deliver the request via a crafted link or review the frontend rendering behavior.
Confirm payload execution in the browser context.

examplePayloads.label: Injecting XSS payload into an API search endpoint error message
JSON string breakout payload

variants: API Error Reflection XSS: Direct reflection in JSON error fields rendered unsafely by frontend clients.
MIME-Confusion XSS: Forcing the browser to interpret JSON error payloads as HTML documents.
mitigation: Ensure all API error responses strictly declare `Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8` and enforce the `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` header to prevent MIME-type sniffing.
Implement robust context-aware output encoding on all error messages, and ensure frontend applications utilize safe DOM methods (like `textContent`) when displaying error text to users.
Apply a strict Content-Security-Policy without `unsafe-inline` so that even if an encoding gap slips through, injected script content cannot execute.

WEB-138.prerequisites: Access to a web application featuring administrative panels, restricted buttons, or management features that are hidden via client-side CSS (`display: none`) or conditional rendering based on user roles. Burp Suite Professional or browser Developer Tools.
WEB-138.whatItIs: Admin-only buttons and menu items are simply hidden from regular users on screen — but the actual backend functions behind them have no matching permission check, so anyone who knows (or guesses) the right request can trigger them directly, without ever seeing the button.
WEB-138.rootCause: This mixes up 'the user can't see it' with 'the user can't do it.' Hiding something in the interface does nothing to stop someone from calling the underlying request directly — that only works if the backend itself checks permissions every time, which it doesn't here.
WEB-138.impact: Standard users or unauthenticated attackers can easily inspect client-side source code, uncover hidden administrative URL paths or API endpoints, and invoke them directly, achieving total vertical privilege escalation and unauthorized administrative access.
stepsToIdentify: Log into the application as a standard, low-privileged user account.
Inspect the client-side HTML source code, bundled JavaScript files, or frontend routing maps (e.g., React/Vue router files) to discover hidden admin paths or commented-out navigation links.
Attempt to navigate directly to the discovered administrative URLs (e.g., `/admin/users` or `/api/admin/delete`) via the browser or Burp Suite.
Observe if the backend server successfully returns the administrative interface or data without enforcing role validation.
exploitationSteps: Extract hidden administrative endpoints from client-side JavaScript bundles using automated tools like `LinkFinder` or manual source review.
Issue direct HTTP requests to these endpoints using low-privileged session credentials.
Verify if administrative actions (such as promoting users or exporting databases) can be successfully executed.
Document the exposed backend endpoints and the lack of server-side access controls.

examplePayloads.label: Directly accessing a hidden administrative API endpoint via curl
Extracting frontend routes via LinkFinder

variants: Hidden DOM Element Access: Invoking functions tied to buttons hidden via CSS.
Exposed Admin Routes: Navigating to client-side routing paths (`/admin`) stripped from standard user navigation menus.
mitigation: Implement rigorous, centralized server-side Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) on every backend endpoint and API route, completely independent of frontend UI rendering logic.
Ensure sensitive administrative components, code, and routes are never bundled into client-facing JavaScript packages delivered to low-privileged users.

Treat any client-side role/permission flag purely as a UI convenience and never as an authorization decision; log and alert on backend requests for admin-only functionality made by non-admin sessions.

WEB-139.prerequisites: Access to a Java-based web application (frequently utilizing Spring Boot) that incorporates the Pebble templating engine and unsafely concatenates user input directly into rendered templates. Burp Suite Professional or `curl`.
WEB-139.whatItIs: Pebble, a Java templating tool, lets templates run real logic. If user input gets mixed directly into the template's own text instead of being passed in as a safe, separate value, an attacker can inject template syntax that reaches into Java itself — potentially running their own code on the server.
WEB-139.rootCause: User input gets pasted directly into the raw template text before it's processed, instead of being passed in safely as a separate value meant to fill into a fixed, pre-written template.
WEB-139.impact: Exploitation yields immediate Remote Code Execution (RCE) on the Java application server, granting the attacker full control over the underlying operating system and internal application state.
stepsToIdentify: Fuzz application inputs with basic mathematical expressions compatible with Pebble, such as `{{7*7}}` or `{{2+2}}`.
Observe the HTTP response; if the server evaluates and reflects the mathematical result, SSTI is confirmed.
Test for access to Java runtime objects and reflection methods via Pebble syntax.
exploitationSteps: Construct a Pebble-specific RCE payload leveraging Java reflection or built-in extension functions to invoke `java.lang.ProcessBuilder` or `Runtime.getRuntime().exec()`.
Submit the payload through the vulnerable input vector.
Verify command execution via reflected output or OOB interaction.
Document the vulnerability and provide the verified proof-of-concept payload.

examplePayloads.label: Pebble SSTI math evaluation test
Pebble SSTI Remote Code Execution via ProcessBuilder

variants: Reflected Pebble SSTI
Sandboxed Pebble Template Escape
mitigation: Never concatenate user input directly into Pebble template strings; always pass parameters securely via context maps.
Enable Pebble's strict sandbox mode if user-defined templates must be supported, restricting access to dangerous Java classes and methods.
Keep the Pebble templating library patched to the latest version and monitor for CVE advisories affecting its sandbox implementation.

WEB-140.prerequisites: Access to a legacy ASP.NET web application utilizing `LosFormatter`, `ObjectStateFormatter`, or `NetDataContractSerializer` to process serialized state tokens (such as hidden `__VIEWSTATE` parameters). Burp Suite Professional and `ysoserial.net`.
WEB-140.whatItIs: Older .NET apps sometimes save a chunk of page state (called ViewState) into data sent to the browser and back, using a format that can reconstruct complex objects when loaded. If that data isn't protected with a proper integrity check, an attacker can craft a malicious version — using widely available tools built exactly for this — that runs their own code the moment the server loads it back.
WEB-140.rootCause: The integrity-check feature that's supposed to detect tampering with this data is either turned off, or uses a weak, predictable key — meaning the server has no reliable way to tell whether that data has been modified before trusting and reconstructing it.
WEB-140.impact: Exploitation results in immediate Remote Code Execution (RCE) on the IIS web server running with application pool privileges, leading to total server compromise. Because the payload rides inside a field (`__VIEWSTATE`) that looks like routine framework noise, the request rarely stands out in access logs, and the resulting shell is instantiated with the application pool's own privileges — often enough to pivot directly into the rest of the internal network from the compromised host.
stepsToIdentify: Inspect HTTP requests for ASP.NET state parameters such as `__VIEWSTATE`, `__EVENTVALIDATION`, or custom serialized tokens.
Check configuration files (`web.config`) for missing MAC validation or disabled viewstate security (`enableViewStateMac="false"`).
Test for gadget chain execution using non-destructive OOB payloads generated via `ysoserial.net`.
exploitationSteps: Identify available .NET libraries and framework versions to select a valid gadget chain (e.g., ActivitySurrogateSelector or TypeConfuseDelegate).
Generate a malicious serialized payload utilizing `ysoserial.net` designed to execute a benign command or OOB callback.
Inject the payload into the `__VIEWSTATE` parameter.
Trigger the application to deserialize the payload and verify execution.
Document the RCE capability and vulnerable configuration settings.

examplePayloads.label: Generating a .NET deserialization payload via ysoserial.net
Transmitting serialized payload via curl

variants: ViewState Deserialization Abuse via weak MachineKey
NetDataContractSerializer RCE in WCF endpoints
mitigation: Ensure `enableViewStateMac="true"` is explicitly enforced and configure strong, cryptographically secure, randomly generated `machineKey` values in `web.config`.
Migrate away from legacy formatters (`LosFormatter`, `BinaryFormatter`) toward safe data serialization formats like JSON.
Apply the latest .NET Framework security patches addressing ViewState deserialization vulnerabilities and audit all pages for legacy formatter usage during code review.

WEB-141.prerequisites: A web browser and an intercepting proxy (Burp Suite Community Edition or OWASP ZAP), a target application login or password reset URL, and a comprehensive username list for testing.
WEB-141.whatItIs: Login, sign-up, and password-reset pages take a measurably different amount of time to respond depending on whether the username or account being checked is real — letting an attacker figure out which accounts exist just by carefully timing responses.
WEB-141.rootCause: The backend does more work — like checking a password hash — only when it finds a real, matching account, and does much less work when it doesn't. That difference in workload creates a small but measurable, exploitable timing gap.
WEB-141.impact: Enables attackers to curate a precise list of valid accounts within the target organization, facilitating targeted credential stuffing, high-impact phishing, or aggressive password spraying campaigns.
stepsToIdentify: Capture a baseline login request using an intercepting proxy and send it to the Intruder tool for automated timing analysis.
Populate the username payload slot with a mix of known-valid internal accounts and definitely-invalid generated strings.
Configure Burp Intruder to record the 'Response received' timestamp and sort requests by execution duration to identify anomalies.
Perform manual verification using cURL with multiple iterations to eliminate network jitter and confirm consistent timing deltas.
Analyze server-side application logic paths, error handling routines, and database query structures during code review or black-box testing.
Document all endpoints that exhibit statistically significant time variances between valid and invalid user submissions.
exploitationSteps: Automate the submission of a large username wordlist against the vulnerable authentication or password-recovery endpoint.
