Filter and sort responses based on precise millisecond response times or subtle HTTP header variations.
Isolate records that consistently trigger the longer execution path to build a verified list of active user accounts.
Confirm scope explicitly authorizes account enumeration activities against the target environment.
Execute the validation checks using low-concurrency threads to avoid triggering rate limiters or crashing application pools.
Export the confirmed list of valid usernames to serve as input for subsequent authorized testing phases.

examplePayloads.label: Automated timing differential check using Burp Intruder cluster bomb
Manual cURL request measuring precise response time for a valid user
Manual cURL request measuring precise response time for an invalid user
Python script snippet for asynchronous timing analysis
Network latency capture via tcpdump for backend query correlation
examplePayloads.command: tcpdump -i eth0 'tcp port 443 and host target.com' -w timing_analysis.pcap

variants: Timing-based account enumeration where the HTTP status code and message text are completely identical, but the database execution time differs due to dummy password-hashing routines.

Enumeration via the password-reset flow itself: even when the login endpoint gives a uniform response, the 'forgot password' endpoint often replies faster for non-existent accounts (short-circuiting before any email-send logic) than for real accounts, leaking the same account-validity signal through a different code path.
mitigation: Implement artificial constant-time processing or dummy cryptographic hashing (e.g., password_verify) for invalid usernames to normalize execution duration.
Return an identical generic response (message, status code, and comparable timing) regardless of whether the account exists.
Apply rate limiting and CAPTCHA challenges globally across all authentication and password recovery entry points.
Enable audit logging and monitor for unusual request frequencies targeting authentication flows.
Conduct regular security testing and vulnerability scanning to detect regression issues.

WEB-146.prerequisites: A web browser, an intercepting proxy (Burp Suite or OWASP ZAP), an authenticated low-privilege user session, and a target API endpoint supporting Cross-Origin Resource Sharing.
WEB-146.whatItIs: The app automatically trusts whatever website claims to be making a cross-origin request and reflects that trust back — while also allowing that request to include the user's login credentials. Combined, this completely defeats the browser's normal protection and lets any malicious website read a logged-in user's private data.
WEB-146.rootCause: Instead of maintaining a fixed, specific list of trusted websites, the server-side code just echoes back whatever site is asking, with no real check — and credentials are still allowed through on top of that.
WEB-146.impact: An attacker-controlled malicious website can silently issue credentialed API requests on behalf of an authenticated victim, directly reading sensitive JSON responses, personal data, or session tokens via JavaScript.
stepsToIdentify: Capture an authenticated API request in an intercepting proxy.
Inject an arbitrary, external domain into the 'Origin' header (e.g., 'https://attacker.com').
Inspect the server response to verify if 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' reflects the injected domain back to the client.
Check whether the response header 'Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true' is present alongside the reflected origin.
Test edge cases such as null origins, prefix matching, or suffix regex flaws in the origin validation logic.
Document all vulnerable endpoints that permit credentialed cross-origin data access.
exploitationSteps: Host a proof-of-concept HTML page on an external attacker-controlled domain.
Write JavaScript code using the Fetch API with 'credentials: include' to query the vulnerable target API endpoint.
Confirm that the browser receives and parses the sensitive JSON response returned by the target server.
Exfiltrate the harvested data back to an attacker-controlled listener.
Verify that engagement scope explicitly authorizes cross-origin exploitation testing.
Record the extracted sample data structure as definitive proof-of-concept evidence.

examplePayloads.label: cURL test for CORS origin reflection and credential allowance
JavaScript Proof-of-Concept snippet for credentialed fetch exfiltration
cURL test for null origin reflection vulnerability
Python script snippet to test multiple candidate origin strings
Network traffic recording via tcpdump during CORS probe

variants: CORS misconfiguration utilizing a permissive regular expression (e.g., allowing any domain ending with the company's public suffix) rather than a literal wildcard or exact match.

Null-origin bypass: a request originating from a sandboxed iframe (`<iframe sandbox>`) or a redirect chain through a `data:`/`file:` context sends `Origin: null`; if the server's allow-list explicitly (and mistakenly) trusts the literal string `null` as a valid origin, any attacker page can trigger this path with credentials included.
mitigation: Maintain a strict, explicit whitelist of trusted partner origins server-side rather than dynamically reflecting the incoming Origin header.
Never combine wildcard or reflected origin values with 'Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true'.
Avoid supporting the 'null' origin in production environments.
Enable audit logging to monitor unusual cross-origin access requests.
Conduct regular security reviews of API gateway and server CORS configurations.

WEB-147.prerequisites: Access to an endpoint that consumes signed XML (SAML assertions, WS-Security SOAP messages, or signed XML API payloads), a valid previously-issued signed XML document to use as a template, an intercepting proxy (Burp Suite), and the SAML Raider or WS-Attacker extension for automated wrapping payload generation.
WEB-147.whatItIs: This attacks how a signed XML document (like a login assertion from a single sign-on system) gets checked. The part of the app that verifies the digital signature looks at one specific piece of the document, while the part that actually processes the data looks somewhere slightly different. An attacker can restructure the document so the signature check passes on the real, untouched piece, while the app actually acts on a different, tampered piece they've smuggled in.
WEB-147.rootCause: The code checking the signature finds the signed content one way, while the code actually using that content later finds it a different way — so an attacker can insert a fake, unsigned copy of the data positioned exactly where the second piece of code will pick it up instead of the genuinely signed original.
WEB-147.impact: Allows complete authentication and authorization bypass in federated single sign-on systems: an attacker can forge a SAML assertion claiming to be any user (including administrators) while keeping a validly signed but unrelated assertion attached, resulting in full account takeover across every service provider trusting that identity provider.
stepsToIdentify: Capture a legitimate signed SAML response or WS-Security SOAP message via an intercepting proxy during a normal login flow.
Decode the base64 SAMLResponse and inspect the <ds:Signature> block to identify the Reference URI and the ID attribute it points to.

Load the captured assertion into SAML Raider and generate the standard XSW payload variants (XSW1 through XSW8), which relocate or clone the Assertion element while preserving the original signed copy elsewhere in the document.

Replay each generated variant to the assertion consumer service endpoint and observe whether the service accepts the forged, unsigned copy's claims (e.g. a different NameID or elevated Role attribute) while still passing signature validation.
Repeat the process against any WS-Security SOAP endpoints using WS-Attacker's XSW plugin, testing wrapping in the SOAP Header/Body relationship.
Confirm impact by modifying the wrapped assertion's NameID/username to a privileged account and checking if the service grants a session under that identity.
exploitationSteps: Use SAML Raider's XSW tab to select the target service provider's endpoint and load the intercepted, validly signed assertion.
Modify the cloned (unsigned) assertion copy's NameID/Subject to a target victim or admin identity while leaving the original signed assertion structurally present but logically orphaned.
Re-encode the tampered XML to base64 and URL-encode it into the SAMLResponse POST parameter.
Submit the forged SAMLResponse to the Assertion Consumer Service URL and capture the resulting authenticated session, confirming the identity now reflects the injected NameID.

examplePayloads.label: XSW1-style wrapped assertion structure (conceptual)
examplePayloads.command:
<samlp:Response>
  <saml:Assertion ID="evil"><saml:Subject><saml:NameID>admin@example.com</saml:NameID></saml:Subject></saml:Assertion>
  <ds:Signature><ds:Reference URI="#original-signed-id">...</ds:Reference></ds:Signature>
  <saml:Assertion ID="original-signed-id">... original signed content moved here as sibling ...</saml:Assertion>
</samlp:Response>

examplePayloads.label: Replaying a forged SAMLResponse via curl
SAML Raider CLI-equivalent Burp extension workflow note
examplePayloads.command: Burp Suite -> SAML Raider tab -> 'Send Message to SAML Raider Certificates' -> 'XSW' sub-tab -> select XSW1..XSW8 -> Save & Forward

variants: WS-Security SOAP wrapping where a signed SOAP Body is moved into a wsse:Security header while an attacker-controlled Body sibling is processed by the service.
Key confusion variant combined with XSW, where the attacker also swaps the signing certificate referenced in KeyInfo to a self-controlled key not properly checked against a trust anchor.
Comment-based wrapping where the original signed NameID is preserved but the actual parsed value is manipulated via an interspersed XML comment that some XML parsers ignore inconsistently.
mitigation: Bind signature validation and business-logic parsing to the exact same DOM node object (not a re-queried element) so the validated element is guaranteed to be the one consumed.
Use canonical, schema-validated XML parsers configured to reject documents containing duplicate IDs or unexpected sibling Assertion/Body elements.
Adopt libraries with built-in XSW protections (e.g. up-to-date OpenSAML, Shibboleth) rather than custom XML-DSig validation logic, and keep them patched.
Enforce strict single-assertion-per-response policies and reject any SAML response containing more than one Assertion element unless explicitly required.

WEB-148.prerequisites: A web browser or intercepting proxy, access to normal application workflows (login, password reset, payment, file access), and access to standard server/proxy access logs or browser history if available for impact verification.
WEB-148.whatItIs: Sensitive values — session tokens, API keys, passwords, personal data, password-reset codes — get put directly into the web address itself, instead of somewhere more private. Since URLs get saved in browser history, written into server logs, and automatically shared with other websites when clicking a link from that page, this ends up leaking sensitive data to places it should never have gone.
WEB-148.rootCause: Sensitive values get passed through the URL because it's simpler — for shareable links, bookmarks, or older integrations — without considering that URLs get logged, cached, and forwarded by all sorts of systems that were never meant to see confidential information.
WEB-148.impact: Exposes credentials and tokens to anyone with access to browser history, shared/public computers, corporate proxy logs, CDN/WAF logs, or third-party sites that receive the Referer header, enabling session hijacking, account takeover, and unauthorized data access without the attacker needing to compromise the application directly.
stepsToIdentify: Crawl the application and log every full URL requested during authentication, password reset, payment, and file-download workflows.
Inspect each captured URL's query string for patterns resembling tokens, session identifiers, JWTs, API keys, or PII (email addresses, card fragments).
Check whether pages that load third-party resources (analytics, ads, fonts, widgets) do so on a page whose own URL contains a sensitive parameter, since the Referer header would leak it.
Review server, load balancer, and CDN access log samples (if available) to confirm sensitive query strings are being persisted in cleartext logs.
Check browser history/autocomplete behavior by revisiting the address bar to confirm the sensitive URL is retained and suggested.
exploitationSteps: Trigger a password-reset or magic-link flow and capture the token delivered via GET request in the confirmation email or SMS link.

Demonstrate Referer leakage by loading a page containing a sensitive query parameter that also embeds a third-party script, then confirm via that third party's request logs (or a Burp Collaborator substitute) that the full URL was forwarded.
Show that the token remains valid and reusable after being retrieved from shared browser history or a corporate proxy log export, completing an account-takeover proof of concept.

Report each specific channel through which the sensitive URL was exposed (browser history, referer leakage, proxy/CDN logs) since remediation differs — moving tokens to the request body or a header, and setting Referrer-Policy: no-referrer for pages carrying sensitive query parameters.

examplePayloads.label: Example vulnerable password-reset link
Checking Referer leakage with curl against a controlled listener
Grepping server logs for leaked tokens (authorized log review)

variants: OAuth access tokens returned in a redirect_uri fragment or query string instead of via POST back-channel exchange.
Payment or PII data (card last-4, order details) embedded in confirmation page URLs indexed by search engines due to missing noindex directives.
File-download endpoints authorizing access purely via a token embedded in the URL query string with no additional binding to session or IP.
mitigation: Transmit all sensitive tokens and identifiers via POST body, HTTP headers (Authorization), or secure cookies instead of URL query parameters.
For necessary one-time links (password reset, email verification), enforce single-use, short-lived tokens and invalidate them immediately after first use.
Set `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` or `strict-origin-when-cross-origin` on pages that must temporarily carry sensitive data in the URL to prevent leakage to third parties.
Configure servers, proxies, and CDNs to redact or avoid logging full query strings for endpoints known to carry sensitive parameters.

WEB-149.prerequisites: Ability to query public DNS records for the target's mail-sending domain (dig/nslookup), an SMTP client or scripting capability able to send raw email (swaks, Python smtplib), and access to a mailbox to receive test messages and inspect authentication headers.
WEB-149.whatItIs: The company's domain is missing (or has misconfigured) the DNS records that prove an email genuinely came from them. Without those records, an attacker can send an email that looks like it's from someone at the real company — like the CEO — with nothing cryptographically proving it's fake, and the recipient's mail server has no instruction telling it to be suspicious.
WEB-149.rootCause: The DNS records that authorize legitimate mail servers to send on the domain's behalf are missing, too permissive, or not actually enforced — and there's no policy telling other mail servers what to do with email that fails those checks, so unauthorized senders just get delivered like normal.
WEB-149.impact: Enables highly convincing business email compromise (BEC), spear-phishing, and invoice-fraud campaigns impersonating the organization's own executives or domain, damaging brand trust, facilitating credential theft against employees/customers, and potentially resulting in fraudulent wire transfers.
stepsToIdentify: Query the target domain's SPF record and check whether it exists and what qualifier terminates it: `dig TXT example.com +short` looking for a `v=spf1 ... -all` (hard fail) versus `~all` (soft fail) or missing entirely.
Query DKIM selectors (common selectors: default, google, selector1, selector2, k1) to confirm public keys are published: `dig TXT default._domainkey.example.com +short`.
Query the DMARC record and evaluate the policy: `dig TXT _dmarc.example.com +short`, checking for `p=reject`, `p=quarantine`, or the weaker/absent `p=none`/no record.

Send a test email using a tool like swaks with a spoofed From address matching the target domain from an unauthorized mail server, and observe whether it is delivered to an inbox rather than rejected or spam-filtered.
Inspect the delivered message's Authentication-Results header to confirm SPF/DKIM/DMARC all show `fail` or `none` yet the message was still delivered to the inbox.
exploitationSteps: Craft a spoofed email using swaks specifying an arbitrary sender at the target domain and a convincing pretext (e.g. HR benefits update, invoice payment change).
Send the message through an attacker-controlled SMTP relay not authorized in the target's SPF record.
Confirm inbox delivery (not spam/junk) at a test recipient and capture the Authentication-Results header showing failed SPF/DKIM but delivery not blocked, as evidence for the report.

Report the specific missing or misconfigured control (absent SPF record, SPF present but not enforced via a strict DMARC policy, missing DKIM) since remediation is applied per-control and a partial configuration is a distinct, lower-severity finding than a complete absence.

examplePayloads.label: Checking SPF record
Checking DMARC policy
Sending a spoofed test email with swaks
examplePayloads.command: swaks --to test-recipient@example.com --from ceo@example.com --header 'Subject: Urgent Wire Transfer Approval' --body 'Please approve the attached invoice today.' --server <attacker-controlled-relay>

variants: Lookalike/homoglyph domain registration combined with a weak DMARC policy on the legitimate domain to increase phishing credibility.
DKIM key rotation gaps where an old, still-published selector uses a weak key length (512/768-bit RSA) that can feasibly be factored.
Subdomain spoofing where the DMARC policy on the root domain is strict but subdomains lack `sp=reject`, allowing spoofing of mail@sub.example.com.
mitigation: Publish an SPF record ending in a hard fail (`-all`) that accurately lists all authorized sending sources.
Enable DKIM signing on all outbound mail streams and publish corresponding public keys using at least 2048-bit RSA keys.
Publish a DMARC record with `p=reject` (or at minimum `p=quarantine` during rollout) and `rua`/`ruf` reporting addresses to monitor abuse, ensuring the subdomain policy (`sp=`) is equally strict.
Regularly review DMARC aggregate reports to detect unauthorized senders attempting to spoof the domain.

WEB-150.prerequisites: A web browser, the ability to control content on an outbound link's destination page (either as the target application under test linking out, or as an attacker-controlled page the target links to), and basic HTML/JavaScript knowledge.
WEB-150.whatItIs: When a page opens a link in a new tab without a specific protective setting, that newly opened page gets a live reference back to the original tab — and can secretly change what that original tab is showing, swapping it out for a convincing fake login page while the user's attention is on the new tab.
WEB-150.rootCause: Links that open in a new tab are missing a specific attribute that would prevent the new page from getting that reference back to the tab that opened it. Without it, any page opened this way can reach back and manipulate the original tab.
WEB-150.impact: Enables convincing credential-phishing attacks where a user who clicked a trusted link is unaware their original browser tab has been silently redirected to a fake login page, increasing the likelihood they will re-enter credentials believing they are still on the legitimate site.
stepsToIdentify: View the page source or use browser DevTools to locate anchor tags using `target="_blank"`, particularly those pointing to user-supplied URLs (profile links, comment links, referral links) or third-party domains.
Confirm the anchor tags lack both `rel="noopener"` and `rel="noreferrer"` attributes.
Open the link in a new tab and, from the destination page's console, execute `window.opener` to confirm a live reference to the originating tab is accessible.
From the destination page, attempt `window.opener.location = 'https://attacker-controlled-phishing-page.example'` and verify the original tab navigates away without any user interaction.
Check any user-generated content areas (forums, chat, markdown renderers) that auto-linkify URLs to confirm they also apply proper `rel` attributes on generated `<a>` tags.
exploitationSteps: Set up an attacker-controlled page that clones the target application's login page pixel-for-pixel.
Get the victim to click any outbound link on the target site that opens the attacker's page in a new tab (e.g. an ad, a partner link, or a link the attacker planted in user-generated content).
From the newly opened attacker tab, execute JavaScript to rewrite the original tab's `window.opener.location` to the cloned phishing page.
Wait for the victim to return to the original tab, now showing the phishing clone, and harvest submitted credentials.

examplePayloads.label: Vulnerable anchor tag missing rel attribute
Malicious destination page script rewriting the opener
Detecting opener access via browser console
examplePayloads.command: console.log(window.opener); // non-null indicates the vulnerability is exploitable

variants: Reverse tabnabbing via user-generated content where a forum post or chat message contains an outbound link that itself points to an attacker page performing the opener redirect.
Tabnabbing combined with a delayed redirect timer so the phishing swap happens only after the user has stopped watching the original tab, increasing believability.
mitigation: Add `rel="noopener noreferrer"` to every anchor tag using `target="_blank"`, especially those rendering user-supplied or third-party URLs.
Where a templating engine or CMS auto-generates external links, update the link-rendering component or auto-linkifier to always emit the `noopener` attribute by default.
Consider using `rel="noopener"` in combination with a Content-Security-Policy that restricts window navigation where feasible.
Educate content moderation/review processes to flag outbound links added via user-generated content that could be used for this technique.

WEB-151.prerequisites: Access to an active GraphQL endpoint and its schema (via introspection or documentation), a GraphQL client (Postman, Altair, or curl), and optionally a load-testing tool to measure server resource consumption.
WEB-151.whatItIs: GraphQL lets a client ask for deeply nested, related data — like a person's friends, and their friends' friends, and so on — in one request. Without a limit on how deep this can go, a single carefully crafted request can force the server to do an enormous, exponentially growing amount of work.
WEB-151.rootCause: The server runs any request that matches its schema, with no limit on how deep or complex a single query is allowed to be, and the code fetching related data doesn't limit or batch how many nested lookups a single request can trigger.
WEB-151.impact: A single malicious request can degrade or completely take down the GraphQL service and its backing database, resulting in denial of service for all legitimate users, and in resolver architectures without connection pooling limits, can exhaust database connections application-wide.
stepsToIdentify: Retrieve the GraphQL schema via introspection (or existing documentation) to identify object types with circular or self-referential relationships (e.g. user.friends[].friends[]).
Construct a moderately nested query (5-6 levels deep) reusing a self-referential relationship and measure response time and payload size compared to a shallow query.
Incrementally increase nesting depth and/or field count at each level, observing whether response time grows non-linearly (indicating exponential resolver fan-out).
Monitor server resource indicators (response latency, timeouts, 5xx errors) as depth increases to identify the point of degradation.
Check whether the server enforces any depth/complexity limit by sending an extremely deep query (15+ levels) and confirming whether it is rejected with a validation error or actually executed.
exploitationSteps: Build a query generator script that programmatically nests a chosen relational field N levels deep with aliases at each level to multiply the fan-out.
Submit the generated query as a single HTTP POST request to the GraphQL endpoint.
Measure the server's response time and, if authorized, monitor backend CPU/memory or database connection count during the request to quantify the amplification factor.
Optionally send multiple such requests concurrently to demonstrate full denial-of-service impact on a non-production/staging environment only.

examplePayloads.label: Self-referential nested query template (Python generator)
Manually crafted 6-level nested query
examplePayloads.command: {"query":"query{ user(id:1){ friends{ friends{ friends{ friends{ friends{ id name } } } } } } }"}

examplePayloads.label: Sending the deep query with curl

variants: Fragment-based amplification where reusable named fragments are nested inside each other, multiplying field resolution exponentially without an obviously deep textual query.
Alias-multiplication combined with nesting, where each nesting level also duplicates the same field dozens of times via aliases to multiply cost further.
Circular fragment spreads that some parsers fail to detect, causing infinite or near-infinite resolution loops.
mitigation: Implement a maximum query depth limit (e.g. reject queries nested beyond 6-8 levels) enforced during query validation before execution.
Adopt query cost/complexity analysis (e.g. graphql-cost-analysis, graphql-query-complexity) assigning weighted costs to fields and rejecting queries exceeding a total budget.
Implement per-field resolver-level batching (DataLoader pattern) to prevent N+1 amplification from turning into unbounded database load.
Disable introspection in production or restrict it to authenticated internal tooling to reduce schema reconnaissance that aids crafting amplification queries.

WEB-152.prerequisites: Access to a feature that transforms XML using an XSLT stylesheet where any part of the stylesheet or its input is influenced by user input (document generation, XML-to-HTML rendering, invoice/report generators), an intercepting proxy, and knowledge of XSLT 1.0/2.0 extension functions for the target processor (libxslt, Saxon, Xalan).
WEB-152.whatItIs: The app takes user input and mixes it into an XSLT stylesheet — a set of instructions for transforming XML data — which then gets processed by an XML engine. Because these stylesheets can include instructions to read files or make network requests, an attacker can inject their own instructions to read local files, reach internal systems, or in some cases run their own code.
WEB-152.rootCause: User input gets pasted directly into the stylesheet's text instead of being kept safely separate, and the XML engine processing it still has powerful features (like file access) turned on by default, with no restriction on what the stylesheet is allowed to do.
WEB-152.impact: Can result in arbitrary local file disclosure, server-side request forgery, and in processors supporting extensible scripting objects, full remote code execution on the server performing the transformation.
stepsToIdentify: Identify features that generate output from XML+XSLT (PDF/report generation, XML-to-HTML rendering endpoints, XML import/export with 'apply stylesheet' options).
Submit a benign XSLT fragment as input (e.g. via an uploaded XML/XSLT file or a parameter reflected into a stylesheet) to confirm it is parsed and executed rather than treated as inert text.
Attempt to inject a `document()` function call referencing a local file path (e.g. `document('/etc/passwd')`) and check whether its contents appear in the rendered output.
Attempt an out-of-band SSRF probe using `document('http://<attacker-listener>/xslt-test')` and monitor the listener for an inbound request confirming server-side execution.
If the processor is identified as Saxon or a .NET-based engine, test processor-specific scripting extensions (`<msxsl:script>` for .NET, Saxon extension elements) to assess code execution potential.
exploitationSteps: Craft a malicious XSLT stylesheet containing a `document()` call targeting a sensitive local file.
Submit the stylesheet through the vulnerable input point (file upload, template parameter, or direct XSLT injection point).
Retrieve the transformed output and extract the disclosed file contents as proof of local file read.
If a scripting extension is supported and enabled, craft a stylesheet embedding a script block that executes an OS command and confirm execution via an out-of-band callback or observable side effect.

examplePayloads.label: Local file disclosure via document()
SSRF probe via document() to attacker listener
.NET msxsl:script remote code execution primitive
examplePayloads.command: <xsl:stylesheet version="1.0" xmlns:xsl="http://www.w3.org/1999/XSL/Transform" xmlns:msxsl="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:xslt" xmlns:user="placeholder"><msxsl:script language="C#" implements-prefix="user">public string Exec(){ return System.Diagnostics.Process.Start("cmd","/c whoami").ToString(); }</msxsl:script></xsl:stylesheet>

variants: Saxon-specific extension function abuse (`saxon:system-property`, `saxon:evaluate`) for dynamic XPath evaluation leading to injection.
XSLT used within SAML/SSO metadata transformation pipelines rather than typical document generation, giving a stealthier attack surface.
Blind XSLT injection where output is not directly reflected but time-based or OOB `document()` calls confirm the vulnerability.
mitigation: Never allow user-controlled input to be inserted directly into XSLT stylesheet source; treat any user-supplied XSLT/XML as data, not executable transformation logic.
Disable or sandbox extension functions and the `document()` function in the XSLT processor configuration where user influence over stylesheets cannot be fully eliminated.
Run XSLT transformation in a restricted, network-isolated execution context with no filesystem access to sensitive paths.
Keep the XSLT processing library patched and prefer processors/configurations with secure-by-default extension handling.

WEB-153.prerequisites: Ability to upload or host user-controlled content on the target's domain (avatar/attachment upload, static asset hosting), an intercepting proxy to inspect response headers, and a web browser for practical exploitation confirmation.
WEB-153.whatItIs: When the app serves an uploaded file without properly declaring what type of file it actually is, browsers sometimes try to guess the type themselves by peeking at its content. An attacker can craft a file that looks like an innocent image but is secretly also valid HTML/JavaScript, and get the browser to run it as a webpage instead of displaying it as a picture.
WEB-153.rootCause: The app doesn't set a strict, correct type label on uploaded files, and it's also missing a specific header that would tell the browser 'don't try to guess the type yourself — trust the label I gave you.' Without that, browsers fall back to guessing based on content, which is exactly what a cleverly disguised file exploits.
WEB-153.impact: Enables stored cross-site scripting by uploading a file that appears benign (e.g. named `image.jpg`) but contains embedded HTML/JavaScript, which the victim's browser executes in the origin's security context when directly navigated to, leading to session theft or account compromise.
stepsToIdentify: Identify file upload or asset-serving endpoints (avatars, attachments, exported reports) and check the `Content-Type` and presence/absence of `X-Content-Type-Options` in the response headers when retrieving an uploaded file.
Upload a polyglot file (valid image header followed by embedded HTML/script content) with an image extension and content-type.
Request the uploaded file directly in a browser tab (not via an `` tag) and observe whether the browser renders it as HTML rather than displaying/downloading it as an image.
If rendered as HTML, confirm embedded script execution by including a benign JavaScript payload that triggers an observable action (e.g. alert or a callback to a listener).
Repeat testing across other user-content endpoints that lack explicit Content-Type enforcement, such as CSV/PDF/report downloads.
exploitationSteps: Craft a GIF/JPEG polyglot file: valid magic bytes for the image format followed by an HTML payload containing a script tag.
Upload the polyglot through the vulnerable file upload feature, ensuring it is stored and served from the target's own origin.
Send the direct URL to the uploaded file to a victim, or embed it as a clickable link, so the browser navigates to and sniffs the content.
Confirm script execution in the victim's session context (e.g. exfiltrate cookies to an attacker-controlled listener) to demonstrate stored XSS impact.

examplePayloads.label: GIF/HTML polyglot payload structure
Checking for missing nosniff header
Uploading a polyglot with curl

variants: SVG upload abuse where SVG files (correctly typed as image/svg+xml) directly embed `<script>` tags, executing without any sniffing needed if served without a strict CSP.
PDF/HTML polyglots where a file valid as both PDF and HTML executes script content when directly opened in-browser rather than downloaded.
Content-Disposition misconfiguration where files that should force a download (`attachment`) are instead served `inline`, increasing the chance of browser rendering.
mitigation: Send `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` on all responses, especially those serving user-uploaded content.
Serve user-uploaded files from a separate, cookie-less domain (a sandboxed content domain) so any script execution cannot access the main application's session.

Force `Content-Disposition: attachment` for file types not intended to be rendered inline, and validate/normalize the Content-Type based on server-side file inspection rather than trusting the client-supplied value.
Strip active content (scripts, embedded objects) from uploaded SVGs and similarly renderable formats before storage.

WEB-154.prerequisites: An intercepting proxy (Burp Suite), access to the form protected by CAPTCHA (login, registration, comment submission), and optionally a scriptable HTTP client to test workflow-level bypasses.
WEB-154.whatItIs: The 'prove you're not a robot' check meant to stop automated abuse can be bypassed entirely — maybe it's only checked in the browser's own JavaScript instead of on the server, maybe the same solved answer can be reused over and over, or maybe the protected action can be triggered directly, skipping the form that shows the check in the first place.
WEB-154.rootCause: The actual verification of whether the check was solved correctly isn't happening on the server — either it's trusted from the client, the same answer never gets invalidated after use, or there's no server-side check confirming a real answer was submitted at all before the protected action runs.
WEB-154.impact: Defeats the anti-automation control entirely, enabling large-scale automated account creation, credential stuffing, comment spam, or brute-force attacks against the very endpoints the CAPTCHA was meant to protect.
stepsToIdentify: Submit the protected form once normally, solving the CAPTCHA, and capture the full request in an intercepting proxy.
Replay the exact same captured request (including the same CAPTCHA response token) multiple times and observe whether the server accepts it repeatedly instead of rejecting reused tokens.
Remove or blank the CAPTCHA response parameter entirely and resubmit, checking whether the server-side logic fails open (accepts the request) rather than rejecting it.

Inspect client-side JavaScript to determine whether CAPTCHA validation occurs purely in the browser before allowing form submission, with no corresponding server-side verification call to the CAPTCHA provider.
Check for an alternate, undocumented, or legacy endpoint performing the same action (e.g. a mobile API endpoint) that does not enforce the CAPTCHA at all.
exploitationSteps: Automate the discovered bypass (token replay, omitted parameter, or unprotected alternate endpoint) using a scripted HTTP client.
Run the automated script against the target action (e.g. account registration or login) at high volume in an authorized test window.
Demonstrate successful completion of hundreds of automated submissions without solving a fresh CAPTCHA per attempt, confirming the control provides no real protection.

Report the specific bypass technique confirmed and recommend server-side, per-session challenge validation (rejecting any submission whose CAPTCHA token was already consumed or was never issued) as the concrete fix.

examplePayloads.label: Replaying a captured, previously-solved CAPTCHA token
Submitting with the CAPTCHA parameter entirely omitted
Automated loop testing token reuse across many accounts
examplePayloads.command: for i in $(seq 1 20); do curl -s -X POST https://example.com/register -d "email=test$i@example.com&password=Test123!&g-recaptcha-response=<reused-token>"; done

variants: Audio CAPTCHA fallback with weaker entropy than the visual challenge, enabling automated speech-to-text solving.
CAPTCHA verification response leaking whether the answer was correct via a distinguishable client-visible signal before the actual form submission, allowing offline brute-forcing of the challenge.
Third-party CAPTCHA solving services successfully bypassing weak-difficulty challenges at scale, indicating insufficient challenge strength even when server-side verification exists.
mitigation: Always verify the CAPTCHA response server-side via the provider's verification API (e.g. Google reCAPTCHA siteverify) before processing the protected action, never trusting client-side validation alone.
Ensure each CAPTCHA solution token is single-use and bound to the specific session/request, rejecting any replay attempts.
Apply the CAPTCHA (or equivalent server-side rate limiting) consistently across every code path and endpoint that performs the protected action, including mobile/API variants.
Combine CAPTCHA with server-side rate limiting and anomaly detection so it is a defense-in-depth layer rather than the sole automation control.

WEB-155.prerequisites: Any endpoint that parses user-supplied XML (SOAP APIs, file uploads accepting XML/DOCX/XLSX/SVG, XML-RPC), an intercepting proxy, and awareness of the target's XML parser to gauge default entity-expansion protections.
WEB-155.whatItIs: A tiny, few-kilobyte XML file defines a handful of nested shortcuts, where each one expands into multiple copies of the previous one — so a small file balloons into gigabytes of data the instant the server tries to read it, exhausting its memory.
WEB-155.rootCause: The XML parser processing this file has no limit on how many times these internal shortcuts are allowed to expand, or how large the final expanded result can get — so a tiny, deliberately crafted file can consume an enormous, disproportionate amount of memory before anything catches it.
WEB-155.impact: A single small request (often under 1KB) can exhaust available memory and CPU on the parsing server, causing a denial of service affecting all users of the application or shared infrastructure.
stepsToIdentify: Identify all endpoints accepting raw XML or XML-based file formats (SOAP, XML-RPC, SVG upload, Office Open XML documents which are zipped XML internally).

Prepare a small-scale, bounded 'billion laughs' style payload (e.g. only 3-4 levels of nesting with modest multiplication) to safely gauge parser behavior without risking a full denial of service on shared infrastructure.
Submit the bounded payload and monitor response time and any error indicating parser-imposed entity expansion limits (e.g. 'entity expansion limit exceeded').

If the bounded payload is processed without any limit being enforced, escalate cautiously and only in a pre-approved, isolated test environment to confirm actual resource exhaustion, coordinating with the client to avoid production impact.
Document parser identification (e.g. via error messages or response fingerprinting) to correlate with known default protections (e.g. libxml2's default `--noent` limits vs. explicit opt-outs).
exploitationSteps: Construct an XML document with a chain of internal entities where each entity references the previous one multiple times (classic Billion Laughs structure).
Submit the crafted document to the identified XML-consuming endpoint in an authorized, non-production environment.
Monitor server-side memory/CPU utilization (with client authorization and monitoring in place) to document the resource exhaustion impact and recovery time.

Report the specific payload structure and resource-exhaustion profile observed, and recommend the XML parser be configured with strict entity-expansion limits and DTD processing disabled by default, rather than relying on runtime resource monitoring alone.

examplePayloads.label: Classic Billion Laughs entity expansion structure
examplePayloads.command:
<?xml version="1.0"?>
<!DOCTYPE lolz [
 <!ENTITY lol "lol">
 <!ENTITY lol2 "&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;">
 <!ENTITY lol3 "&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;">
 <!ENTITY lol4 "&lol3;&lol3;&lol3;&lol3;&lol3;&lol3;&lol3;&lol3;&lol3;&lol3;">
]>
<lolz>&lol4;</lolz>

examplePayloads.label: Submitting the bounded test payload with curl

variants: Quadratic blowup variant using a single large entity referenced many times without deep nesting, evading naive depth-based defenses.
Zip-bomb-in-XML variant via Office Open XML (docx/xlsx) uploads, where the zip container itself as well as internal XML entities can both be weaponized.
External DTD-based expansion pulling a remote, attacker-hosted DTD that defines the expansion bomb, moving the malicious definition off the wire payload itself.
mitigation: Disable DTD processing and external entity resolution entirely in the XML parser configuration wherever DTDs are not a legitimate business requirement.

Configure the XML parser with explicit limits on entity expansion depth, total entity count, and maximum expanded document size (e.g. libxml2's `XML_PARSE_NOENT` disabled, entity expansion limits in Xerces/Saxon).
Enforce a strict maximum input size for any endpoint accepting XML before parsing begins.
Run XML parsing in a resource-constrained, isolated worker process/container with strict memory and CPU limits so a parsing bomb cannot impact the main application.
